istanbul-coffeehouses-open-1554.summary: Ottoman historian İbrahim Peçevi, writing in the 1640s, records that in 962 AH (1554 to 1555) Hakam from Aleppo and Şems from Damascus each opened a kahvehane in Tahtakale, Istanbul's market quarter by the Golden Horn. Patrons sat on divans, drank coffee, played chess and backgammon, read poetry and talked politics, and Peçevi notes dismissed officials and judges among them. Coffee had reached Cairo's al-Azhar quarter about 1510 and Mecca's jurists tried to ban it in 1511. Within a generation Istanbul held hundreds of coffeehouses, giving men a gathering place outside mosque, home and tavern; preachers and sultans repeatedly tried to close them. Ralph Hattox's 1985 study traces this chain from Yemeni Sufi lodges to an urban trade in cups and conversation that reached Venice and London a century later.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses: The Origins of a Social Beverage in the Medieval Near East (University of Washington Press, 1985), chs. 5-6
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Peçevi's account of two Syrians opening coffeehouses in Istanbul in 962 AH; social life of coffeehouses; Meccan ban of 1511.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses, full text (Internet Archive)
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Translated passage from Peçevi on Hakam and Shams in Tahtakale, 962 AH, chess, backgammon, poetry and dismissed officials among patrons.

sources.author: Grehan, James
sources.confirms: Coffeehouses as centres of Ottoman urban sociability from the mid-sixteenth century and repeated attempts at closure.

picture.credit: Unknown Ottoman miniaturist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

patio-process-1554.summary: In 1554 Bartolomé de Medina used mercury to pull silver from poor ore, and Mexico's mines paid. By the 1550s New Spain's richest silver ores were running out, and smelting lower grades cost too much. Bartolomé de Medina, a Seville merchant, learned from an unknown German called Maestro Lorenzo that silver could be drawn from crushed ore with mercury and salt brine. In Pachuca in 1554 he built a model refinery and is credited with adding magistral, an impure copper sulfate, to speed its reaction. Amalgamation made remote Potosí viable; Spanish America produced three fifths of world silver before 1900.

sources.title: Patio process - Wikipedia
Probert, Alan, 'Bartolome de Medina: The Patio Process and the Sixteenth Century Silver Crisis', in Mines of Silver and Gold in the Americas (Routledge, 1997), pp. 96-130
sources.author: Probert, Alan
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'patio process'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the process broadly to the 16th century through the early 20th century; it gives no specific year. It does not confirm that Medina introduced it in 1554.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pachuca'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives no specific year; it says the patio process was perfected in Pachuca in the 16th century. It supports the broad claim that Bartolomé de Medina perfected the process in Pachuca, but does not confirm 1554.

patio-process-1554.detail: Crushed ore was heaped with salt, water, magistral and mercury. Labourers or mules trod it in a shallow walled patio for six to eight weeks; it was then washed, and heated to drive off mercury.

agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.summary: In 1556 Agricola's De re metallica put the mining trade's guarded know-how in 292 woodcuts. It stayed the standard text for nearly 200 years. Georg Bauer, a physician who Latinised his name to Georgius Agricola, spent nine years in the Bohemian mining town of Joachimsthal and then lived in Chemnitz in Saxony's Ore Mountains, watching how metals were found, mined, refined and smelted. His De re metallica, in twelve Latin books, appeared in Basel in 1556, a year after his death. Latin let educated Europeans read it, and its detailed machinery made it a working reference for more than a century.

sources.title: De re metallica
Agricola, Georgius, De re metallica, trans. H. C. and L. H. Hoover (London: Mining Magazine, 1912), from the first Latin edition of 1556
sources.author: Agricola, Georgius; Hoover, Herbert Clark; Hoover, Lou Henry
sources.confirms: Catalogue states the translation is from the first Latin edition of 1556.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'De re metallica'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1556 and says the work was published posthumously. It confirms that De re metallica was a major mining and metallurgy text, described in cited coverage as the leading textbook for nearly two centuries; it does not confirm 292 woodcuts.

agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.verification_note: Published posthumously (Agricola died 1555). Title implies he published it.
agricola-de-re-metallica-1556.detail: Publication was delayed while its 292 woodcuts were cut from drawings by Blasius Weffring. Herbert and Lou Henry Hoover published its first English translation in 1912.

picture.alt: Woodcut from De re metallica, Basel 1556, page 131, showing a machine for drawing water out of a mine.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

cassava-africa-portuguese-1558.summary: Portuguese ships carry Brazilian cassava cuttings to Africa's Atlantic coast in the 16th century; FAO dates cassava's first African record to 1558. Dutch trader Samuel Brun saw it at Loango in 1611, and travelers found it a staple around Malebo Pool by 1698. Cassava tolerates poor soil and drought, stores in the ground for up to two years and resists locusts, so African farmers adopted it as famine reserve and then as staple, developing soaking and fermenting to remove cyanide. Jan Vansina showed in 1997 that adoption in Kongo, Angola and Loango took generations and varied by place. Nigeria now leads world output.

sources.title: Vansina, J., 'Histoire du manioc en Afrique Centrale avant 1850', Paideuma 43 (1997), 255-279
sources.author: Vansina, Jan
sources.confirms: Traces cassava's history in Kongo, Angola and Loango before 1850 and shows adoption as staple took variable time by locality.
sources.qualifies: Argues the supposed rapid cassava agricultural revolution in central Africa is far from proven.

sources.title: Guira, F. et al., 'Origins, production, and utilization of cassava in Burkina Faso', Food Science and Nutrition 5 (2016), 415-423
sources.author: Guira, Flibert; Some, Koussao; Kabore, Donatien; Sawadogo-Lingani, Hagretou; Traore, Yves; Savadogo, Aly
sources.confirms: States cassava was introduced into Africa from America by the Portuguese in 1558, citing Jones (1959) and Lebot (2003).

sources.title: FAO, 'Roots, tubers, plantains and bananas in human nutrition', ch. 1 (cassava in Congo basin 1558)
sources.author: FAO
sources.confirms: Gives Portuguese introduction into Congo basin as early as 1558.

sources.title: Carter, S. E. et al., 'Introduction and diffusion of cassava in Africa', IITA Research Guide
sources.author: Carter, Simon E.; Fresco, Louise O.; Jones, Peter G.; Fairbairn, J. N.
sources.confirms: Documents Brun's 1611 observation at Loango and cassava as staple around Malebo Pool by 1698.

cassava-africa-portuguese-1558.detail: Cassava also entered east Africa via Portuguese Mozambique and Indian Ocean trade in the 18th century. Its labour demands fell mostly on women, who processed roots into gari, fufu and chikwangue. Dependence brought risks: konzo paralysis from poorly processed bitter varieties, and mosaic virus epidemics in the 20th century that IITA breeding later addressed. Vansina argues claims of a cassava-driven transformation of central African farming are unproven.

picture.credit: Lebu Ayiga, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

index-librorum-prohibitorum-1559.summary: In 1559 Rome published a list of books Catholics could not print or read, censorship that lasted until 1966. Index Librorum Prohibitorum was the Church's changing list of books judged heretical or immoral; Catholic states could enforce it by law. A first Roman Index printed in 1557 under Pope Paul IV was withdrawn for unclear reasons. In 1559 his new Index appeared, banning every work of some 550 authors as well as individual titles, on a principle that an author's religious convictions contaminated all his writing. Even Catholic scholars found it too severe, and in 1564 the Council of Trent's Tridentine Index replaced it.

Barbierato, Federico, 'Index of Prohibited Books', in Encyclopedia of Renaissance Philosophy (Springer, 2022), pp. 1670-1676
sources.author: Barbierato, Federico
sources.confirms: Abstract: 'the first official Roman Index dates to 1559'; indices in force 1559 to 1966.
sources.qualifies: Legal force was 'in substance almost limited to the Italian territory'; France never received it, Spain and Portugal kept their own lists.

sources.title: Grendler, Paul F., 'Printing and censorship', in The Cambridge History of Renaissance Philosophy (Cambridge, 1988), pp. 25-54

index-librorum-prohibitorum-1559.detail: Later lists named Copernicus, Galileo, Descartes, Kant and many others.

huancavelica-mercury-mine-1563.summary: In 1563 and 1564 Amador de Cabrera registered cinnabar outcrops at Huancavelica, in Peru's central highlands, after an Andean worker named Ñahuincopa showed him its cinnabar. Within a decade, under Viceroy Toledo, Crown-controlled mines there supplied quicksilver to Potosí's refineries, where mercury amalgamation replaced smelting of low-grade ores from 1572. Indigenous mitayos drafted from surrounding provinces dug ore underground and roasted it in furnaces, inhaling mercury vapour; Kendall Brown's study documents tremors, tooth loss and early death that made Huancavelica notorious as 'mina de la muerte'. Output averaged several thousand quintals a year, and Huancavelica and Potosí together anchored Spain's American silver economy for two centuries.

sources.title: Brown, Kendall W., 'Workers' Health and Colonial Mercury Mining at Huancavelica, Peru', The Americas 57 (2001)
sources.author: Brown, Kendall W.
sources.confirms: Discovery in 1563 to 1564, mita labour, mercury poisoning symptoms and the mine's role in Andean silver refining.

sources.title: Robins, Nicholas A., Mercury, Mining, and Empire: The Human and Ecological Cost of Colonial Silver Mining in the Andes (Indiana University Press, 2011), ch. 2-3
sources.author: Robins, Nicholas A.
sources.confirms: Estimates of mercury emissions and health effects at Huancavelica and Potosí.

sources.title: Brown, Kendall, 'Mercury and Silver Mining in the Colonial Atlantic', Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History (Oxford University Press, 2017)
sources.author: Brown, Kendall
sources.confirms: Overview of mercury supply from Huancavelica, Almadén and Idrija to American refineries.

huancavelica-mercury-mine-1563.detail: Mercury was shipped by llama train to coastal ports, by sea to Arica and overland to Potosí, roughly 1,500 kilometres. Nicholas Robins estimates that Huancavelica released about 17,000 tonnes of mercury vapour into air and soil between 1564 and 1810, with Potosí's refineries adding far more. A 1786 gallery collapse cut production; Spain later imported Almadén and Idrija mercury to make up shortfalls.

picture.credit: LITOUS, via Wikimedia Commons

kirkcesme-water-supply-istanbul-1563.summary: Sultan Süleyman orders chief architect Sinan in 1554 to end Istanbul's water shortage. Sinan surveys streams in Belgrad Forest north of the city, gathers two branches of springs in covered masonry galleries and joins them at a deep collecting pool south of Kemerburgaz. A single gravity line then crosses valleys on aqueducts, among them Mağlova, 36 metres high and about 250 metres long with two tiers of arches, and Uzunkemer, before reaching distribution chambers at Eğrikapı and fountains across the walled city. Floods on 20 September 1563 wrecked Mağlova and damaged others; Sinan rebuilt them and water flowed again in 1564. A survey in 1568 counted 94 public fountains, 19 wells, 15 troughs, 13 baths and seven palaces served, and later dams raised supply to around 17,500 cubic metres a day. Parts remain in use.

sources.title: Uyumaz, A. and Dabanlı, İ., 'Architect Sinan's Kırkçeşme water supply system outside the city of Istanbul and city network', Water Supply 13 (2013), 626-637
sources.author: Uyumaz, Ali; Dabanlı, İsmail
sources.venue: Water Science and Technology: Water Supply
sources.confirms: Two branches fed from Kağıthane tributaries, collection at Başhavuz south of Kemerburgaz, crossing over Mağlova aqueduct, opening 1564, dams added 1620 to 1818.

sources.title: Kurt, B., 'The Ottoman State Between Urban Space and Environment: Preserving the Drinking Water of Istanbul', Belleten 85 (2021), 933-966
sources.author: Kurt, Burcu
sources.confirms: Süleyman ordered water from Belgrad Forest canals to new fountains; Kırkçeşme facilities built in response.

sources.title: Museum With No Frontiers, 'Kırkçeşme water-supply system', Discover Islamic Art
sources.author: Museum With No Frontiers
sources.confirms: Ordered 1554, completed 1563, flood damage rebuilt 1564; galleries about 55 km, 33 aqueducts, over 300 fountains at first.

manila-galleon-trade-1565.summary: In 1565 Spain found a way back across the Pacific, and galleons traded silver for silk. Augustinian friar Andrés de Urdaneta, and separately Alonso de Arellano, found this return route, the tornaviaje, by riding the Kuroshio Current north past Japan and then east. Spanish ships had crossed from Mexico to Asia for decades without finding a return; in 1552 Francis Xavier had asked that no more fleets try. From then until 1815 galleons made one or two round trips a year, carrying Chinese silk, porcelain and other Asian goods west to America and returning with New World silver for trade with China.

sources.title: Manila galleon - Wikipedia
Flynn, Dennis O.; Giraldez, Arturo, 'Silk for Silver: Manila-Macao Trade in the 17th Century', Philippine Studies 44.1 (1996)
sources.author: Flynn, Dennis O.; Giraldez, Arturo
sources.confirms: Landing page shows bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline, 'The Manila Galleon Trade (1565-1815)'
sources.author: Metropolitan Museum of Art
sources.confirms: The title gives 1565-1815; the page does not give a separate date for the route’s discovery. it confirms trade between China and Mexico involving Asian goods and New World silver.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Manila galleon'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1565-1815. The page says galleons made annual round trips between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese silk and other goods west and Mexican silver back.

manila-galleon-trade-1565.detail: Galleons were mostly built at Cavite in Manila Bay, left Manila about July and took at least four months to reach Acapulco. Mexico's war of independence ended this route.

chinese-variolation-1567.summary: By the 1500s Chinese doctors gave children a mild case of smallpox to protect them: vaccination's root. Variolation deliberately infected a person with smallpox matter in hope of a mild case that would protect for life. About 1 to 2 percent of those variolated died, against about 30 percent of those who caught smallpox naturally. China's oldest documented practice dates to the 16th century, and sinologist Joseph Needham places its first use between 1567 and 1572. Practitioners chose donors with mild cases, dried their scabs for some time since fresh ones risked full infection, ground them to powder and blew it through a pipe into one nostril. Reports reached London's Royal Society in 1700.

sources.title: Variolation - Wikipedia
Boylston, Arthur, 'The origins of inoculation', Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 105.7 (2012), pp. 309-313
sources.author: Boylston, Arthur
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
sources.confirms: Full text: inoculation first practised in China between 1567 and 1572 by nasal insufflation; earliest written discussion in a 1549 book.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'variolation'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives the date as the 16th century; it does not give 1567 or a more precise date. broadly: it says 16th-century Chinese accounts describe nasal insufflation using powdered dried smallpox scabs blown through a pipe.

chinese-variolation-1567.detail: Three or four scabs were ground, sometimes with one grain of musk. Wan Quan and others recorded such methods, and the Kangxi Emperor later inoculated his children and troops.

potato-canary-islands-europe-1567.summary: On 28 November 1567 notary Lorenzo Palenzuela in Gran Canaria records three medium barrels of potatoes, oranges and green lemons shipped to Antwerp, the earliest known written record of potatoes in Europe. A second notary record of 24 April 1574 notes potatoes sent from Tenerife to Rouen, and Seville's Hospital de la Sangre bought potatoes on 27 December 1573, its first mention on mainland Europe. Tubers must have been planted in the Canaries by about 1562 to yield an export crop. A 2007 DNA study of Canary landraces finds both Andean and Chilean types, pointing to multiple introductions. Potatoes later fed Europe's population growth and, through blight in 1845, its worst 19th-century famine.

sources.title: Rios, D., Ghislain, M., Rodriguez, F. and Spooner, D. M., 'What Is the Origin of the European Potato? Evidence from Canary Island Landraces', Crop Science 47 (2007), 1271-1280
sources.author: Rios, Domingo; Ghislain, Marc; Rodriguez, Flor; Spooner, David M.
sources.confirms: States the potato was first recorded in Europe in the Canary Islands in 1567 and quotes the 1567 Palenzuela and 1574 Tenerife notarial records; DNA shows Andean and Chilean types among Canary landraces.
sources.qualifies: Argues the early European potato was selected from Chilean rather than only Andean introductions.

sources.title: Rios, D., Devaux, A. and Ruiz de Galarreta, J. I., 'Ancient Potato Varieties of the Canary Islands: Their History, Diversity and Origin of the Potato in Europe', Potato Research 67 (2024), 963-994
sources.author: Rios, Domingo; Devaux, Andre; Ruiz de Galarreta, Jose Ignacio
sources.confirms: Reviews the 1567 and 1574 shipping records, the 1573 Seville hospital purchase and the estimate of planting by about 1562.

sources.title: Hawkes, J. G. and Francisco-Ortega, J., 'The early history of the potato in Europe', Euphytica 70 (1993), 1-7
sources.author: Hawkes, J. G.; Francisco-Ortega, J.
sources.confirms: Argues potatoes were cultivated in the Canaries by about 1562 and documents the 1567 and 1574 shipments.

potato-canary-islands-europe-1567.detail: The Canaries sat outside Seville's monopoly on American trade, so they became a hub for plants moving between continents. Ancient Canary landraces still grown on Tenerife carry Andean genetics; Domingo Rios's group argues early European potatoes were selected from Chilean introductions long before the 1840s. Potatoes remained a garden curiosity in much of Europe until Prussia and France promoted them in the 18th century.

picture.alt: Papas antiguas, old potato landraces of Canary Islands
picture.credit: Koppchen, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

florentine-codex-1569.summary: By 1569 Nahua scholars with Sahagún had recorded Aztec life in 2,400 pages, in their own words. This Franciscan friar spent from 1545 until his death in 1590 compiling La Historia General de las Cosas de Nueva España. It was meant to help missionaries and to record a vanishing heritage. He worked with Nahua elders and with former students of his Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, crediting them by name, gathering testimony through questionnaires and writing in Nahuatl with Spanish alongside. Its Nahuatl text, completed in 1569 in a manuscript that does not survive, ran to 2,500 pages in twelve books with more than 2,000 illustrations by native artists.

sources.title: Florentine Codex - Wikipedia
Sahagun, Bernardino de, Historia general de las cosas de Nueva Espana (Florentine Codex, 1575-77), Library of Congress / World Digital Library
sources.author: Sahagun, Bernardino de
sources.confirms: The page says the complete copy was prepared in 1575-77; it gives 1577 as the publication year.

sources.title: Terraciano, Kevin, 'Three Texts in One: Book XII of the Florentine Codex', Ethnohistory 57 (2010), 51-72
sources.author: Terraciano, Kevin
sources.confirms: The Florentine Codex is a sixteenth-century manuscript of twelve books on Nahua culture in parallel Nahuatl and Castilian columns with many illustrations by Nahua artists.

florentine-codex-1569.verification_note: Terraciano (Ethnohistory 2010) describes twelve books in parallel Nahuatl and Castilian columns with Nahua illustrations; Library of Congress dates the surviving codex to 1575 to 1577, while 1569 marks Sahagún's completed Nahuatl text, whose manuscript is lost.
florentine-codex-1569.detail: Its books cover gods, society and natural history, and Book 12 tells the conquest as seen from Tenochtitlan. Its best manuscript, in Florence's Laurentian Library and made in 1575 to 1577, gives it its name.

picture.alt: Opening page of Book XI, on earthly matters and natural history, in Sahagún's Florentine Codex, completed about 1577, from Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana via World Digital Library.
picture.credit: Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua scribes, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, public domain, via Library of Congress World Digital Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

mercator-projection-1569.summary: In 1569 Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator published a world map, 202 by 124 cm in eighteen sheets, on which a straight line is a fixed compass course; it is still in use. Sailors follow rhumb lines, paths of constant bearing, which Portuguese cosmographer Pedro Nunes had analysed in 1537. Mercator titled his map a new description of Earth corrected for navigators' use. By spacing parallels ever wider toward both poles, it draws every rhumb line straight, so courses can be laid with a ruler. Its price is area: lands far from the equator swell, until Greenland looks as large as Africa, which is 14 times bigger.

sources.title: Mercator projection - Wikipedia
Monmonier, Mark, Rhumb Lines and Map Wars: A Social History of the Mercator Projection (Chicago, 2004)
sources.author: Monmonier, Mark
sources.confirms: Book page: Mercator's 1569 world map introduced the projection with straight rhumb lines.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mercator projection'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1569. The page says any straight line on a Mercator map is a line of constant true bearing, useful for plotting a straight-line course.

mercator-projection-1569.detail: Edward Wright published accurate construction tables in 1599. Mercator's projection became standard for navigation in the 18th century and returned in Web Mercator maps.

picture.alt: Composite of all sheets of Gerardus Mercator's 1569 world map Nova et aucta orbis terrae descriptio, from Basel copy.
picture.credit: Gerardus Mercator, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.summary: Between 1572 and 1575 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo reorganised silver production at Potosí, in present Bolivia. He imposed a rotating labour draft, la mita, which obliged sixteen highland provinces to send about 13,500 men each year to mines and refineries, and he financed a chain of about 20 reservoirs in Kari Kari hills above town whose water drove more than a hundred ingenios, stamp mills that crushed ore for mercury amalgamation. Indigenous guayra wind furnaces, which had smelted rich ores since 1545, gave way to this water-powered industrial complex. Output climbed to over 200 tonnes of silver a year around 1592, flowing to Seville and, through Manila, to China.

sources.title: Bakewell, Peter, Miners of the Red Mountain: Indian Labor in Potosí, 1545-1650 (University of New Mexico Press, 1984), ch. 2-3
sources.author: Bakewell, Peter
sources.confirms: Toledo's mita quotas, reservoirs and ingenios, and the shift from guayra smelting to amalgamation.

sources.title: Saignes, Thierry, 'The Miners in Colonial Potosí' (review of Bakewell and Cole), Bulletin of Latin American Research 6 (1987)
sources.author: Saignes, Thierry
sources.confirms: Scholarly assessment of mita size and operation as reconstructed by Bakewell and Cole.

sources.title: Cook, Noble David, review of Bakewell, Silver and Entrepreneurship in Seventeenth-Century Potosí, Technology and Culture 32 (1991)
sources.author: Cook, Noble David
sources.confirms: Mill ownership and refining technology at seventeenth-century Potosí.

potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.verification_note: Mita quota figures range from about 13,000 to 14,000 men per year across sources; reservoir counts range from 18 to 32 depending on period. Toledo's ordinances date from 1572 to 1575, so 1573 is a mid-point of the reorganisation.
potosi-mita-ingenios-1573.detail: Peter Bakewell's Miners of the Red Mountain reconstructs labour arrangements and this shift from Indigenous smelting to amalgamation; Jeffrey Cole traces mita operations to 1700. A reservoir dam failure in 1626 destroyed many mills and killed hundreds. Mitayos walked up to two months from Cusco's hinterland with families and llamas; many stayed as paid mingas. Potosí's population reached about 160,000 around 1610.

picture.alt: Drawing of Cerro Rico above Potosí from Diego de Ocaña's account of about 1600, showing mine workings on the hill
picture.credit: José Fuertes, via Wikimedia Commons

li-shizhen-bencao-gangmu-1578.summary: In 1578 Li Shizhen finished a catalogue of every drug in Chinese medicine, 1,892 entries doctors still consult. The Ming physician's Bencao gangmu, Compendium of Materia Medica, took more than three decades of work. It lists every drug then known to Chinese medicine: 1,892 entries of plants, animals and minerals, 374 added by Li, with 11,096 prescriptions and 1,160 drawings across 53 volumes, each entry giving names, appearance, nature, uses and side effects. Ming emperors ignored it, and it was printed only in 1596 in Nanjing, three years after his death. It carries errors too, such as holding mercury non-toxic.

sources.title: Bencao Gangmu - Wikipedia
Tsai et al., 'Bencao Gangmu and the foundations of Chinese pharmacology', Frontiers in Pharmacology 17 (2026)
sources.author: Tsai et al.
sources.confirms: Full text: Li Shizhen completed the Bencao gangmu in 1578; first printed 1596.

sources.title: Metailie, Georges, 'Des mots et des plantes dans le Bencao gangmu de Li Shizhen', Extreme-Orient Extreme-Occident 10 (1988), pp. 27-43
sources.author: Metailie, Georges
sources.confirms: Full text on Persee discusses the work's nomenclature; gives no completion date.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bencao gangmu'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1578. It says the Bencao gangmu was completed in 1578 and described 1,892 drugs, but does not call it a first draft or say it listed every drug then known.

li-shizhen-bencao-gangmu-1578.detail: Entries are arranged in 16 divisions and 60 orders. Li drew on literary and historical texts as well as earlier herbals, and editions followed in 1603, 1606 and 1640.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

tamil-type-quilon-1578.summary: On 20 October 1578 a Jesuit press at Quilon (Kollam), Kerala, printed Thambiran Vanakkam, a sixteen page Tamil translation of a Portuguese catechism, using metal type cut for Tamil script. Henrique Henriques prepared text and Joao Gonsalves, a Spanish lay brother and former blacksmith, with Tamil assistants, cut and cast fifty or so sorts with ligatures for vowel signs. This was first book printed in an Indian script with movable type. A Goa printing of 1577 preceded it but no copy survives; one Quilon copy is held at Harvard. Printing in Tamil continued at Cochin and Punnaikayal with grammars and a dictionary, two centuries before Bengali type.

constantinople-observatory-destroyed-158.summary: In 1580 the sultan razed Istanbul's new observatory, and Ottoman astronomy lost its tools. Chief astronomer Taqi ad-Din had asked Murad III to fund an observatory to rival Ulugh Beg's at Samarkand. Built by 1577 on a hill above Constantinople's European quarter, almost as Tycho Brahe's Uraniborg opened, it housed instruments Taqi ad-Din made, including his giant armillary sphere and his mechanical clock for timing planets, with its aim of replacing outdated astronomical tables. Within months a great comet appeared; pressed for his forecast, Taqi ad-Din called it a sign of well-being and of conquest in Persia, and plague followed. It was razed in 1580.

sources.author: Sen, A. Tunc

constantinople-observatory-destroyed-158.detail: Its two buildings held library and staff in one and instruments in the other. Its work left his zij, or table set, more accurate than Tycho's or Copernicus's.

akbar-arsenal-gun-machines-1582.summary: Abu'l Fazl's Ain-i Akbari records two devices in Akbar's imperial arsenal around 1582: a geared wheel turned by one ox that cleaned or bored sixteen matchlock barrels at once, and a mounting that let seventeen guns fire together from a single match. Irfan Habib credits Mir Fathullah Shirazi, an Iranian scholar who joined Akbar's court in 1583, with these and with a cart whose wheels drove a grain mill. Ain also describes rolled and welded barrels made from twisted iron sheet. These court machines show gearing applied to metalworking, but Habib notes they stayed curiosities and did not pass into general workshop practice.

sources.author: Irfan Habib
sources.confirms: 1582 devices, Shirazi attribution, boring interpretation

akbar-arsenal-gun-machines-1582.detail: Blochmann's English translation of Ain-i Akbari (1873) gives Ain 36 to 38 on guns, including machine for cleaning guns with a plate. Habib's 'Akbar and Technology' (Social Scientist, 1992) analyses a manuscript diagram in British Library Add. 7652 and argues that barghu here means boring the barrel interior rather than cleaning. Ain attributes inventions to Akbar himself; Habib and later writers credit Shirazi.

gregorian-calendar-1582.summary: In October 1582 ten days vanished as Catholic Europe adopted the Gregorian calendar, now used worldwide. Julius Caesar's calendar year of 365.25 days ran about 11 minutes longer than Earth's solar year. By the 16th century its spring equinox, which sets Easter, had slipped some ten days from its date at the Council of Nicaea. Pope Gregory XIII's bull Inter gravissimas adopted a scheme from Calabrian doctor Aloysius Lilius, worked out by mathematician Christopher Clavius: drop three leap years in every 400, keeping only centurial years divisible by 400, for an average year of 365.2425 days. To reset its equinox, Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October.

gregorian-calendar-1582.detail: Catholic states changed first; Protestant and Orthodox countries followed over three centuries, Britain in 1752 and Greece last in 1923.

lahore-astrolabe-workshop-1587.summary: In Lahore, instrument maker Allahdad and his descendants dominate production of astrolabes and celestial globes in the later 16th century and through the 17th, according to Abbasi and Sarma's 2014 study in Islamic Studies. About 120 astrolabes and 25 globes signed by family members survive in collections from India to the United States. A dated astrolabe of 1587 now in Moscow is among its earliest; Muhammad Muqim alone signed instruments from 1609 to the 1650s. They also cast celestial globes as single hollow spheres without a joint by lost-wax casting, a feat European founders did not match. Sarma records that Allahdad migrated from Samarqand and worked under Emperor Humayun's patronage.

lahore-astrolabe-workshop-1587.detail: Nearly 125 astrolabes and globes by seven makers over four generations are catalogued in Sarma's survey of Indian astronomical instruments, published open access by the University of Halle. Their instruments combine Persian and Indian traditions, with Sanskrit as well as Arabic inscriptions on some pieces, and their output outnumbers that of any other Islamic-world workshop after 1600; Hamid ibn Muhammad Muqim signed the Khalili Collection astrolabe pictured here.

lee-patent-refused-1589.summary: Around 1589 Elizabeth I is said to have refused Lee a patent for his knitting machine, to protect knitters. Its row of bearded needles knitted a whole course of loops at once instead of stitch by stitch. Accounts say he sought a patent from Elizabeth I and was refused out of concern for hand-knitters' employment; his often-quoted answer from her, "Thou aimest high, Master Lee. Consider thou what the invention could do to my poor subjects," comes from an account modern scholarship rejects. Lee took nine frames to Rouen under Henry IV of France's patent.

william-lee-stocking-frame-1589.summary: In 1589 William Lee built the first knitting machine; the queen is said to have refused him a patent. It imitated hand knitters' movements: hooked, bearded needles in one row held old loops while sinkers pressed yarn between them into new loops, so whole courses of stitches formed at once. His first frame had eight needles to each inch and knitted coarse fabric; he later fitted 20 and by late 1590s knitted silk. Lee demonstrated it at court and sought a patent, but a story that Elizabeth I refused him is later tradition historians treat as unverified.

william-lee-stocking-frame-1589.detail: He took frames and workmen to France. Frames spread through England's Midlands, and frame-breaking by displaced workers led to protective legislation in 1788.

janssen-microscope-1590.summary: Around 1590 Dutch lens makers put two lenses in a tube: the microscope opened a hidden world. Who first did it is unknown. One claim, made by Zacharias Janssen's son, dates it to 1590 in Middelburg's spectacle-making trade; rival claims name Janssen's father Hans Martens, their neighbour Hans Lippershey, who sought the first telescope patent in 1608, and Cornelis Drebbel, who had one in London in 1619. Earliest known compound microscopes appeared in Europe around 1620, apparently from refocusing telescopes on near objects; Galileo described such an instrument in 1624 and named it occhiolino.

janssen-microscope-1590.detail: Dutch scientist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes later reached 270 times magnification, and Robert Hooke's Micrographia of 1665 made microscope drawings famous.

turtle-ship-yi-sun-sin-1592.summary: In 1592 Yi Sun-sin's spike-roofed turtle ships, proof against boarding, helped destroy Japan's invasion fleet. When Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Japan invaded in 1592, Admiral Yi Sun-sin is credited with an improved design: sturdy oared warships with sails, dragon heads at their bows and closed roofs studded with iron spikes against Japanese boarding tactics. From their first action at Sacheon his turtle ships helped win 16 battles through 1598. Whether they were ironclad is disputed; no Korean source from Yi's time calls them so.

sources.author: Hong, Sung-hee

sources.qualifies: Author notes no Korean record of the period calls the ship ironclad.

turtle-ship-yi-sun-sin-1592.detail: Each carried four classes of chongtong cannon, heaven, earth, black and yellow, with ranges up to 1,200 metres, and seungja arquebuses.

chen-zhenlong-sweet-potato-fujian-1593.summary: Merchant Chen Zhenlong of Changle, Fujian, trading in Spanish Manila, carries sweet potato vines home to Fujian in 1593 and plants them successfully. When drought ruins Fujian's grain in 1594, his son Chen Jinglun presents sweet potato and its benefits to governor Jin Xuezeng, who prints cultivation instructions and orders farmers to plant it; roots earn a name, jinshu, golden tuber. It grows on hillsides and sandy soil unfit for rice, yields heavily and stores through winter, and over two centuries spreads to every province, underpinning Qing population growth from about 150 million to over 400 million. Scholars have treated 1594 as its introduction year since 1937, while Manuel Perez Garcia stresses other routes via Guangdong and Yunnan.

sources.author: Zhang, L.; Wang, Q.; Liu, Q.; Wang, Q.
sources.confirms: Recounts Chen Zhenlong bringing vines from Luzon to Fujian in 1593 and the 1594 famine promotion by governor Jin Xuezeng.

sources.author: Ho, Ping-ti

chen-zhenlong-sweet-potato-fujian-1593.detail: This story survives in family record Jinshu chuanxi lu and later gazetteers rather than eyewitness text, so details are probable rather than certain. Perez Garcia argued in 2017 for multiple entry points through Manila galleon trade and challenged a single national origin narrative. Ho Ping-ti wrote in 1955 what became standard English reading on American crops entering China. Xu Guangqi promoted sweet potato in Jiangnan and wrote Ganshu shu on its cultivation, later folded into his 1639 encyclopedia.

naqsh-e-jahan-isfahan-1598.summary: In 1598 Shah Abbas made Isfahan his capital and built one of the world's largest squares. He moved his court from Qazvin and began remaking Isfahan. Its centrepiece, Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Image of the World, was built between 1598 and 1629: 160 metres wide and 560 long, nearly 90,000 square metres. Each side held one function of his state: mosque, palace, a second mosque and bazaar gate. Shopkeepers traded around it, polo was played on it for the Shah watching from his palace, and Nowruz was celebrated there. UNESCO lists it as World Heritage.

banaue-ifugao-terraces-1600.summary: Stone and earth terraces climbing hillsides at Banaue, Batad and Hungduan carry wet rice fed by channels from mountain forests, with each field drained into fields below. Radiocarbon dates from Stephen Acabado's excavations in Ifugao put terrace construction and wet-rice adoption in sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, as lowland groups moved uphill away from Spanish control after 1565, rather than two thousand years ago as earlier guidebooks and UNESCO's 1995 listing stated. Communal water rights, forest reserves called muyong and ritual calendars managed labour. Terraces remain farmed, and depopulation and erosion put stretches on UNESCO's danger list from 2001 to 2012.

english-east-india-company-1600.summary: On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I chartered the East India Company, a trading firm that would come to rule India. James Lancaster had sailed round the Cape of Good Hope to India in 1591, and Dutch fleets were returning from Asia with profit. Her charter went to 216 petitioners, George, Earl of Cumberland, and 215 others, incorporating them as the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. Its trade grew into territorial rule; after 1757 it governed growing parts of India with its own army until Britain's Crown took over in 1858.

gilbert-de-magnete-1600.summary: In 1600 William Gilbert showed the Earth is a giant magnet, which is why compasses point north. Elizabeth I's physician published De Magnete after years of trials. He carved lodestone into spheres he called terrellae, little Earths, and moved compass needles over them: they pointed to its poles and dipped as latitude changed, just as needles do on Earth. From this he argued that Earth is one great magnet, explaining why compasses point north and why dip varies. Separately he studied amber rubbed to attract light objects and called such attraction electricus, from the Greek for amber, insisting it differed from magnetism. His experimental method and influence reached Kepler and Galileo.

indian-calico-trade-1600.summary: After 1600 cheap printed Indian cotton flooded Europe; the demand it created later drove Britain to mechanise spinning. It is named for Calicut in south-west India, where weavers had made it since the 11th century and dyed or printed it in bright colours. The East India Company then shipped cheap Indian calico prints to Europe, where they grew popular in England. Wool interests fought back: Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721 banned imports and then wearing of printed cotton. Demand shifted to plain grey calico imported for printing in southern England, laying groundwork for Britain's cotton industry.

karakuri-ningyo-1600.summary: From the 1600s Japanese craftsmen built karakuri, clockwork puppets that served tea, ancestors of its robots. Karakuri ningyo are mechanical puppets made from the 17th to 19th centuries; karakuri came to mean any device that awes by hiding its workings. Japan's Nihon Shoki records a south-pointing chariot in 658, but karakuri developed after European clockmaking arrived in early 17th century Japan. Three types followed: life-size stage figures, small dolls for wealthy homes, and figures on festival floats, which made them widely popular. Best known is its tea-serving doll: set a cup on its tray and a whalebone spring, steered by cams and levers, walks it to your guest, bows, and returns when that cup is lifted.

sources.title: Karakuri puppet - Wikipedia
Gutierrez Montanes, Maria, 'Dolls made in Japan: From Karakuri-ningyo to Danny Choo', Mirai. Estudios Japoneses 4 (2020), pp. 99-105
sources.author: Gutierrez Montanes, Maria
sources.confirms: Abstract places development of traditional doll types including karakuri in the Edo period (1603-1868).

sources.title: 'Karakuri', in Japanese Robot Culture (Routledge), pp. 90-101
sources.author: Routledge chapter
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

karakuri-ningyo-1600.verification_note: Sources confirm only an Edo-period dating; none dates karakuri to 1600 or describes a tea-serving doll mechanism.
karakuri-ningyo-1600.detail: Stage figures, butai karakuri, were first built by clockmaker Takeda Omi in Osaka in 1662; household dolls are zashiki karakuri and float figures dashi karakuri.

kongo-raffia-cloth-1600.summary: Men in the kingdoms of Kongo and Loango wove fibre stripped from raffia palm leaflets into plain-weave cloths, then added supplementary wefts that were cut and brushed into velvet-like pile, forming interlaced geometric patterns that Met conservator Christine Giuntini calls patterns without end. Such cloths served as currency, tribute and burial wealth at home. Portuguese captain Duarte Pacheco Pereira judged them equal to Italian work; two were in Rudolf II's Prague Kunstkammer by 1607 and another entered the Danish royal collection by 1674. About 65 presentation cloths and cushion covers from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries survive in European museums, most catalogued for the 2015 exhibition Kongo: Power and Majesty.

sources.title: Giuntini, Christine and Brown, Susan, 'Patterns without End: The Techniques and Designs of Kongo Textiles', Metropolitan Museum of Art, Kongo: Power and Majesty exhibition blog, 18 December 2015
sources.author: Giuntini, Christine; Brown, Susan
sources.confirms: Raffia fibre preparation, plain weave, supplementary weft pile cut and brushed, about 65 surviving cloths all of raffia, male weavers, interlace patterns; cushion covers inventoried 1737 and dated 16th-18th century

sources.title: Thornton, Dora, 'Made of Straw of Rare Beauty: Kongo Textiles in Renaissance European Collections', Metropolitan Museum of Art, Kongo: Power and Majesty exhibition blog, 2 October 2015
sources.author: Thornton, Dora
sources.confirms: Two cloths in Rudolf II's Prague Kunstkammer by 1607; a cushion cover inventoried in the Royal Danish Kunstkammer in 1674; Pacheco Pereira's and Zuchelli's descriptions

sources.title: Fromont, Cécile, 'Common Threads: Cloth, Colour, and the Slave Trade in Early Modern Kongo and Angola', Art History 41 (2018)
sources.author: Fromont, Cécile
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of cloth, colour and exchange in Kongo and Angola
sources.qualifies: Landing page did not render; metadata confirmed through Crossref

kongo-raffia-cloth-1600.detail: Cécile Fromont has traced how imported Indian and European textiles entered Kongo dress alongside raffia and how cloth figured in slave-trade accounting. Missionary Antonio Zuchelli described finishers cutting cloth with a knife and rubbing it by hand so it looked like patterned velvet. Raffia squares, called mpusu or libongo, circulated as money in Luanda under Portuguese rule. Dates here bracket the surviving pieces; weaving as a craft predates European contact.

picture.alt: Openwork raffia palm fibre kinzembe from Kongo-related peoples, Textile Museum, George Washington University; an example of the fibre craft behind Kongo cloth
picture.credit: Daderot

konso-terraces-1600.summary: In Ethiopia's southern highlands, Konso communities shaped more than 230 square kilometres of steep, dry hillside into stepped fields held by dry-stone walls up to five metres high. Terraces retain soil, slow runoff and feed sorghum, maize, cotton and moringa plots that are manured and intercropped under a system of communal work parties organised by generation grades. Walled towns called paleta, ringed by up to six stone walls, sit on hilltops with communal spaces called mora and carved wooden waka grave markers. UNESCO's inscription in 2011 records a tradition reaching back 21 generations, over 400 years, which places its consolidation around 1600. Elizabeth Watson's fieldwork documents how this landscape is maintained and contested today.

sources.title: Watson, Elizabeth E., Living Terraces in Ethiopia: Konso Landscape, Culture and Development (James Currey, 2009)
sources.author: Watson, Elizabeth E.
sources.confirms: Monograph on Konso terracing, social organisation and development interventions

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Konso Cultural Landscape', World Heritage List no. 1333
sources.confirms: Dry-stone terraces up to 5 m high over 230 km2; tradition of 21 generations, more than 400 years; walled towns (paletas) with one to six walls; moras; waka statues

konso-terraces-1600.detail: Watson's Living Terraces in Ethiopia shows terrace work as social as much as technical: labour groups, ritual leaders called poqalla and age-grade obligations govern wall building and repair. Population pressure, out-migration and state interventions in the twentieth century strained maintenance while food aid altered incentives. Konso terracing is one of several indigenous African intensive systems, alongside Nyanga in Zimbabwe and Engaruka in Tanzania. Dating comes from genealogical reckoning, so the year is approximate.

picture.alt: Stone-walled agricultural terraces in the Konso Cultural Landscape, southern Ethiopia
picture.credit: JosepMGracia

ottoman-tobacco-arrives-1600.summary: Peçevi dates tobacco's arrival in Istanbul to 1009 AH (1600 to 1601), brought by English merchants who sold it as a remedy. Smoking spread through coffeehouses in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo and Istanbul so quickly that jurists, preachers and sultans debated it for a century. Ahmed I banned it in 1609, Murad IV executed smokers in the 1630s alongside his coffeehouse closures, and in 1646 Shaykh al-Islam Bahai Efendi ruled it licit; by the 1690s treasury officials taxed it instead. Farmers in Macedonia, Anatolia and Syria planted it, Latakia and Yenice leaf became export goods, and long pipes and later water pipes became fixtures of male sociability. James Grehan reads the debate as an argument over new public leisure as much as over health or law.

sources.title: Grehan, J., 'Smoking and Early Modern Sociability: The Great Tobacco Debate in the Ottoman Middle East (Seventeenth to Eighteenth Centuries)', American Historical Review 111 (2006), 1352-1377
sources.author: Grehan, James
sources.confirms: Tobacco arrived around 1600, spread through coffeehouses, was banned under Ahmed I and Murad IV, ruled licit mid-century and taxed thereafter.

sources.title: Grehan, J., Everyday Life and Consumer Culture in Eighteenth-Century Damascus (University of Washington Press, 2007), ch. 4
sources.author: Grehan, James
sources.confirms: Tobacco and coffee consumption in Ottoman Damascus; pipes and water pipes.

ottoman-tobacco-arrives-1600.verification_note: Peçevi's 1009 AH date is a chronicler's recollection; tobacco may have arrived in Egypt or Syria a few years earlier. Grehan's chapter on Damascus is cited for context.

rapa-nui-palm-forest-loss-1600.summary: Rapa Nui once carried a forest of Paschalococos palms and other trees. Soil profiles studied by Mieth and Bork record millions of palm root casts, charcoal layers and erosion that date forest clearance mainly to between about 1250 and 1650, with Poike peninsula cleared by around 1400 and remaining stands gone by roughly 1600 to 1650. Hunt and Lipo argue that Polynesian rats, which gnawed palm nuts, prevented regeneration and that islanders adapted successfully through rock gardens rather than collapsing. Mieth and Bork stress human burning and slash-and-burn cultivation. Both camps agree forest loss was complete before Dutch visitors arrived in 1722, leaving an open grassland island whose farming depended on lithic mulch.

sources.title: Mieth, Andreas; Bork, Hans-Rudolf, 'History, origin and extent of soil erosion on Easter Island (Rapa Nui)', Catena 63 (2005)
sources.author: Mieth, Andreas; Bork, Hans-Rudolf
sources.confirms: Soil erosion and charcoal record forest clearance by fire between about 1250 and 1650
sources.qualifies: Emphasises human burning

sources.title: Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P., 'Revisiting Rapa Nui (Easter Island) "ecocide"', Pacific Science 63 (2009)
sources.author: Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P.
sources.confirms: Argues rats and adaptation, not ecocide, explain deforestation and demography
sources.qualifies: Rejects collapse narrative, contested by other authors

sources.title: Mieth, Andreas; Bork, Hans-Rudolf, 'A vanished landscape: phenomena and eco-cultural consequences of extensive deforestation in the prehistory of Rapa Nui', in Cultural and Environmental Change on Rapa Nui (Routledge, 2017)
sources.author: Mieth, Andreas; Bork, Hans-Rudolf
sources.confirms: Estimates palm numbers and consequences of deforestation
sources.qualifies: Chapter synthesises earlier fieldwork

rapa-nui-palm-forest-loss-1600.verification_note: Scholars disagree sharply on causes: Mieth and Bork emphasise human fire and clearance; Hunt and Lipo emphasise rats and deny pre-contact collapse. Date of final clearance (c. 1600 to 1650) is common ground.
rapa-nui-palm-forest-loss-1600.detail: Jared Diamond popularised an ecocide narrative of self-destruction; Hunt and Lipo's 2009 Pacific Science paper rejects collapse before contact and points to disease and slave raids after 1722 as causes of population decline. Mieth and Bork's 2017 chapter counts root casts to estimate up to 16 million palms. Rat-gnawed nuts are abundant, but charcoal shows fire also. Dating relies on buried soils and charcoal, with regional differences across island.

picture.alt: Treeless grassland around Rano Raraku crater, Rapa Nui, where a palm forest once stood
picture.credit: Bjørn Christian Tørrissen

upper-guinea-rice-1600.summary: Along estuaries from Casamance to Sierra Leone, Baga, Balanta, Diola and Temne farmers turned mangrove swamps into rice fields by building earth dykes, cutting hollow-log sluices and letting rain and tide leach salt over several seasons, then transplanting African rice, Oryza glaberrima, domesticated in Niger's inland delta. Women managed seed selection, transplanting and parboiling. Judith Carney argued in 2001 that enslaved people from this region carried the system to Carolina's tidal plantations. David Eltis, Philip Morgan and David Richardson replied in 2007 with slave-trade data showing few Carolina captives came from rice regions, setting off a debate about African agency that continues.

sources.title: Carney, Judith A., 'Rice Origins and Indigenous Knowledge', in Black Rice: The African Origins of Rice Cultivation in the Americas (Harvard University Press, 2001), ch. 2
sources.author: Carney, Judith A.
sources.confirms: Rice central to subsistence and identity in West Africa; dense populations on the Upper Guinea coast through 350 years of Atlantic slaving; women's role in cultivation and processing

sources.title: Eltis, David; Morgan, Philip and Richardson, David, 'Agency and Diaspora in Atlantic History: Reassessing the African Contribution to Rice Cultivation in the Americas', American Historical Review 112 (2007)
sources.author: Eltis, David; Morgan, Philip; Richardson, David
sources.confirms: Critique of the rice-transfer thesis using slave-trade data; framing of inheritance versus environment in Atlantic history

upper-guinea-rice-1600.verification_note: Carney and Eltis, Morgan and Richardson disagree over whether Upper Guinea rice technology was carried across to Spanish and Portuguese America; both accept its African development, which is all this entry describes.
upper-guinea-rice-1600.detail: Rice sustained dense populations on the Upper Guinea coast through 350 years of Atlantic slaving, with women central to cultivation and processing. Eltis, Morgan and Richardson accept African origins of the technology but dispute its transfer. Mangrove rice remains Guinea-Bissau's staple system. Year 1600 marks when European accounts first describe these works in detail and is approximate.

picture.alt: Bunded mangrove rice field (bolanha) prepared for transplanting, Guinea-Bissau
picture.credit: Demétrio Delizoicov Neto

wootz-crucible-steel-making-1600.summary: Ironworkers around Konasamudram and Nirmal in Telangana, in Mysore and at Mel-siruvalur in Tamil country sealed wrought iron with carbon-rich leaves and wood in small clay crucibles, fired dozens together in charcoal furnaces for many hours and produced cakes of high carbon steel, called ukku or wootz. Smiths from Persia, Syria and Arabia bought these cakes and forged them slowly into watered blades. Excavations and surveys by Sharada Srinivasan find crucible fragments and slag at these sites; travellers of seventeenth century describe caravans of steel cakes leaving Golconda ports. Production ran on this scale through Mughal period until British iron imports and bans on arms undercut it.

sources.title: Sharada Srinivasan, 'Wootz crucible steel: a newly discovered production site in South India', Papers from the Institute of Archaeology 5 (1994)
sources.author: Sharada Srinivasan
sources.venue: Papers from the Institute of Archaeology
sources.confirms: Mel-siruvalur site, crucible process, hypereutectoid steel

sources.title: R. K. Dube, 'Wootz: Erroneous Transliteration of Sanskrit Utsa used for Indian Crucible Steel', JOM 66 (2014)
sources.author: R. K. Dube
sources.confirms: wootz terminology and Indian crucible steel tradition

wootz-crucible-steel-making-1600.verification_note: Srinivasan's 1994 abstract supports site identifications; Dube is cited as supporting literature; travellers' accounts such as Tavernier's are cited secondhand.
wootz-crucible-steel-making-1600.detail: Srinivasan's 1994 field report identifies south Indian crucible steel sites and a cooling process that yielded hypereutectoid steel; her later metallurgical studies examine carbide banding. Dube's JOM review sets wootz within long run of Indian iron making. Pearson analysed wootz chemically in London in 1795. Year 1600 is approximate.

picture.alt: Close view of the watered pattern on a South Indian wootz steel blade
picture.credit: Mr McIntyre

amsterdam-stock-exchange-1602.summary: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company's shares could be sold on to anyone, and Amsterdam grew the first stock market. A secondary market soon formed at Amsterdam's East India House, where its official bookkeeper entered each sale in a capital book, giving buyers confidence that ownership moved in fact and not only on paper. Secondary markets for similar instruments had existed elsewhere; what was new in Amsterdam was volume, liquidity, publicity and freedom to speculate. It is counted as the oldest modern securities market and is now part of Euronext.

sources.title: Euronext Amsterdam - Wikipedia

Gelderblom, Oscar; Jonker, Joost, 'Completing a Financial Revolution: The Finance of the Dutch East India Trade and the Rise of the Amsterdam Capital Market, 1595-1612', Journal of Economic History 64.3 (2004), pp. 641-672
sources.author: Gelderblom, Oscar; Jonker, Joost
sources.confirms: Abstract: VOC share trading created a secondary market in Amsterdam after 1602; market strong by 1609.

sources.title: Petram, Lodewijk, The World's First Stock Exchange (Columbia, 2014)
sources.author: Petram, Lodewijk
sources.confirms: Book page: VOC share issue of 1602 initiated the transformation into a securities market.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Amsterdam Stock Exchange'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives early 1600s and says Dutch East India Company shares were traded there by the early 1600s; it does not give 1602 specifically.

amsterdam-stock-exchange-1602.detail: Turnover jumped after 1623, when VOC directors skipped its chartered 21-year liquidation and shareholders had to sell to get out. Joseph de la Vega's Confusion of Confusions described this market in 1688.

picture.alt: Claes Jansz Visscher's 1611 print of Hendrick de Keyser's new exchange building on Rokin in Amsterdam, where VOC shares changed hands.
picture.credit: Claes Jansz. Visscher (II), public domain (CC0), via Rijksmuseum

campanella-city-of-sun-1602.summary: In 1602 Campanella, in prison, wrote City of the Sun, La città del Sole, in Italian, a utopia run by scientist-priests with shared property; his Latin version, written in 1613 to 1614, was printed in Frankfurt in 1623. Inspired by Plato's Republic, it describes a theocratic city on a hill ringed by seven walls painted with all knowledge, from stars and mathematics to inventors and lawgivers, ruled by its priest Hoh, or Metaphysic. Goods are held in common, idleness is despised, and shared labour cuts each person's work to four hours daily.

sources.title: The City of the Sun - Wikipedia
Tommaso Campanella | Italian Philosopher, Poet, Theologian ...
La Città del Sole: Dialogo Poetico / The City of the Sun: A Poetical Dialogue
sources.author: Campanella, Tommaso; Donno, Daniel J. (trans. and intro.)
sources.venue: University of California Press, Berkeley and Los Angeles
sources.confirms: Critical Italian text with facing English translation and an introduction placing the composition in the Naples prison in 1602 and the first printing in Latin at Frankfurt in 1623.

sources.title: Tommaso Campanella
sources.author: De Lucca, Jean-Paul
sources.confirms: After escaping execution by feigning madness, Campanella wrote The City of the Sun as a poetical dialogue between a Genoese sailor and a Knight Hospitaller; it first appeared in Latin as an appendix to his Politica, Frankfurt 1623.

campanella-city-of-sun-1602.detail: It is framed as dialogue between a Knight Hospitaller and a Genoese sea captain. Citizens all learn every trade.

picture.alt: Engraved title page of Campanella's Realis philosophiae epilogisticae partes quatuor, Frankfurt 1623, first printing of his City of the Sun written in 1602.
picture.credit: Tommaso Campanella, National Central Library of Rome, public domain, via Internet Archive

dutch-east-india-company-1602.summary: On 20 March 1602 the Dutch East India Company sold shares to public buyers, and stock markets began. The States General merged competing Dutch trading companies into one Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, or VOC, with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade. Any Dutch Republic citizen could buy shares, which changed hands in open-air secondary markets, one of which became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange; it is counted among history's first joint-stock companies. Its charter let it wage war, make treaties, strike coins, imprison and execute, and found colonies, so some call it history's first multinational corporation. Bankruptcy came in 1799.

sources.title: Dutch East India Company - Wikipedia
Gelderblom, Oscar; de Jong, Abe; Jonker, Joost, 'The Formative Years of the Modern Corporation: The Dutch East India Company VOC, 1602-1623', Journal of Economic History 73.4 (2013)
sources.author: Gelderblom, Oscar; de Jong, Abe; Jonker, Joost
sources.confirms: Abstract treats VOC from its 1602 charter as the first company with transferable shares and limited liability evolving 1602-1623.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Dutch East India Company'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1602; it does not give a specific date. It does not confirm that shares were sold publicly on 20 March or that this began the stock market.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Amsterdam Stock Exchange'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives only the early 1600s; it does not give a specific date. It confirms broadly that Dutch East India Company shares were traded in Amsterdam by the early 1600s and that the exchange was among the world’s earliest.

dutch-east-india-company-1602.detail: From 1602 to 1796 it sent nearly one million Europeans to Asia on 4,785 ships, ruled from Batavia after 1619, and paid dividends averaging 18 percent.

picture.alt: Engraved title page of Begin ende voortgang vande Vereenigde Nederlandtsche geoctroyeerde Oost-Indische Compagnie, 1646, showing VOC ships and trade.
picture.credit: Hessel Gerritsz, public domain (CC0), via Rijksmuseum

matteo-ricci-world-map-1602.summary: In 1602 Matteo Ricci printed a world map in Chinese for the Wanli Emperor with China near its centre and Pacific Ocean mid-sheet. At Wanli's request Ricci worked in Beijing with mandarin Zhong Wentao, translator Li Zhizao and other scholars to produce his third map, Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, Complete Map of Ten Thousand Countries of the World, China's earliest known world map built on European cartography and its first to show American continents. Copies soon reached Korea and Japan, where they reshaped geographic ideas.

sources.title: Kunyu Wanguo Quantu - Wikipedia
Livieratos, Evangelos, 'On the cartography of Matteo Ricci's 1602 world map', International Journal of Cartography 2.2 (2016), pp. 186-201
sources.author: Livieratos, Evangelos
sources.confirms: Abstract dates the Kunyu wanguo quantu to 1602 and discusses its Chinese printing.

sources.title: Ricci, Matteo; Li Zhizao, Kunyu wanguo quantu (Beijing, 1602), Library of Congress
sources.author: Ricci, Matteo; Li Zhizao
sources.confirms: 1602; created/published in Beijing, China. The page identifies Ricci’s 1602 Chinese world map and says it depicts North and South America.

matteo-ricci-world-map-1602.detail: Carved on six woodblocks and printed on six mulberry paper panels, it stands 1.52 metres high and 3.66 wide.

edo-period-era-1603.summary: From 1603 the Tokugawa shoguns gave Japan 265 years of peace and near-closure to the outside world, until Western ships forced it open. His dynasty ruled from Edo, now Tokyo, over some 300 daimyo until 1868. To keep lords in check, from 1635 each daimyo spent alternate years in Edo, leaving his family there; by 1639 foreigners were expelled under sakoku, except Dutch traders confined to Dejima in Nagasaki. Two centuries of peace made samurai into administrators and enriched merchants. Commodore Perry forced Japan open in 1853; the Meiji Restoration ended Tokugawa rule in 1868.

sources.title: Edo period - Wikipedia
Hall, John Whitney, 'The bakuhan system', in The Cambridge History of Japan vol. 4 (Cambridge, 1991), pp. 128-182
sources.author: Hall, John Whitney
sources.confirms: Chapter: Ieyasu became shogun in 1603; the bakuhan order reached stable form in the 1630s-40s.

sources.title: Nakabayashi, Masaki, chapter in The Cambridge History of Capitalism / Japanese economy (Cambridge, 2021)
sources.author: Nakabayashi, Masaki
sources.confirms: Chapter abstract on Tokugawa rule from 1603.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tokugawa period'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the Tokugawa period to 1603-1867. It broadly confirms the claim: the period brought internal peace and stability, and the shogunate adopted national seclusion.

edo-period-era-1603.detail: Merchant houses of this era later became zaibatsu, and a commoner culture of kabuki and ukiyo-e grew in Edo, Osaka and Kyoto.

picture.alt: Horse Race at Kamo Shrine, Japanese screen painting from early to mid 1600s, first decades of Edo period.
picture.credit: Japan, Edo period (1615 to 1868), CC0, via Cleveland Museum of Art

janissary-volley-fire-1605.summary: Historians of Europe's military revolution dated musketry volley fire, in which ranks shoot in turn so that fire never stops, to Dutch drill of 1590s and to battlefield use only after 1620. Günhan Börekçi's 2006 study of overlooked Ottoman narrative and visual sources from Ottoman-Habsburg warfare of 1593 to 1606 shows janissary musketeers using volley fire in action during their 1605 campaign in Hungary, and possibly earlier. Janissaries had carried matchlock muskets since the fifteenth century and were salaried professionals drilled at Istanbul barracks, conditions that made coordinated fire by rank workable. Börekçi argues this evidence upends a story in which Ottoman armies only borrowed European tactics and asks whether volley fire was invented once or several times, since Japanese arquebusiers used rotating ranks in 1570s as well.

sources.title: Börekçi, G., 'A Contribution to the Military Revolution Debate: The Janissaries Use of Volley Fire during the Long Ottoman-Habsburg War of 1593-1606 and the Problem of Origins', Acta Orientalia Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae 59 (2006), 407-438
sources.author: Börekçi, Günhan
sources.confirms: Janissaries used volley fire in action in 1605 and possibly before, per Ottoman narrative and visual sources; European armies, except possibly the Dutch in 1600, did not use it in action until the 1620s.

sources.title: Agoston, G., Guns for the Sultan: Military Power and the Weapons Industry in the Ottoman Empire (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
sources.author: Agoston, Gabor
sources.confirms: Ottoman firearms production and janissary musketry, including volley fire in the Long War of 1593-1606.

janissary-volley-fire-1605.verification_note: Börekçi's abstract supports volley fire in 1605; which engagements and which miniature he cites rests on his full text.

picture.alt: Woodcut of an Ottoman janissary soldier printed in 1562, four decades before janissaries adopted volley fire with matchlock muskets.
picture.credit: François Desprez, public domain (CC0), via Rijksmuseum

new-julfa-armenian-silk-network-1605.summary: During his 1604 campaign against Ottoman forces, Safavid shah Abbas I deports tens of thousands of Armenians from Julfa on the Aras river and burns their town. Merchant families are settled in 1605 across the Zayandeh river from Isfahan in a new suburb named New Julfa, granted land, churches, their own mayor and a leading role in exporting Iran's raw silk, which Abbas made a royal monopoly in 1619. Over the following century New Julfa houses sent agents on commenda contracts to Aleppo, Venice, Amsterdam, Moscow, Surat, Madras, Lhasa, Canton and Manila, linked by Armenian-language letters, a shared commercial law and trust built on kinship. Sebouh Aslanian's archival study of this trade circulation society shows an Asian merchant network operating by its own rules alongside European chartered companies.

sources.author: Aslanian, Sebouh David
sources.confirms: Deportation of Julfa Armenians in 1604, settlement at New Julfa in 1605, silk monopoly and later global network of commenda agents.

sources.author: Herzig, Edmund

sources.title: Herzig, E., 'Julfa iv. Armenians of New Julfa', Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.author: Herzig, Edmund
sources.confirms: Founding of New Julfa in 1605 across the Zayanda-rud, privileges, kalantar, silk trade and later trading network.

picture.credit: Unknown photographer (scan by MJJR), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

relation-first-newspaper-1605.summary: In 1605 Johann Carolus of Strasbourg set his weekly newsletter in type, the first printed newspaper. Copying was slow, so he bought Thomas Jobin's former printing workshop and set his Relation aller Fürnemmen und gedenckwürdigen Historien in type instead. His petition to Strasbourg's council for protection from copying, found in its archive in the 1980s, states he had printed twelve weekly issues; in 2005 the World Association of Newspapers accepted it as proof that printing began in 1605, not 1609. Under functional criteria, regular issues of current news, it counts as history's first newspaper.

sources.title: Johann Carolus - Wikipedia
Weber, Johannes, 'Strassburg, 1605: The Origins of the Newspaper in Europe', German History 24.3 (2006), pp. 387-412
sources.author: Weber, Johannes
sources.confirms: Abstract: 'the first periodical news sheet, which appeared in Strassburg in 1605', printed by Johann Carolus.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'The first newspapers'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates Johann Carolus’s Relation to 1609. It does not confirm the record’s central claim that Carolus printed it in 1605. The page says the Relation was first printed in 1609 by Johann Carolus.

relation-first-newspaper-1605.detail: Printing historian Stanley Morison dissented, calling it a newsbook and giving first-newspaper status to a Dutch courante of 1618.

picture.alt: Title page of Johann Carolus's Relation aller Fürnemmen und gedenckwürdigen Historien, 1609 volume of newspaper begun in Strasbourg in 1605, from Heidelberg University Library.
picture.credit: Johann Carolus, public domain, via Heidelberg University Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

mexico-desague-huehuetoca-1607.summary: After floods in 1604 and 1607, Viceroy Luis de Velasco approved cosmographer Enrico Martínez's plan to cut an outlet from Lake Zumpango through hills at Nochistongo, near Huehuetoca, into Tula's river valley. Work began in November 1607 with about 60,000 Indigenous labourers drafted by repartimiento; in eleven months they dug a tunnel of roughly 6.6 kilometres plus an open canal of some 8 kilometres. Martínez had replaced prehispanic dikes, which kept water in, with a scheme to send it out of Mexico's basin. Collapses, silting and disputes with engineer Adrian Boot followed; a 1629 flood left Mexico City under water for five years, and workers slowly converted into an open cut, finished in 1789.

sources.author: Mathes, W. Michael

mexico-desague-huehuetoca-1607.verification_note: Labour figures of 60,000 and tunnel length of about 6.6 kilometres come from Mathes and colonial reports; other accounts give 4,000 to 6,000 workers at a time. The open cut's completion is given as 1788 or 1789.
mexico-desague-huehuetoca-1607.detail: W. Michael Mathes's 1970 article narrates this 1607 to 1608 campaign; Vera Candiani's Dreaming of Dry Land follows Desagüe works through two centuries as a project of elites that drained lakes, ended chinampa agriculture around Mexico City and displaced lakeside towns. Thousands of workers died underground, and Martínez was jailed after 1629. Mexico City continued to sink and flood into living memory, until deep drainage tunnels replaced Nochistongo's cut after 1975.

xu-guangqi-euclid-translation-1607.summary: In 1607 Xu Guangqi and Matteo Ricci translated Euclid into Chinese; the words they coined for point, line and parallel are still used. He became one of China's Three Pillars of Catholicism. Working together in 1607, Xu and Ricci rendered the first parts of Euclid's Elements, a work on geometry and logic, into Chinese; they also translated Confucian texts into Latin. After his circle correctly predicted a solar eclipse in 1629, Xu led the Chongzhen Emperor's calendar reform with Jesuit help. Some Chinese scholars credit him with starting China's enlightenment.

lippershey-telescope-patent-1608.summary: In 1608 Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey sought a patent for a tube that drew the distant near; Galileo soon improved it. Born in Wesel around 1570, Lipperhey had settled in Middelburg in 1594 as a master lens grinder. He was refused because other spectacle makers claimed it too, but Dutch authorities paid him handsomely for copies. News spread across Europe within months.

bank-of-amsterdam-1609.summary: In 1609 Amsterdam founded a bank where merchants settled debts by moving entries in a ledger instead of coins. Some 500 kinds of coin, legal and illegal, circulated in Amsterdam with no good way to fix exchange rates. Merchants deposited coin and received credit in stable bank money; depositors who withdrew got full-weight coin. It was the first public bank whose accounts were not directly convertible into coin, and its bank guilder traded at a premium over current money. Some call it the first true central bank; others dispute that label.

bank-of-amsterdam-1609.detail: Adam Smith later explained its bank guilder at length. Large unsecured advances to the Dutch East India Company, on which it defaulted, broke confidence: its premium vanished in 1790, Amsterdam's city took control in 1791 and liquidation came in 1819.

galileo-telescope-1609.summary: In 1609 Galileo saw moons circling Jupiter through a telescope: not everything orbits Earth. Hearing descriptions of a Dutch spyglass, he worked out its optics and built his own, first at eight or nine times magnification, later about thirty. Turned to the Moon, it showed an uneven boundary between light and dark, from which he deduced mountains and craters. On 7 January 1610 he saw three points of light near Jupiter; by 15 January he concluded they were moons orbiting Jupiter, proof that not everything circled Earth and support for Copernicus. He published all of it in Sidereus Nuncius, Starry Messenger, in March 1610.

sources.author: Galilei, Galileo
sources.confirms: Original 1610 publication of the telescopic observations of the Moon and Jupiter's satellites.

sources.confirms: The page dates the telescope’s development to spring 1609, its presentation to August 1609, and Galileo’s discovery of Jupiter’s moons to January 1610. It says the moons showed there was more than one centre of motion in the universe.

galileo-telescope-1609.detail: On 25 August 1609 he demonstrated a telescope to Venetian lawmakers. He named Jupiter's moons Medicean stars for Cosimo II de' Medici.

picture.alt: Title page of Galileo's Sidereus nuncius, Venice 1610, which reported what his telescope showed of Moon, stars and Jupiter's moons.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

kepler-astronomia-nova-1609.summary: In 1609 Kepler showed Mars moves in an ellipse, not a circle, and asked what force moves planets: astronomy became physics. Where astronomers treated Copernicus's circles as a computing device, Kepler asked what physically moved planets. His best circular model missed Tycho's data by eight arcminutes; trusting Tycho, he said that error would lead to reforming all of astronomy. He found that a line from Sun to planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, tried an oval, and settled on an ellipse with our Sun at one focus. He argued strongly for a Sun-centred system.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Astronomia nova
Kepler, Johannes, Astronomia nova (Heidelberg, 1609), digitized by Smithsonian Libraries

sources.confirms: Original 1609 edition presenting the elliptical orbit of Mars.

kepler-astronomia-nova-1609.detail: He proposed that some force from that Sun, which he likened to magnetism, drove planets.

picture.credit: Johannes Kepler, public domain, via Internet Archive (Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, University of Toronto)

brazil-engenho-three-roller-mill-1612.summary: A royal survey of 1612 attributed to Diogo de Campos Moreno counted 192 engenhos in Brazil, mostly in Pernambuco and Bahia, exporting more than 10,000 tonnes of sugar a year. In these same years millwrights introduced a vertical three-roller mill, three upright wooden cylinders sheathed in iron and geared so that a water wheel or oxen turned a middle roller, which drove two outer ones. Cane fed through twice gave more juice with fewer workers than older edge-runner and two-roller presses. John and Christian Daniels' 1988 study in Technology and Culture places its appearance in Brazil and Peru about 1608 to 1613; from Brazil it spread to Barbados and across Caribbean islands. Stuart Schwartz's Bahia study details each engenho as a combined farm and factory worked by enslaved Africans.

sources.title: Daniels, John and Daniels, Christian, 'The Origin of the Sugarcane Roller Mill', Technology and Culture 29 (1988)
sources.author: Daniels, John; Daniels, Christian

brazil-engenho-three-roller-mill-1612.verification_note: Daniels and Daniels date the three-roller mill's appearance to a window of about 1608 to 1613 rather than one year; the 1612 engenho count varies between 170 (captaincies covered by the report) and 192 (Schwartz's total).
brazil-engenho-three-roller-mill-1612.detail: Daniels and Daniels reject earlier attributions of three-roller mills to Sicily or China and argue for an American origin. Brandônio's 1618 Diálogos das grandezas do Brasil praised these new 'engenhos de palitos'. Mill counts grew to 346 by 1629; each engenho needed a boiling house, purging house for claying sugar, firewood, oxen and 60 to 100 enslaved workers.

picture.credit: Frans Post, via Wikimedia Commons

rolfe-tobacco-1612.summary: In 1612 Rolfe grew sweet tobacco in Virginia, a crop that saved the colony and drew slavery. His crop was North America's first marketable tobacco; Orinoco, a variety often linked with him, dominated only from about 1650. Accounts differ on his first export: March 1614, or 28 June 1614 in a Library of Congress timeline, or 1617 for a first substantial shipment. Plantations spread along the James River, and one tally has exports rising from 2,500 pounds in 1616 to 50,000 in 1628. Tobacco planting later ran on enslaved labour.

rolfe-tobacco-1612.detail: By December 1618 tobacco served as money in Virginia. In August 1619 Virginia's first Africans arrived and were exchanged for supplies.

santorio-clinical-thermometer-1612.summary: Santorio Santorio (1561 to 1636), professor of medical theory at Padua from 1611, took an air thermoscope circulating among Galileo's friends, added a scale and shaped its bulb to fit in mouth or hand. Around 1612 he described measuring a patient's heat by watching how far its column moved in a fixed time counted on a pendulum, and he published engravings of it in his commentaries on Galen (1612) and Avicenna (1625). He also built a pulsilogium, a pendulum for timing pulses, and a weighing chair on which he sat for thirty years to measure what he ate and excreted. Readings were crude and unrepeatable, since air pressure moved its column too, but Santorio made temperature a number a doctor could record.

sources.author: Grodzinsky, Ewa; Sund Levander, Marta
sources.confirms: Confirms that around 1612 Santorio calibrated the tube and tried to measure human temperature with a thermoscope whose bulb was placed in the mouth, with limited success.
