sources.confirms: Confirms birth 1561 and death 1636, the Padua chair 1611 to 1624, the clinical thermometer of 1612, the pulse clock, and the weighing chair experiments.

santorio-clinical-thermometer-1612.verification_note: 1612 is the date of his Galen commentary, which first describes the instrument; his Avicenna commentary with the better-known engraving dates to 1625. Marked approximate.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

heo-jun-donguibogam-1613.summary: Court physician Heo Jun, ordered by King Seonjo in 1596 to compile a medical reference after Japanese invasions, finished Donguibogam in 1610 and saw it printed with wooden movable type in 1613. Its 25 volumes arrange internal medicine, external symptoms, miscellaneous diseases, materia medica and acupuncture around a view of body as a system to be kept in balance, with Korean plant names written in hangul beside Chinese. It drew on some 86 Chinese and Korean texts and became a standard work reprinted in China and Japan. UNESCO added it to Memory of World register in 2009, and it still underpins traditional medicine training in Korea.

Donguibogam prioritised preventive regimen and accessible remedies for a population recovering from war. Printed copies survive in Korean national library and museum collections.

napier-logarithms-1614.summary: In 1614 Napier of Merchiston, near Edinburgh, published Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio: fifty-seven pages of explanation and ninety of tables. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction, so astronomers and navigators could replace long hand calculations with table look-ups. Henry Briggs visited him in 1615 and they agreed to rescale to base ten; Napier left Briggs to compute revised tables. In 1617 he published rabdology, numbered rods now called Napier's bones, which carry out lattice multiplication by hand.

qeswachaka-bridge-1615.summary: In 1615 Quechua author Huamán Poma illustrated Guambo's Inca grass rope bridge in use in his First New Chronicle; one such bridge, Q'iswa Chaka over the Apurímac River, is still rewoven yearly by villagers. Rope bridges hung over canyons and rivers as part of Inca roads. Since Inca people used no wheeled transport, bridges carried only people and livestock, among them chasqui runners relaying messages across their empire. Villagers wove ichu grass into thick cables and replaced every cable each year as labour owed to their state, dangerous work that cost lives. Poma praised Spanish masonry bridges as an improvement.

oughtred-slide-rule-1600.summary: Around 1622 William Oughtred, Cambridge-trained clergyman, made his slide rule, engineers' calculator for 350 years. John Napier had published logarithms in 1614, and Edmund Gunter then laid one logarithmic scale along a rule, read with dividers to multiply and divide. Oughtred set two such scales sliding against each other: lining up lengths adds logarithms, so products and quotients appear directly, with no dividers and fewer errors than working on paper; Cambridge's Centre for Computing History credits him with its invention in 1622. Slide rules stayed standard calculating tools for engineers until cheap pocket electronic calculators, beginning with Hewlett-Packard's HP-35 in 1972, made them obsolete.

schickard-calculating-clock-1623.summary: In 1623 Wilhelm Schickard described to Kepler a machine that added and carried tens on its own, two decades before Pascal's. His drawing shows an adding machine worked by rotating knobs, its result shown in small windows, with rotating Napier's bones above to help multiply. His letters lay unknown for three centuries until Kepler's biographer Franz Hammer publicised them in the 20th century, arguing that Schickard had preceded Pascal's calculator by twenty years. Critics answered that his design was incomplete and that its single-tooth carry mechanism could not work reliably.

statute-of-monopolies-1624.summary: In 1624 England banned royal monopolies except for true inventions, the root of patent law. English monarchs had long issued letters patent giving one holder a monopoly over some trade, originally to attract skilled foreigners with new techniques. Under Elizabeth I this became a way to raise money without a tax: patents covered common goods such as starch and salt, prices rose and protest grew. James I kept selling them despite Sir Edward Coke's Committee of Grievances. Parliament passed the Statute of Monopolies on 29 May 1624, voiding past and future monopolies but excepting patents for any new manner of manufacture, limited to fourteen years. It counts as England's first statutory expression of patent law.

bacon-new-atlantis-1626.summary: In 1626 Francis Bacon's New Atlantis imagined a state-funded house of researchers, a blueprint for research labs. He left it unfinished at his death; his chaplain William Rawley published it with Sylva Sylvarum in a volume catalogues date 1626 or 1627 (its title page reads 1627). Sailors blown off course from Peru reach Bensalem, an island whose people are generous, learned and devout. Its chief institution, Salomon's House, is a state-funded college of researchers who travel to gather knowledge, run experiments in caves, towers and laboratories, and decide which inventions to publish. Readers took it as a blueprint for organised, cooperative science, and it helped inspire the Royal Society's founding in 1660.

qiqi-tushuo-western-machines-1627.summary: In 1627 a Jesuit and a Chinese scholar published European machines in Chinese, the first such book in China. Johann Schreck, a German Jesuit who had studied under Galileo at Padua, had been recruited by Nicolas Trigault to bring European science to China. Nicolas Trigault recruited him to bring European science to China, and in 1616 they toured Europe collecting books, mechanical equipment and instruments, including China's first Western telescope. After reaching Beijing late in 1623, Schreck worked closely with Wang Zheng, a judge and military inspector from Shaanxi, and in 1627 they published Diagrams and Explanations of Wonderful Machines of the Far West. In 1629 his eclipse prediction beat Chinese astronomers', and Emperor Chongzhen asked Jesuits to reform China's calendar.

harvey-circulation-1628.summary: William Harvey, physician to St Bartholomew's Hospital and Lumleian lecturer at London's College of Physicians, published Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus at Frankfurt in 1628, a 72-page book printed by William Fitzer. By ligature experiments on arms and by vivisection of snakes, eels and dogs he showed that valves in veins admit flow only toward the heart, and he calculated that it pumps more blood in half an hour than the body contains, so blood must return in a circle, which overturned Galen's model of liver-made blood consumed in tissues. He concluded that blood in animal bodies moves around in a circle continuously, and that the heart's action or function is to drive this by pumping.

sources.author: Ribatti, Domenico

harvey-circulation-1628.detail: Ibn al-Nafis had described pulmonary transit in Damascus in 1242 and Realdo Colombo in Padua in 1559, but neither proposed a full systemic circuit. Harvey could not see capillaries; Marcello Malpighi found them with a microscope in 1661. Printed abroad in a small run with many typographical errors, it drew critics, among them Jean Riolan in Paris, whom Harvey spent years answering in letters published in 1649.

vasa-ship-sinks-1628.summary: In August 1628 Sweden's warship Vasa sank a mile into its maiden voyage, top-heavy with guns. King Gustavus Adolphus had ordered it for his war with Poland-Lithuania, and Stockholm's navy yard built it between 1626 and 1628. It was an early warship with two full-length gun decks, built when shipbuilding theory was poorly understood: its heavy hull and upper works placed its centre of gravity too high for its ballast. The king's officers knew and lacked courage to postpone. On 10 August 1628, after sailing about 1,300 metres on its maiden voyage, a gust stronger than a breeze heeled it over and it sank in Stockholm harbour. Its hull was raised largely intact in 1961.

cinchona-bark-europe-1631.summary: Quechua healers in the Andes used quina bark against shivering. Agustino Salumbrino, a Jesuit apothecary who reached Lima in 1605, tested it on fever patients at the order's college and sent a consignment from Callao on 31 May 1631 to Rome, where malaria killed cardinals and popes each summer. Within two decades "Jesuit's bark" sold across Catholic Europe, and Spanish sources record its arrival in Seville in the 1630s. It worked because it carried quinine, isolated by Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou in Paris in 1820. It was the first specific remedy for a named disease Europe possessed, and demand for it drove Dutch plantations in Java that supplied most quinine worldwide by 1900.

taj-mahal-construction-1632.summary: In 1632 Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal for his dead wife; 20,000 workers took two decades and Mughal coffers paid dearly. He commissioned her tomb that year on the Yamuna's right bank at Agra. More than 20,000 workers and artisans laboured under court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori, raising an ivory-white marble mausoleum inlaid with semi-precious stones, with red sandstone for its mosque, guest house and walls around 17 hectares of formal garden. Its mausoleum was finished in 1648 and the whole complex by 1653 at about 32 million rupees.

galileo-trial-1633.summary: In 1633 Rome's Inquisition made Galileo recant that the Earth moves and confined him for life. Pope Urban VIII, Galileo's patron, allowed him to write on Copernican ideas as hypothesis, but his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632 put geocentric arguments in the mouth of one Simplicio, portrayed as a fool, and read as advocacy. Tried in 1633, Galileo was found vehemently suspect of heresy for holding that the Sun stands still and Earth moves. He was made to abjure, curse and detest those opinions; imprisonment was commuted next day to house arrest at Arcetri near Florence for life.

galileo-trial-1633.detail: His Dialogue was banned along with any future work, yet he finished his book on mechanics, printed in Holland in 1638. His legendary mutter, and yet it moves, has no evidence behind it.

ottoman-coffeehouse-ban-1632.summary: In 1633 Ottoman sultan Murad IV shut Istanbul's coffeehouses and made smoking tobacco punishable by death; smokers caught red-handed were executed on the spot (James Grehan, American Historical Review, 2006). Rulers feared places where people gathered and talked. Murad had come to power aged 11 in 1623 under his mother Kösem's regency while cavalry and Janissaries forced executions of officials; in 1632 spahi cavalry invaded his palace and took heads of his grand vizier and sixteen others, after which Murad seized full control and ruled ruthlessly. Britannica records that he banned tobacco and closed coffeehouses and wineshops as nests of sedition, executing violators and mere suspects. Fire was his practical argument, since Istanbul's wooden buildings burned often. Ottoman authorities soon gave up: by 1650 tobacco was formally legal again.

sakoku-isolation-1633.summary: From 1633 Japan closed its ports to nearly all foreigners for 220 years, keeping out Christianity and trade. Christian converts had multiplied through missionary work, and the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637 to 1638, an uprising of some 40,000 mostly Christian peasants, is said to have triggered its final form; missionaries were blamed and expelled. Japan was never sealed: trade continued at Nagasaki and through Tsushima and Satsuma. Seclusion ended after Matthew Perry's expedition of 1853 forced treaties opening Japan to Western trade.

sakoku-isolation-1633.detail: Chinese merchants traded at Nagasaki. Europeans traded only through Dejima island there, whose Dutch post supplied books that fed Rangaku, Dutch learning; Korea dealt via Tsushima domain and Ryukyu via Satsuma.

royal-mail-public-1635.summary: On 31 July 1635 England's royal post opened to all, and anyone could send a letter across England. This royal post began in 1516, when Henry VIII made Brian Tuke Master of the Posts to carry crown letters. Its monopoly was farmed out to Thomas Witherings, who was to build six Great Roads and get mail to Edinburgh and back within six days. Senders began paying only in 1839, with adhesive penny stamps following in 1840.

descartes-discourse-method-1637.summary: In 1637 Descartes argued a machine could never hold a conversation or reason in every situation, the first test set for thinking machines. Part IV gives his famous starting point, I think, therefore I am. Part V treats animal bodies as machines and asks how we could tell a machine imitating a human from a human. He names two tests: no machine could arrange words to give meaningful answers to whatever is said in its presence, and none could act through reason in all of life's contingencies, as opposed to performing a few set tasks.

Wikipedia: Discourse on the Method

sources.author: Gunderson, Keith
sources.confirms: Descartes argued in the Discourse that no machine could use language flexibly or act from reason in all situations, a test for distinguishing men from machines.

descartes-discourse-method-1637.detail: This Discourse prefaced essays on optics, meteorology and geometry. Philosophers since Gunderson in 1964 have read Part V as a forerunner of Turing's test, with Descartes confident no machine could pass.

tiangong-kaiwu-1637.summary: In 1637 Song Yingxing published an illustrated encyclopedia of every Chinese craft; it survived only in Japan. It is a technical encyclopedia: growing grain, silk and cotton, boats and carts, casting and forging metal, sulfur and saltpetre, gunpowder weapons, brick and tile making, each process pictured, down to a brick-maker dressing clay in his wooden mould. Unusually, Song rarely cited earlier texts, writing as if from direct observation, which he put down to his poverty and low standing. Copies grew scarce under Qing rule, whose state monopolies covered industries it described.

tulip-mania-1637.summary: In February 1637 Dutch tulip prices collapsed after rare bulbs such as Semper Augustus had sold for 10,000 guilders. Tulips had reached the Dutch Republic from Ottoman lands and become luxuries. Bulbs infected with mosaic virus produced flamed petals that could not be bred reliably, so such rare kinds stayed scarce. In 1636 traders began buying and selling contracts for bulbs still in the ground, meeting in tavern colleges and paying no margin, in what critics called windhandel, air trade. When prices broke, no bulbs were delivered. Charles Mackay's 1841 tale of mass ruin is disputed by scholars who find its damage limited.

Garber, Peter M., 'Tulipmania', Journal of Political Economy 97.3 (1989), pp. 535-560
sources.author: Garber, Peter M.
sources.confirms: Abstract confirms the 1637 collapse of tulip bulb prices.

tulip-mania-1637.detail: By November 1636 even common bulbs fetched hundreds of guilders, rare ones over ten times a skilled artisan's yearly income, and some contracts changed hands five times. By one account prices broke after a Haarlem auction found no buyers. Legislators cancelled contracts, and Haarlem let buyers settle for 3.5 percent.

picture.credit: Anonymous, Tulpenboek, Six Collection, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stephen-daye-press-1638.summary: In 1638 Stephen Daye set up a printing press at Cambridge, Massachusetts, British North America's first, 18 years after Plymouth. Glover, its owner, died during their crossing; his widow Elizabeth became owner of press and contract. Its first items in 1639 were a broadside of the Oath of a Freeman, sworn by every new colonist, and William Pierce's almanac; in 1640 came its first book, the Bay Psalm Book, all 150 psalms in English verse for congregational singing.

sources.title: Stephen Daye - Wikipedia

xu-guangqi-nongzheng-quanshu-1639.summary: Six years after Xu Guangqi's death, his student Chen Zilong edits and prints Nongzheng quanshu, Complete Treatise on Agricultural Administration, at Pinglu Hall in 1639. Sixty chapters and about 700,000 characters cover land systems, water control, tools, crops, sericulture, forestry, animal husbandry and famine administration, quoting 225 earlier works alongside Xu's own trials. Xu, grand secretary and convert who translated Euclid with Matteo Ricci, folds in his Ganshu shu on sweet potato and Western hydraulics learned from Jesuit Sabatino de Ursis. Eighteen chapters on famine relief list 414 wild plants safe to eat. Bray treats such treatises as instruments of a state science of agronomy, and the book becomes a reference for Qing administrators.

sources.author: Bray, Francesca

xu-guangqi-nongzheng-quanshu-1639.detail: Xu farmed experimentally in Shanghai and Tianjin, testing cotton, sweet potato and irrigation methods before writing. His emphasis on state responsibility for water works and grain reserves reflected late Ming crises of flood, drought and rebellion that toppled the dynasty five years after printing. Via Japan and Korea the work shaped farming reform across East Asia. Its water-control chapters reproduce Taixi shuifa, the hydraulic text Xu compiled with de Ursis in 1612.

picture.credit: Ciked, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

abel-tasman-new-zealand-1642.summary: In 1642 Abel Tasman was the first European to sight Tasmania and New Zealand: the southern ocean held land. The Dutch East India Company had sent him with two ships, Heemskerck and Zeehaen, to find a Southern Continent thought to lie across the Pacific. Sailing from Batavia by way of Mauritius and far south, he sighted Tasmania's west coast on 24 November and named it Van Diemen's Land after Governor-General Anthony van Diemen. Blown off its coast by westerlies through Bass Strait, he turned east and on 13 December became the first European to see New Zealand. Company directors judged his voyage a failure, since no trade followed.

van Meijl, Toon, 'Tasman's 1642 encounter', Journal of New Zealand Studies NS40 (2025)
sources.author: van Meijl, Toon

abel-tasman-new-zealand-1642.detail: He named New Zealand Staten Landt, guessing it joined land of that name off South America. Off Golden Bay, Māori in canoes attacked one boat and clubbed four sailors to death; Tasman called it Murderers' Bay and left without landing, going on to Tonga and Fiji. Over a century later James Cook built on Tasman's charts.

pascaline-1642.summary: In 1642 Pascal, aged 19, built an adding machine that carried tens: the first calculator sold. Numbers were entered by turning dials with a stylus; results showed in windows above, and a mechanism carried tens automatically from one wheel to the next. It added and subtracted directly, using nines' complements for subtraction, and multiplied or divided by repeated steps. Its cost and complexity kept it from wide use, but many later calculators followed its design.

pascaline-1642.detail: He made versions for accounting, surveying and science, and in 1649 Louis XIV granted him a royal privilege, an exclusive right to make and sell calculating machines in France. He had sold about twenty by 1654; nine survive in museums.

torricelli-barometer-1643.summary: In 1643 Torricelli held up mercury with the weight of air, making the barometer and a vacuum. Well diggers knew that suction pumps raise water no higher than about 10 metres, and Galileo's appeal to a force of vacuum could not explain why. Evangelista Torricelli, Galileo's secretary in his last months, proposed that we live at the bottom of a sea of air whose weight presses on everything. Air pressing on a basin should then hold up about 10 metres of water, or one thirteenth of that in mercury, thirteen times denser. In 1643 he upended his mercury-filled tube in a basin: mercury fell to about 76 centimetres, leaving history's first sustained vacuum above.

torricelli-barometer-1643.detail: His tube was about a metre long and sealed at one end. He set out his sea-of-air idea in a letter to Michelangelo Ricci on 11 June 1644. Blaise Pascal later showed that this column drops on towers and mountains; physics gained its concept of atmospheric pressure, and weather forecasting and altimetry gained their instrument.

fasil-ghebbi-gondar-1645.summary: Around 1645 Ethiopia's emperor built a stone castle at Gondar and ended rule from tent camps. Ethiopian emperors had long moved from camp to camp with their courts, living off local peasants. Fasilides broke that pattern: he founded Gondar as his fixed capital and ordered an imposing castle there, core of Fasil Ghebbi, ghebbi being Amharic for an enclosure. One Yemeni ambassador who saw it in 1648, when it was a few years old, named its architect as Abdal Kerim, an Indian who had built for Fasilides's father. Later emperors added palaces, library, chancellery and halls, until this compound covered about 70,000 square metres. UNESCO listed it in 1979.

fasil-ghebbi-gondar-1645.detail: Walls of brown basalt trimmed with wine-coloured tuff carried Portuguese, Hindu and Arab influences. Yohannes I, Iyasu I and Dawit III were the emperors who extended it, and Italian occupiers and independent Ethiopia both restored it.

historia-naturalis-brasiliae-1648.summary: In 1648 Leiden and Amsterdam printers issued Historia Naturalis Brasiliae, compiled from fieldwork at Recife under Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen. Physician Willem Piso described tropical diseases and remedies learned from Tupi and African informants, including ipecacuanha root for dysentery; naturalist Georg Marcgrave catalogued hundreds of plants, fish, birds and mammals with woodcuts after paintings by Albert Eckhout and others, and ran an observatory on Recife's Antonio Vaz island from 1639. Marcgrave died in Angola in 1644 and Johannes de Laet edited his notes. Linnaeus drew on it a century later, and Brazilian common names it recorded still anchor zoological nomenclature.

Piso's section De medicina Brasiliensi runs to four books on climate, diseases, poisons and plant remedies. A 2023 census by Alsemgeest and Bos locates surviving copies worldwide. Dutch rule in Pernambuco ended in 1654, but this book remained Europe's standard reference on Brazilian nature until about 1820.

wilkins-mathematical-magick-1648.summary: In 1648 John Wilkins imagined submarines, land yachts and a flying chariot in a book on what machines might do. Newly Warden of Wadham College, Oxford, he published Mathematical Magick surveying what levers, pulleys, gears and springs could achieve. Magick here meant marvels, nothing occult. Its first book, Archimedes, explains mechanical powers; its second, Daedalus, imagines land yachts, submarines, perpetual motion and flight. Wilkins lists four ways a person might fly, by spirits, by birds, by wings fixed to one's body, or by a flying chariot, and argues that practice and research would make this last possible: a vehicle contrived to carry one person with an engine, or several people working it in turn.

In the 1650s Wilkins and Robert Hooke tested one model in Wadham's garden that, Hooke recorded, rose and stayed up by springs and wings.

barbados-sugar-revolution-1650.summary: Through 1640 to 1660 English planters on Barbados, taught by Dutch and Sephardic traders who had worked in Pernambuco, replaced tobacco and cotton with sugar cane. They built cattle- and wind-driven three-roller mills, boiling houses with trains of copper kettles, and curing houses, and bought enslaved Africans in growing numbers; by 1660 enslaved people outnumbered Europeans there. Russell Menard's work shows that Barbadian planters financed this change largely from their own tobacco profits and English credit, built an integrated plantation combining field and factory, and made Barbados England's richest colony by 1660. Richard Dunn's study follows planter families and demographic costs borne by enslaved workers.

barbados-sugar-revolution-1650.detail: Windmills suited Barbados's trade winds; by 1750 several hundred stone mill towers stood across Barbados. Ligon's 1657 True and Exact History records mill layouts and boiling schedules. Sugar exports rose from near zero in 1640 to roughly 7,000 tonnes a year by 1660, and this Barbados model spread to Jamaica after 1655 and to French Antilles colonies.

bihar-saltpetre-trade-1650.summary: Nuniya caste workers in Bihar scraped nitrous earth from village soils, leached it in clay vats, and boiled brine to crystallise potassium nitrate. Dutch and English East India companies set up refineries at Patna and Chhapra in 1650s to re-boil this crude saltpetre and shipped thousands of tons a year from Hughli as ballast. By late seventeenth century Bengal saltpetre supplied most gunpowder made in Amsterdam and London. European states fought for access, and Mughal governors taxed and licensed trade. Indian soil chemistry, climate and cheap labour, not European technique, made this possible; refining stayed in Indian hands into nineteenth century.

sources.title: James W. Frey, 'The Indian Saltpeter Trade, the Military Revolution, and the Rise of Britain as a Global Superpower', The Historian 71 (2009)

Prakash's Princeton study of Dutch company trade in Bengal gives export volumes and locations of refineries. Dates are approximate; Dutch Patna factory operated from 1638 and English from 1650s.

edo-night-soil-1650.summary: By mid-seventeenth century, when Edo passed half a million residents, landlords sold rights to tenants' excrement to farmers from surrounding villages, who hauled it by boat and cart and composted it for vegetables and rice. Prices rose through eighteenth century, guilds formed, and disputes over rates reached magistrates. Susan Hanley argued that this trade, with piped water from Tamagawa and Kanda aqueducts, kept Edo cleaner than contemporary London or Paris and spared it waterborne epidemics on European scale until cholera arrived in 1858. Farmers gained fertiliser cheaper than fish meal, and city streets gained removal of waste that elsewhere flowed into rivers.

sources.author: Hanley, Susan B.

sources.author: Hanley, Susan B.
sources.confirms: Expanded treatment of sanitation and living standards in Tokugawa cities

edo-night-soil-1650.verification_note: Both sources support this trade; a mid-century date approximates a gradual development.
edo-night-soil-1650.detail: Hanley's 1987 article in Journal of Interdisciplinary History sets out this argument and its demographic evidence; her 1997 book expands it. Critics note that smallpox and measles still struck Edo hard, so sanitation gains were specific to intestinal disease. Dating is approximate since trade grew gradually from early 1600s.

kircher-arca-musarithmica-1650.summary: In 1650 Kircher described a box of slats that let anyone compose music by combining them. The Jesuit scholar's Arca Musarithmica, musical ark, appears in Musurgia Universalis, whose eighth book treats composing by combinatorics. It is a box of wooden slats he called tariffa. Each carries rows of numbers standing for notes in a scale or mode, plus rhythmic patterns for them; different sets suit Latin texts in different poetic metres. A user picks slats for the text's metre, reads off numbers and writes out four-part church music without musical training; the combinations run to millions of pieces.

kircher-arca-musarithmica-1650.detail: Metres served include Sapphic and Archilochian, and some slats serve plain four-part harmony while others give the florid style in which voices move independently. Kircher's pupil Gaspar Schott later described his Organum Mathematicum, a similar cabinet for arithmetic and astronomy as well as music. Few Baroque arcas survive; one is in Samuel Pepys's library at Cambridge.

hobbes-leviathan-reckoning-1651.summary: In 1651 Hobbes's Leviathan called reasoning reckoning, adding and subtracting: thought as sums. That idea, that thinking is calculation, is the root of treating minds as computers. Its first part, Of Man, builds this on an account of sense, language and reasoning. Hobbes wrote that "words are wise mens counters, they do but reckon by them", while "words are the mony of fooles" who value them on Aristotle's authority. Reasoning, for him, was adding and subtracting with words, starting from definitions.

hobbes-leviathan-reckoning-1651.detail: Hobbes held that nothing in the world is universal but names, and admired how geometry proceeds from definitions. No conclusion, he wrote, is certain without certainty of every affirmation and negation it rests on.

tamagawa-aqueduct-1653.summary: In 1653 townsmen brothers Shoemon and Seiemon, commissioned by shogunate officials, dug a 43-kilometre channel to bring the Tama River to Edo, soon the world's largest city. Work began in April 1653; their open channel from Hamura to Yotsuya was finished by November, and its whole system, with buried wooden and stone conduits under Edo's streets, was running by June 1654. Over its length it drops only about 92 metres, enough for gravity to move water with no pumping.

tamagawa-aqueduct-1653.detail: Both brothers were granted their family name Tamagawa. More than thirty branch canals later irrigated Musashino Plateau farmland around Edo, and its upstream reach still carries raw water for Tokyo today.

magdeburg-hemispheres-1654.summary: In 1654 Otto von Guericke emptied two joined bowls of air and 30 horses could not part them. The mayor of Magdeburg, a city whose population had fallen from 20,000 to 4,000 in the Thirty Years' War, had built an air pump to study vacuum. To show what it did, he made two copper hemispheres about 50 centimetres across with mating rims. Greased together and pumped empty, they were held shut by nothing but surrounding air pressing on their joint. On 8 May 1654, before the Imperial Diet and Emperor Ferdinand III at Regensburg, two teams of fifteen horses failed to pull them apart; once he opened a valve, they fell apart by hand.

tarikh-al-sudan-timbuktu-1655.summary: Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, a Timbuktu scholar and imam who served Arma administrators as secretary and envoy, finished his Tarikh al-Sudan in 1653 and revised it to 1656. In Arabic prose he ran a connected history from Ghana and Mali through the Songhay askiyas to the Moroccan conquest of 1591 and the pashas who followed, with biographies of Timbuktu and Jenne scholars and reports of famines, floods and prices. Paulo Fernando de Moraes Farias reads it, together with Ibn al-Mukhtar's Tarikh al-fattash of 1664, as a new genre invented to make sense of post-conquest politics and to unite Arma, askiya lineages and urban elites.

John Hunwick's annotated English translation of 1999 runs to 1613 and remains standard. Farias warns that both chronicles' early dynastic lists are unreliable and shaped by their authors' political aims. Anchor year 1655, where its narrative ends, sits between completion and revision.

huygens-pendulum-clock-1656.summary: In 1656 Huygens's pendulum clock cut a clock's drift from 15 minutes a day to 15 seconds. Galileo had noticed around 1602 that a pendulum's swing takes about equal time whatever its width, but no working clock had followed. Huygens contracted Salomon Coster of The Hague to build it and patented it in 1657; clockmakers rushed to fit pendulums to old verge-and-foliot movements. No timekeeper was more precise than pendulum clocks until the 1930s.

In Horologium Oscillatorium of 1673 Huygens showed that pendulums swinging on cycloids keep time regardless of amplitude.

royal-society-founded-1660.summary: In 1660 the Royal Society formed in London to settle questions by experiment; it still does. Robert Boyle wrote of an invisible college, John Wilkins ran his Philosophical Society at Wadham College, Oxford, and after the Restoration one circle met at Gresham College in London. On 28 November 1660 twelve of them resolved to found a college for promoting experimental learning. Charles II approved, and charters of 1662 and 1663 created the Royal Society of London for the Improvement of Natural Knowledge. Its motto, Nullius in verba, take nobody's word for it, stated its method.

royal-society-founded-1660.detail: Those twelve founders included Christopher Wren, Boyle, Wilkins, William Brouncker and Robert Moray. Charters came on 15 July 1662 and 23 April 1663, with Brouncker as president and Robert Hooke as Curator of Experiments. No scientific academy has existed longer without a break.

malpighi-capillaries-1661.summary: Harvey had argued in 1628 that blood must pass from arteries to veins, but he could not see how. Marcello Malpighi (1628 to 1694), a physician trained at Bologna and a friend of mathematician Giovanni Borelli, turned a new compound microscope on lung tissue and in 1661 described a network of fine vessels, capillaries, joining smallest arteries to veins. Blood, he showed, stays inside vessels throughout its circuit and is not turned into flesh in outlying tissues, as Galen had taught. Malpighi went on using microscopes for almost forty years on plant structure, embryos, human organs and diseased tissue, founding microscopic anatomy and making them a tool of medical research rather than a curiosity.

sources.author: Ribatti, Domenico

boyle-law-1662.summary: In 1662 Robert Boyle measured that halving a gas's volume doubles its pressure, an early exact law of nature. He pictured air as a fluid of particles at rest between tiny invisible springs, and set out to measure how it resists compression. Using a closed J-shaped glass tube built by his assistant Robert Hooke, he poured mercury into its long open arm and watched trapped air in its short sealed arm shrink; repeating with different amounts of mercury, he found that doubling pressure halved volume. He published this in 1662. Stated today, pressure times volume is constant for a fixed mass of gas at fixed temperature.

sources.title: Boyle's law - Wikipedia
West, John B., 'The original presentation of Boyle's law', Journal of Applied Physiology 87.4 (1999), pp. 1543-1545
sources.author: West, John B.
sources.confirms: Full text: Boyle's 1662 appendix reports J-tube data supporting the inverse pressure-volume relation.
sources.qualifies: West: Boyle framed it as a hypothesis checked against data, not as an exact law; Towneley suggested it.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Boyles law'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1662. The page says Boyle formulated the relation in 1662: for a given quantity of gas at constant temperature, pressure varies inversely with volume (\(pv=k\)).

boyle-law-1662.detail: His result confirmed what Richard Towneley and Henry Power had noted earlier in that century. Edme Mariotte found this relation independently in 1679 and added that temperature must stay constant, so France calls it Mariotte's law.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

descartes-treatise-on-man-1664.summary: In 1664 Descartes's Treatise on Man appeared in French, describing the body as a machine of pipes and valves; only our rational soul stands outside. It was published after his death, in Latin first in 1662. To avoid asking how God made us, it describes an imagined being like us. Food becomes blood in its liver; its heart pushes blood round, and blood's subtlest part is distilled in its pineal gland into fine flame, animal spirits. These spirits run through nerves as through pipes, inflating muscles like springs and valves.

descartes-treatise-on-man-1664.detail: Claude Clerselier edited that French edition in 106 numbered articles. Descartes likened spirits in nerves to water driving garden fountains; pain, in his account, is one nerve tugged, hunger liquor acting on an empty stomach.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

micrographia-1665.summary: In 1665 Robert Hooke published the first pictures of fleas and cork under a microscope, and named cells. Micrographia was the Royal Society's first major book. Hooke examined everything from razor edges to fly eyes, and in a sliver of cork saw walled compartments that reminded him of monks' cells; his word cell became biology's term for life's unit. Copperplate engravings fold out larger than its folio pages, one louse unfolding to four times book size, showing readers a world no one had seen. It became science's first best-seller and drew people to microscopy.

sources.confirms: 1665. The page says Hooke first used “cell” for the microscopic honeycomb cavities he observed in cork.

micrographia-1665.detail: Hooke also discussed distant planets, wave theory of light and fossils' organic origin. Samuel Pepys called it the most ingenious book he had ever read.

great-fire-of-london-1666.summary: In September 1666 fire destroyed 13,000 houses in London in four days; the city was rebuilt in brick with wider streets and fire insurance. London was still a medieval warren of narrow lanes and timber houses, and Lord Mayor Thomas Bloodworth hesitated to pull down buildings for firebreaks until a strong east wind had driven flames beyond control. By Wednesday they had consumed about 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral, leaving perhaps 70,000 of 80,000 residents homeless. London rose again on essentially its medieval street plan under a 1666 Act banning wood from exteriors.

great-fire-of-london-1666.detail: Dropping wind and gunpowder firebreaks laid by soldiers from the Tower finally stopped it. Only a handful of deaths were recorded, which some historians dispute. Christopher Wren, Robert Hooke and others proposed grid plans, all rejected; its Fire Court settled rebuilding disputes within a day, and Nicholas Barbon's Fire Office, history's first fire insurer, followed.

leibniz-de-arte-combinatoria-1666.summary: In 1666 the 19-year-old Leibniz proposed turning ideas into symbols and arguments into sums. Its governing idea, which he credited to Descartes, is an alphabet of human thought: every concept combines a small number of simple concepts, as words combine letters, so every truth can be expressed by combining concepts and analysed back into simples. Given any subject, one could then list every predicate fitting it, and in reverse. He later called it immature, yet it was his first step toward a universal characteristic, a language of ideas with a calculus for reasoning.

sources.author: Centrone, Stefania

sources.confirms: The page says the work was published in 1666. It partly confirms the general aim: Leibniz sought to reduce reasoning and discovery to combinations of basic elements.

leibniz-de-arte-combinatoria-1666.detail: Ramon Llull's Ars Magna inspired this, though Leibniz faulted Llull's arbitrary categories. He defined terms for permutations and for combinations of two, three or more elements, and prefaced it all with a geometrical proof of God from motion.

newton-reflecting-telescope-1668.summary: In 1668 Newton built a telescope with a mirror, not a lens, as great telescopes are built now. Refracting telescopes of his day smeared bright objects with coloured fringes. Isaac Newton, working out his theory of colour, concluded that lenses split white light into spectra just as his prisms did, so any telescope forming its image with a mirror would be free of this fault. In late 1668 he ground his 1.3-inch mirror of speculum metal, a tin-copper alloy, choosing a spherical curve for ease of making, and added a small flat mirror set diagonally to throw its image out to his eyepiece at the tube's side. He saw Jupiter's four moons and Venus's crescent without colour.

Mills, A. A.; Turvey, P. J., 'Newton's Telescope: An Examination of the Reflecting Telescope Attributed to Sir Isaac Newton', Notes and Records 33.2 (1979), pp. 133-155
sources.author: Mills, A. A.; Turvey, P. J.
sources.venue: Notes and Records of the Royal Society

sources.title: Newton, Isaac, letter on light and colours, Philosophical Transactions 6 (1672)

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'reflecting telescope'

sources.confirms: The page dates Newton’s reflecting telescope to 1668. It says Newton invented the reflecting telescope in 1668.

newton-reflecting-telescope-1668.detail:
Galileo and others had discussed mirrors, and James Gregory had published one design in 1663, but none had been made to work. Isaac Barrow showed a second instrument to the Royal Society late in 1671; Charles II saw it in January 1672 and Newton was elected a fellow.

Speculum tarnished soon and gave dim views, so reflectors spread slowly until John Hadley's parabolic mirror of 1721.

picture.credit: Science Museum, London, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

wilkins-real-character-1668.summary: In 1668 John Wilkins published a universal language in which each word's letters spelled out its place in a classification of the world. At the Royal Society's request in 1662, John Wilkins set out to design a replacement; his Essay of 1668 first sorts everything knowable into forty genera, each divided into differences and then species. Every word is then built from that classification: Zi is his genus of beasts, Zit dog-like rapacious beasts, Zitα dogs, so a word's letters state what it names. His written character gave each concept its own symbol independent of any spoken tongue. Interest soon faded.

sources.confirms: Title dates the Essay to 1668; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1668. The page confirms that John Wilkins’s Essay Towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language was published in 1668, but does not describe the classification scheme.

wilkins-real-character-1668.detail: Naturalists John Ray and Francis Willughby helped him, and London's Great Fire of 1666 destroyed part of his draft. His idea of symbols standing for concepts directly drew on mistaken European accounts of Chinese writing. Wilkins meant his scheme as an auxiliary to natural languages and, it is said, as proof of concept.

picture.alt: Title page of John Wilkins's 1668 Essay towards a universal character and a philosophical language, London.
picture.credit: John Wilkins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

song-iyeong-armillary-clock-1669.summary: In 1669, tenth year of King Hyeonjong, Song I-yeong (1619 to 1692), professor of astronomy at Joseon's Bureau of Astronomy (Gwansanggam), completes an armillary clock for the Hongmungwan: a traditional Korean armillary sphere about 40 cm across, turned by a weight-driven clock movement built on a Western alarm clock's principle, inside a wooden case 99 cm high and 118.5 cm long. One weight drives the time wheel, regulated by a pendulum and escapement, and shows hours on a plaque at a window; a second weight strikes a bell through a bead-signal mechanism. It is East Asia's only surviving armillary clock, designated National Treasure No. 230 in 1985 and held by Korea University Museum, and its pendulum regulation shows a European invention of 1656 reaching Korea within a generation.

sources.venue: Journal of Astronomy and Space Sciences
sources.confirms: Abstract read: National Treasure No. 230 at Korea University Museum; the only surviving armillary clock in East Asia; not working because parts are broken or missing; authors measured it and rebuilt a working model of the solar and lunar drives.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies), 'Honcheonui mit honcheonsigye' (Armillary sphere and armillary clock)
sources.author: Academy of Korean Studies

song-iyeong-armillary-clock-1669.verification_note: Its 1669 date, maker, mechanism, designation and museum are confirmed by all three sources. A link to Huygens's pendulum of 1656 is inferred from pendulum and escapement described by Encyclopedia of Korean Culture; Springer's entry speaks only of a Western alarm-clock weight drive.
song-iyeong-armillary-clock-1669.detail: Records show it repaired in 1687 to 1688; it then vanishes from records until businessman Kim Seong-su bought it in an Insa-dong antique shop in the early 1930s and gave it to his university's museum. Lee and Kim's 2007 study measured surviving parts and rebuilt a working model of its sun and moon drives. Korea had made armillary spheres since Sejong's reign, and Jang Yeong-sil's self-striking water clock of 1434 is its ancestor.

hudsons-bay-company-1670.summary: In 1670 Charles II chartered the Hudson's Bay Company with a monopoly over a third of Canada; a company governed a territory for 200 years. In 1668 to 1669 their ketch Nonsuch wintered at James Bay and came home with furs that sold for £1,233, proving this trade. On 2 May 1670 Charles II chartered the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay, with Rupert as first governor. Its charter granted sole trade over lands draining into Hudson Strait not already held by another Christian power, about 3.9 million square kilometres named Rupert's Land. That monopoly lasted two centuries.

sources.title: Hudson's Bay Company - Wikipedia
The Royal Charter for incorporating The Hudson's Bay Company, A.D. May 2, 1670.
Agency Problems in Early Chartered Companies: The Case of the Hudson's Bay Company
sources.author: Carlos, Ann M.; Nicholas, Stephen
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of the Hudson's Bay Company as a chartered company founded in 1670, drawing on Rich's history of the company 1670-1870.

sources.title: Hudson's Bay Company
sources.author: Canadian Encyclopedia (Historica Canada)
sources.confirms: Charter granted 2 May 1670 after the Nonsuch voyage dispatched in June 1668; the company is the oldest incorporated joint-stock merchandising company in the English-speaking world.

hudsons-bay-company-1670.detail: Nonsuch's crew built Charles Fort at the Rupert River. Its charter's words covered sole trade and commerce of all seas, bays, rivers and lands within Hudson Strait, plus fishing and mines. In 1870 the company surrendered Rupert's Land to Canada for £300,000 and one twentieth of farmland opened for settlement.

leibniz-stepped-reckoner-1673.summary: In 1673 Leibniz showed a multiplying machine; its stepped drum ran calculators for 300 years. He had conceived it in Paris in 1672 after seeing pedometers at work, then read of Pascal's calculator and resolved to go beyond addition. On 1 February 1673 he showed a wooden model to London's Royal Society. Its heart was a cylinder with nine teeth of increasing length, now called a stepped drum or Leibniz wheel: sliding a gear along it sets one digit, and each crank turn adds that whole number to its 16-digit accumulator, so repeated turns multiply. Brass prototypes never worked reliably, yet stepped drums drove calculating machines for two centuries.

sources.title: Stepped reckoner - Wikipedia
Leibniz, G. W., letter to the Royal Society, 1 June 1673, in Leibniz Samtliche Schriften (De Gruyter), pp. 95-96
sources.author: Leibniz, Gottfried Wilhelm
sources.confirms: Letter of 1 June 1673 promises the finished machine ('machinam mox dabimus absolutam') after the London showing.
sources.qualifies: Leibniz's letter shows the machine still unfinished in June 1673; the record gives 1 February 1673 for the wooden model.

sources.title: Jones, Matthew L., 'Calculating Machine', in The Oxford Handbook of Leibniz (Oxford, 2018), pp. 509-525
sources.author: Jones, Matthew L.
sources.confirms: Chapter abstract: Leibniz worked on the machine for decades.

sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors

leibniz-stepped-reckoner-1673.verification_note: 1673 London presentation of a model is consistent with Leibniz's own June 1673 letter; Jones (Oxford Handbook) finds that no adequately working machine was ever produced.
leibniz-stepped-reckoner-1673.detail: Shifting its carriage one place multiplies by ten, and division runs in reverse by repeated subtraction. Prototypes built between 1674 and 1694 failed because such gearwork exceeded contemporary craftsmanship and their carry mechanism was flawed; of two built, one survives in Hanover. Stepped drums were still at work in 1970s Curta hand calculators.

verbiest-beijing-observatory-1673.summary: In 1673 the Jesuit Verbiest re-equipped Beijing's observatory, and Jesuits ran China's calendar for a century. It reported celestial movements to emperors, who as Sons of Heaven treated them as affairs of state, and aided sea navigation with Muslim scholars recruited for their expertise. In the mid-17th century Flemish Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest won an astronomy contest and was given complete charge of it by Emperor Kangxi's court. In 1673 he supervised rebuilding some of its instruments, and he and other Jesuits advanced its observations of stars and planets. Bronze instruments still stand on its platform.

ribbon-loom-riots-1675.summary: In 1675 London's silk weavers smashed looms that wove several ribbons at once, an early riot against machines. Silk weaving was East London's staple trade, done at home on handlooms for piece rates. From 1616 weavers fought the Dutch engine loom, which used multiple shuttles to weave several ribbons or tapes at once; since outsiders ran these looms, masters and journeymen of London's Weavers' Company found common cause in keeping them out. Machine looms began replacing handlooms for ribbon in the 1660s. In August 1675 bands of weavers roamed London for three days, smashing engine looms or burning them in the streets. Soldiers put down this riot, but full mechanisation of Spitalfields silk was delayed about a century.

ribbon-loom-riots-1675.detail: The Weavers' Company petitioned against engine looms. Dozens of bands took part; rioters also attacked French weavers accused of taking work, and some wore green aprons, once Leveller colours, alarming a government fearful of republican plots, though it soon saw their grievances were economic. Parliament and government favoured engine looms even so.

leeuwenhoek-microorganisms-1676.summary: In 1676 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek reported living creatures in a drop of water, a world no one knew existed. He had taken up lens grinding to inspect thread more closely than shop magnifiers allowed; his microscopes were single tiny glass beads held in silver or copper frames, some magnifying about 275 times. He met scepticism even so, and at his insistence the Royal Society had Delft ministers and other witnesses look for themselves; in 1677 it accepted his findings. He was later first to document bacteria, spermatozoa and red blood cells.

leeuwenhoek-microorganisms-1676.detail: He wrote only in colloquial Dutch; Henry Oldenburg translated his letters for London's Royal Society and coined their word animalcules for creatures he described. It elected him a fellow in 1680, and he was also first to document blood flowing in capillaries.

hortus-malabaricus-1678.summary: Between 1678 and 1693 Amsterdam printers issued twelve folio volumes of Hortus Indicus Malabaricus, describing 742 plants of Malabar coast with 794 copperplate engravings. Dutch governor Hendrik van Rheede organised it in Cochin, but plant knowledge came from Itty Achuden, an Ezhava physician, three Konkani Brahmin scholars (Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit, Appu Bhat) and a Carmelite friar. Names appear in Malayalam, Konkani, Arabic and Latin scripts. Local collectors brought specimens, and artists drew them from life. Linnaeus drew on this work for South Asian species. It remains a reference for Kerala ethnobotany, and Kerala University published a full English translation in 2003.

Heniger's monograph on Van Rheede and Hortus Malabaricus details Itty Achuden's certificate and Brahmin contributors. Biodiversity Heritage Library holds scans of original volumes.

papin-steam-digester-1679.summary: In 1679 Denis Papin built a pressure cooker with a safety valve, the first control of steam. The French Huguenot physician had worked with Christiaan Huygens in Paris on using vacuum for motive power before moving to London in 1675 to assist Robert Boyle. Between 1676 and 1679 he invented his steam digester, a tightly sealed vessel in which steam built up pressure, raising water's boiling point so that bones softened and tough food cooked through; a weighted safety valve, his own invention, let excess steam escape before it burst. Watching atmospheric pressure act on his digester, he built in 1690 a model piston steam engine, first of its kind.

dockwra-penny-post-1680.summary: In 1680 London got a penny post with several deliveries a day, cheap enough for anyone to write to anyone. London held about half a million people, yet its General Post Office carried only letters leaving town; within it, people paid porters and private couriers. William Dockwra, a customs officer, and Robert Murray, an excise clerk, opened their London Penny Post on 27 March 1680: any letter or packet up to one pound, anywhere in town or suburbs, for one penny paid in advance. Seven districts each had a sorting office, with hourly collections and up to ten deliveries daily in central districts. In 1682 (Britannica says 1683) Crown officials took it over after legal action in James, Duke of York's interest; he held Post Office revenues under a Crown monopoly dating from 1635.

sources.author: Graveson, S.
sources.venue: Journal of the Friends Historical Society

dockwra-penny-post-1680.verification_note: Graveson dates this Crown takeover to 1682 and Britannica to 1683, after legal action in James, Duke of York's interest as holder of Post Office revenues; that postal monopoly had been Crown property since 1635.
dockwra-penny-post-1680.detail: Hundreds of receiving houses took in letters, and delivery within four hours was guaranteed. Each item was hand-stamped to show postage paid, with a heart-shaped mark giving its time, history's first postmarks. Porters attacked its messengers, and Murray was jailed for circulating tracts against the Duke of York, who drew Post Office profits. Afterwards Crown officials ran it as their own Penny Post.

pueblo-revolt-horses-1680.summary: In 1680 Pueblo peoples drove Spain from New Mexico, and horses left behind sped a Plains horse culture already under way. Spanish friars had outlawed Kachina dances and burned Pueblo masks and prayer sticks, and drought and Apache raids in the 1670s brought famine. Po'pay, a religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh who had been flogged and jailed, united two dozen pueblos speaking six languages. Runners carried knotted cords counting down to rising day; it began on 10 August 1680, with Puebloans seizing Spanish horses so colonists could not flee. Some 400 colonists died and 2,000 escaped south; Spain did not return until 1692. Historians long held that Pueblos then sold thousands of Spanish horses along Indigenous trade routes.

sources.title: Pueblo Revolt - Wikipedia
Horse nations
W. T. T. Taylor et al., 'Early dispersal of domestic horses into the Great Plains and northern Rockies', Science 379 (2023), 1316-1323
sources.author: William Timothy Treal Taylor et al.
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and genomic data show Spanish-descended horses integrated into Indigenous societies in the Rockies and Plains by the first half of the 1600s.
sources.qualifies: Dispersal began before the 1680 Pueblo Revolt.

pueblo-revolt-horses-1680.verification_note: Taylor et al. (Science 2023) show horses of Spanish descent in northern Rockies and central Plains sites before 1650, so this 1680 revolt accelerated a spread already begun.
pueblo-revolt-horses-1680.detail: When two runners were caught and tortured, it began early. In that older account horses reached northwestern Plains peoples by the 1730s; radiocarbon dating published in Science in 2023 showed Plains and Rocky Mountain peoples already keeping and riding horses by 1650, so this revolt sped a spread begun generations earlier.

canal-du-midi-1681.summary: In May 1681 the Canal du Midi opens between Toulouse and the Mediterranean, 240 km of waterway that Pierre-Paul Riquet, a Languedoc tax farmer, had begun in 1667 under a licence from Louis XIV and Colbert. Riquet died eight months before it opened. It climbs 63 metres through 26 locks to its summit at Naurouze and descends 189 metres through 74 more, fed by Montagne Noire reservoirs and passing through the first canal tunnel, at Malpas. UNESCO lists 328 structures along 360 navigable km. Chandra Mukerji's Princeton study argues Riquet's project drew on tacit knowledge of local women and peasant engineers as much as on court mathematics.

Riquet put much of his own fortune into construction and died in debt; his family recovered that investment from tolls over following decades, and grain, wine and passengers moved on it until a Bordeaux to Sete railway took its traffic in the 1850s.

seki-takakazu-1683.summary: In 1683 Seki Takakazu found determinants in Japan, ten years before Leibniz and apart from him. In 1683, in Kaifukudai no Hō, he attacked elimination theory: given several equations in several unknowns, how to combine them into one equation in one unknown, whose roots numerical methods could then find. That combining quantity is called a resultant, and to express it he developed his notion of determinant. His formula for 5×5 cases was wrong, giving zero in each case; a correct general formula appears in Taisei Sankei.

Majima, Hideyuki, 'Seki Takakazu, His Life and Bibliography', in Seki, Founder of Modern Mathematics in Japan (Springer, 2013), pp. 3-20
sources.author: Majima, Hideyuki

seki-takakazu-1683.detail: Taisei Sankei was written with Takebe Katahiro and his brothers between 1683 and 1710. Tanaka and Izeki reached similar ideas independently in Japan. Leibniz's first notes on determinants, of these same years, went only to 3×3, and Europe forgot them until Cramer in 1750.

picture.credit: Momotarou2012, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

lopburi-eclipse-observatory-1685.summary: On 11 December 1685, at Thale Chup Son outside Lopburi, six French Jesuit mathematicians who had arrived with Chevalier de Chaumont's embassy set up telescopes in a gallery while King Narai of Ayutthaya observed a lunar eclipse from an adjoining room, asking about moon's surface and timing. Fr Guy Tachard's account records a five-foot telescope offered to king and his permission for Jesuits to stand in his presence. Narai then funded an observatory at Wat San Paolo in Lopburi, and on 30 April 1688 watched a partial solar eclipse with Jesuits there weeks before Phetracha's coup ended French presence. Michael Smithies' 2003 study collates these accounts and their images.

sources.author: Smithies, Michael

sources.author: UNESCO/IAU Portal to the Heritage of Astronomy
sources.confirms: Jesuits arrived 1685; lunar eclipse 1685; observatory at Lopburi

lopburi-eclipse-observatory-1685.detail: Jesuit observations of this eclipse, compared with Paris timings, helped fix Siam's longitude. Fontaney, Bouvet, Gerbillon, Le Comte, Visdelou and Tachard continued to Beijing and served Kangxi's court. UNESCO's astronomical heritage portal lists Lopburi observatory ruins and both eclipses.

picture.credit: C. Vermeleun, in Guy Tachard, Voyage de Siam (1686)

enlightenment-era-1687.summary: From about 1687 Enlightenment thinkers argued that reason and evidence, not kings or churches, should rule. Its thinkers held that reason and evidence, not inherited authority, should settle what people believe and how they are governed; Kant summed up its spirit as dare to know. From that starting point they argued for individual liberty, representative government, rule of law and religious freedom, and for progress through science. Both revolutions of its closing decades, American and French, drew on its arguments.

sources.title: Age of Enlightenment - Wikipedia
Outram, Dorinda, The Enlightenment, 4th ed. (Cambridge, 2019)

enlightenment-era-1687.detail: Ideas travelled through scientific academies, salons, coffeehouses and cheap print, provoking Counter-Enlightenment defences of faith and tradition.

picture.credit: Joseph Wright of Derby, Derby Museum and Art Gallery, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

newton-principia-1687.summary: In 1687 Newton's Principia showed one gravity moves apples and planets: the universe had rules. It began in 1684, when Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke were debating whether an attraction falling off with distance squared would produce Kepler's orbits. Halley took that question to Newton at Cambridge, found he had already worked it out, and pressed him to write it up; a short De motu grew into Principia's three books.

sources.title: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica - Wikipedia

sources.author: Newton, Isaac
sources.confirms: Original 1687 first edition.

newton-principia-1687.detail: Samuel Pepys, as Royal Society president, licensed it in July 1686. Newton proved his results geometrically, keeping his calculus methods out of sight, and in later editions declined to speculate on gravity's cause: hypotheses non fingo. Revised editions followed in 1713 and 1726.

lloyds-coffee-house-1689.summary: Around 1689 Edward Lloyd's coffee house became the place where shipowners found men to insure their voyages; it is now Lloyd's of London. Sailors, merchants and shipowners met there because Lloyd supplied reliable shipping news, and customers began wagering on whether particular ships would come home. Those bets grew into marine insurance: merchants seeking cover found underwriters willing to take a share of each ship's risk for a premium. Much of what was insured was Britain's slave trade; Lloyd's covered slave ships and their human cargo in what Eric Williams described as a near monopoly until abolition in 1807.

sources.title: Lloyd's of London

lloyds-coffee-house-1689.detail: After Christmas 1691 Lloyd moved to 16 Lombard Street, where business continued after his death in 1713. In 1773 John Julius Angerstein took rooms at London's Royal Exchange for his Society of Lloyd's, and Parliament's Act of 1871 incorporated it.

bank-of-england-1694.summary: In 1694 the Bank of England was founded to lend the state money for war: England's national debt. After losing to France at Beachy Head in 1690, England's new regime under William III needed money to rebuild its fleet, and its credit was poor. William Paterson had proposed in 1691 that lenders form a company and lend their capital to the crown; Charles Montagu steered that scheme through Parliament. Under the Tonnage Act of 1694 subscribers lent £1.2 million at 8 per cent interest, with duties on ship tonnage, beer and ale pledged to pay it. That sum was raised in twelve days by 1,268 people, and it received its charter on 27 July 1694.

sources.title: Bank of England
Bowen, H. V., 'The Bank of England during the Long Eighteenth Century, 1694-1820', in The Bank of England: Money, Power and Influence 1694-1994 (Oxford, 1995), pp. 1-18
sources.author: Bowen, H. V.
sources.confirms: Chapter abstract dates the founding to 1694.
sources.qualifies: Bowen: the Bank was not established as a modern central bank; it was a private lender to the state.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bank of England'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors

bank-of-england-1694.detail: Terms included a £4,000 management fee, and no one could subscribe more than £10,000; roughly one in eight subscribers were women. It served as government banker and debt manager, moved to Threadneedle Street in 1734, gained sole right to issue banknotes in England and Wales, and remained privately owned until nationalisation in 1946.

minas-gerais-gold-rush-1695.summary: Between 1693 and 1695 bandeirantes from São Paulo panned gold in streams draining Serra do Espinhaço, in what became Minas Gerais. Tens of thousands of Portuguese migrants and enslaved Africans followed, founding Vila Rica (Ouro Preto), Sabará and Mariana. Miners worked gravel beds with bateia pans, diverted rivers, and later cut hillsides with water channels; Portugal's Crown took a fifth and built smelting houses to stamp bars. Charles Boxer's study calculates Brazilian output at roughly 10 to 15 tonnes a year at its 1750s peak, much of it passing through Lisbon to London. Diamonds found near Tijuco in 1729 added a second monopoly. Gold shifted Brazil's centre from its sugar coast to its interior and moved Brazil's capital to Rio de Janeiro in 1763.

sources.title: Boxer, C. R., 'The Gold Rush in Minas Gerais', in The Golden Age of Brazil, 1695-1750 (University of California Press, 1962), ch. 2
sources.author: Boxer, C. R.
sources.confirms: Discovery in the 1690s, rush migration, Crown fifth and output estimates.

sources.title: Bergad, Laird W., Slavery and the Demographic and Economic History of Minas Gerais, Brazil, 1720-1888 (Cambridge University Press, 1999), ch. 2
sources.author: Bergad, Laird W.
sources.confirms: Slave population growth and the regional economy during and after the gold cycle.

sources.title: Boxer, C. R., The Golden Age of Brazil, 1695-1750: Growing Pains of a Colonial Society (University of California Press, 1962), full text
sources.author: Boxer, C. R.
sources.confirms: Digitised full text for chapter references on mining methods and the diamond district.

minas-gerais-gold-rush-1695.verification_note: Discovery dates range from 1693 to 1695 depending on which strike is counted; peak output estimates differ (Boxer gives about 10 to 15 tonnes a year in the 1750s, others higher).
minas-gerais-gold-rush-1695.detail: Laird Bergad's economic history of Minas Gerais shows a slave population exceeding 100,000 by 1735 and a regional economy of food farming and mule trains that outlived gold. Output fell steeply after 1760 as alluvial deposits ran out and deep ores resisted colonial technology; British companies reopened Gongo Soco and Morro Velho mines with steam pumps from 1824 onward.

picture.credit: Johann Moritz Rugendas, via Wikimedia Commons

savery-steam-pump-1698.summary: On 2 July 1698 Thomas Savery patented a steam pump to drain mines, the first steam engine sold. It had no piston. Steam filled its vessel, cold water poured over its outside condensed it, and vacuum sucked water up a suction pipe; fresh steam then forced that water up a delivery pipe, and this cycle repeated. Four faults limited it: heat was wasted at every cycle, soldered joints burst under pressure, and suction lifted water only about 30 feet, so pumps worked in series, deep inside their mines.

savery-steam-pump-1698.detail: Savery demonstrated it to the Royal Society in June 1699 and described it in his Miner's Friend of 1702. Parliament's Fire Engine Act of 1699 extended his patent to 1733 and made it cover any engine raising water by fire, which later obliged Thomas Newcomen to work under Savery's grant.

picture.credit: Thomas Savery, The Miner's Friend (1702), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

calico-acts-1700.summary: In 1700 England banned Indian printed cotton to protect its weavers, which pushed Britain to make its own. An act of 1698, often dated 1700 (11 Will. 3 c. 10), barred imports of printed cottons from India, Persia and China but set no penalty for selling them, so smuggled cloth kept arriving. A second act in 1721 banned sale and use of almost all cotton textiles, imported or home-made, exempting thread fustian and raw cotton. That exemption nurtured Lancashire's fustian trade, whose mill owners won repeal in 1774.

calico-acts-1700.detail: Imports of raw cotton grew from about 2,000 bales yearly to 7,000 by the 1770s, and fustian making encouraged mechanised spinning. After repeal, demand for raw cotton doubled within a few years. Fustian mixed cotton weft with linen warp.

dhaka-muslin-weaving-1700.summary: Around Dhaka in Bengal, spinners worked phuti karpas, a short staple cotton grown on Meghna river banks, in humid early morning hours to draw thread finer than any machine would match until nineteenth century. Weavers on pit looms produced muslins so sheer that Mughal court names called them woven air and running water. Sixteen separate specialist crafts handled ginning, bowing, spinning, warping, weaving, washing and embroidery. Mughal karkhanas took finest grades as tribute; Dutch and English companies exported bulk grades to Europe and West Asia. Machine spun yarn from Lancashire and loss of court patronage collapsed this trade after 1820, and phuti karpas went extinct as a crop.

dhaka-muslin-weaving-1700.detail: Riello's Cambridge study of cotton situates Bengal muslin within global textile competition and explains why European mechanisation targeted Indian quality. Marshall's volume on eighteenth century Bengal documents company purchases and weaver conditions. Victoria and Albert Museum holds dated muslin samples. Thread counts quoted for best pieces range from 300 to over 1000 in later accounts and are not standardised.

guarani-mission-press-loreto-1700.summary: In 1700 Jesuit missionaries Juan Bautista Neumann and José Serrano, with Guaraní metalworkers and carpenters of Paraguay's reductions, assembled a printing press of local manufacture at Loreto, on upper Paraná riverbanks, and printed a Spanish Martirologio romano. No press had operated in Río de la Plata lands before. In 1705 it issued Nieremberg's De la diferencia entre lo temporal y eterno translated into Guaraní, a volume of more than 400 pages with 43 full-page copperplate engravings cut by Guaraní artisans including Juan Yaparí. Later imprints included Ruiz de Montoya's Guaraní vocabulary (1722) and grammar (1724). Printing continued until 1727; roughly half its known titles survive in libraries worldwide.

sources.title: Hendrickson, D. Scott, 'Early Guaraní Printing: Nieremberg's De la diferencia and the Global Dissemination of Seventeenth-Century Spanish Asceticism', Journal of Jesuit Studies 5 (2018)
sources.author: Hendrickson, D. Scott
sources.confirms: Press inaugurated in 1700 with the Martirologio, the 1705 Guaraní Nieremberg and the role of Guaraní craftsmen.

sources.author: Neumann, Eduardo
sources.confirms: Mission organisation, Guaraní literacy and the press within reduction life.

sources.title: Wilde, Guillermo, 'Jesuit Missions and the Guaraní Ethnogenesis', in Big Water: The Making of the Borderlands Between Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay (University of Arizona Press, 2018)
sources.author: Wilde, Guillermo
sources.confirms: Guaraní participation in mission crafts and textual culture.

guarani-mission-press-loreto-1700.detail: D. Scott Hendrickson's 2018 study situates this 1705 imprint in Jesuit book networks and credits Guaraní craftsmen with type-casting, presswork and engraving. Guillermo Wilde's work on mission print culture shows books circulating among reductions and Jesuit colleges. Type was cast from tin and lead available locally; paper came from Europe. After Jesuit expulsion in 1767 it disappears from inventories.

macassan-trepang-arnhem-land-1700.summary: Each December, fleets of praus from Makassar in Sulawesi rode northwest monsoon winds to Marege, their name for Arnhem Land coast, to gather and process trepang (sea cucumber) for Chinese markets. Crews built stone hearths and smokehouses, boiled trepang in iron cauldrons and dried it over fires, sometimes with Yolngu labour. Macknight's fieldwork and reading of Dutch records dated industry's beginning to about 1700 or soon after, with up to 1,000 men visiting yearly by early 1800s. Yolngu people gained iron blades, dugout canoe designs, cloth, tobacco and loanwords such as rupiah and balanda, and recorded praus in bark paintings and song cycles. South Australian government licensing ended voyages in 1907.

sources.author: Macknight, Campbell C.

sources.qualifies: Start date inferred from Dutch records

sources.qualifies: Author revises some earlier conclusions

macassan-trepang-arnhem-land-1700.detail: Trepang sites with tamarind trees, stone lines and pottery sherds dot Arnhem Land and Kimberley coasts. Macknight's 1972 Oceania paper and later work argued for an eighteenth-century start; some radiocarbon dates on beeswax and rock art hint at earlier contact, which Macknight treats cautiously. This exchange preceded British settlement by a century and connected Aboriginal Australians to Asian commerce. Yolngu artists still depict praus and Makassar figures.

new-guinea-highlands-sweet-potato-1700.summary: Sweet potato reached New Guinea's interior sometime after Portuguese and Spanish ships introduced it to eastern Indonesia in sixteenth century, passing from garden to garden along trade routes. In Wahgi valley at Kuk Swamp, Golson's team found a sixth phase of drainage ditches linked to sweet potato cultivation and dated to about 1700 or a little earlier. Unlike taro, sweet potato tolerates poor soils, altitude up to 2,700 metres and short fallows, and makes good pig fodder. Highlanders responded by expanding settlement into higher valleys and building up pig herds for ceremonial exchange. Direct dating puts charred sweet potato at Nombe rockshelter at roughly 1750 to 1800.

sources.title: Bayliss-Smith, Tim; Golson, Jack; Hughes, Philip, 'Phase 6: impact of the sweet potato on swamp landuse, pig rearing and exchange relations', in Ten Thousand Years of Cultivation at Kuk Swamp (ANU Press, 2017)
sources.author: Bayliss-Smith, Tim; Golson, Jack; Hughes, Philip

sources.qualifies: Date of first arrival remains inferred

sources.qualifies: Argues narrative shaped interpretation

new-guinea-highlands-sweet-potato-1700.detail: Watson's 1965 'Ipomoean revolution' hypothesis held that sweet potato transformed highland societies; Chris Ballard argues this narrative shaped archaeological interpretation. Some scholars argue populations were already large and sweet potato intensified rather than created exchange systems. Kuk's earlier phases, dated back 7,000 to 10,000 years, make this swamp a centre of independent agricultural origins; Phase 6 marks its last and most extensive drainage network before abandonment.

tull-seed-drill-1701.summary: In 1701 Jethro Tull's drill sowed seed in even rows, so crops could be hoed and less wasted. Farmers had sown by scattering seed over ploughed ground, which wasted grain and left plants too crowded to hoe. Jethro Tull, a Berkshire farmer frustrated by servants who refused his ways of working, built a horse-drawn drill in 1701 that dropped seed from a hopper through a grooved rotating cylinder into a furrow at even depth and spacing, then covered it. Straight rows let him hoe between plants with a horse-drawn hoe to pulverise soil and kill weeds. Other drills had been tried before his; Tull's reputation rests on making one that worked and on pairing it with row cultivation.

tull-seed-drill-1701.detail: He had seen vine-dressers in southern France hoe between rows. His Horse-hoeing Husbandry of 1731 spread both ideas, though it also argued, wrongly, that pulverised soil made manure unnecessary.

leibniz-binary-i-ching-1703.summary: In 1703 Leibniz explained counting with only 0 and 1, the binary arithmetic every computer runs on. His Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire showed how each place stands for a power of two and how to add and multiply in that notation. Leibniz saw more in it than a curiosity: for him 1 and 0 pictured God creating everything from nothing. In 1700 he described his notation to Joachim Bouvet, a Jesuit in China steeped in the I Ching, who replied that its 64 hexagrams, read with broken lines as 0 and solid lines as 1, already ran from 0 to 63 in binary order.

sources.author: Strickland, Lloyd; Lewis, Harry
sources.confirms: Open-access edition; chapter 30 prints the Explication text dated 7 April 1703 with the I Ching correspondence.

leibniz-binary-i-ching-1703.detail: Leibniz treated Bouvet's hexagram order as parallel discovery, attributed to Fu Xi. Thomas Harriot had explored such systems a century earlier without publishing, and John Napier's location arithmetic of 1617 did binary sums with letters. Leibniz tied binary to his dream of a universal characteristic, his formal language for reasoning that George Boole and Gottlob Frege later took up.

boston-news-letter-1704.summary: On 24 April 1704 John Campbell, Boston's postmaster and a bookseller, sold his first weekly Boston News-Letter, the first newspaper in America to last: one small sheet printed on both sides, filled with news lifted from London journals. For over a year he had been sending handwritten newsletters of European events to New England's governors; to save himself trouble he had printer Bartholomew Green set them in type. Publick Occurrences had been shut down after a single issue in 1690; Campbell avoided that fate because its royal governor approved every copy before it appeared. Loyalist to the end, it closed when British troops left Boston in March 1776.

boston-news-letter-1704.detail: His paper was heavily subsidised. Under Green and then Boston's Draper family it grew to four pages of colonial news. Three copies and a fragment of its first issue survive.

darby-coke-smelting-1709.summary: In 1709 Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke, not charcoal, freeing iron from the forests. Iron furnaces had burned charcoal, and woodland could not supply enough; raw coal was plentiful but its sulphur made iron brittle. Abraham Darby, a Quaker who had worked malt mills and brass in Bristol, leased an old furnace at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire and in January 1709 blew it in with coke, coal baked to drive off its impurities, much as maltsters had long roasted barley. Coke-smelted iron suited his thin-walled castings, so he sold cheap pots and kettles, though it was poorer for working into wrought iron. Coke eventually freed iron-making from forests and let furnaces grow.

darby-coke-smelting-1709.detail: Darby had patented sand-casting of iron pots in 1707. Local clod coal was low in sulphur, which helped. Other ironmasters stayed with charcoal for decades; his son Abraham Darby II built further coke furnaces in the 1750s.

statute-of-anne-1710.summary: In 1710 Britain's Statute of Anne, in force from 10 April, gave whoever held a book's copy 14 years' exclusive rights from publication, renewable for 14 more if its author lived, and 21 years for books already in print; afterwards works passed to public use. Lyman Ray Patterson (Copyright in Historical Perspective, Vanderbilt, 1968) read it as trade regulation rather than an authors' charter or England's first copyright act: the Licensing Act, which gave Stationers' Company members perpetual rights in registered books, lapsed in the mid-1690s, leaving booksellers in chaos. London booksellers lobbied for protection and got limited terms. Britannica credits it with recognising authors as copyright's primary beneficiaries and limited duration, a model for Britain, its colonies and America.

sources.title: Statute of Anne
Patterson, Lyman Ray, 'The Statute of Anne', in Copyright in Historical Perspective (Vanderbilt, 1968), pp. 143-150
sources.author: Patterson, Lyman Ray
