statute-of-anne-1710.detail: Owners had to register titles with Stationers' Company and deposit copies for named libraries. London booksellers argued for decades that common law still gave them perpetual rights; in Donaldson v Becket in 1774 Britain's House of Lords ruled against them.

java-coffee-priangan-1711.summary: Coffee seedlings from Malabar planted around Batavia in 1696 and 1699 bore enough fruit for Dutch East India Company (VOC) to send a first commercial shipment to Amsterdam in 1711. Within a decade Priangan regents in West Java's highlands were obliged to deliver fixed quotas at prices set by company, a system Jan Breman calls forced cultivation under indirect rule. Java supplied most of Europe's coffee by 1720s and broke Mocha's monopoly. Compulsory deliveries and village labour burdens set patterns later formalised in nineteenth-century Cultivation System, and Javanese smallholders carried risks of price swings and leaf rust that reached Java in 1876.

sources.title: Breman, Jan, Mobilizing Labour for the Global Coffee Market: Profits from an Unfree Work Regime in Colonial Java (Amsterdam: Amsterdam University Press, 2015)
sources.author: Breman, Jan
sources.confirms: VOC coffee cultivation in Priangan from early 18th century; forced deliveries through regents

sources.confirms: University-press survey of coffee's global spread from 1500 including the Dutch move of cultivation to Java; chapter page would not open, record confirmed through Crossref.

sources.author: Breman, Jan
sources.confirms: Abstract states coffee was grown on Java for the commercial market from the early eighteenth century when the VOC began buying from peasant producers in the Priangan highlands, a trade that became forced cultivation.

java-coffee-priangan-1711.detail: Breman's 2015 study (Mobilizing Labour for the Global Coffee Market) documents Priangan quotas, regent intermediaries and coercion in VOC coffee. VOC records give 1711 for first auctioned Java coffee; some accounts cite 1712 for larger shipments. Arabica trees from this stock reached Suriname and Caribbean via Amsterdam.

newcomen-engine-1712.summary: In 1712 Newcomen's engine pumped out a flooded coal mine, the first steam engine in daily use. Newcomen, an ironmonger from Dartmouth, built it with his partner John Calley at Conygree, Tipton, on Lord Dudley's land. Denis Papin had shown in 1690 that steam condensing under a piston let air pressure drive it down; Newcomen made that idea work at mine scale, under Thomas Savery's patent. Low-pressure steam filled his brass cylinder beneath its piston; cold water sprayed in condensed it, and air pressure pushed that piston down, rocking its great beam to lift pump rods.

Allen, J. S., 'The 1712 and other Newcomen engines of the Earls of Dudley', Transactions of the Newcomen Society 69 (1997)
sources.author: Allen, John S.
sources.confirms: Abstract dates the first Newcomen engine to 1712 at the Dudley estates.

sources.author: Andrew, Jim; Allen, John S.
sources.venue: International Journal for the History of Engineering and Technology
sources.confirms: Abstract: first successful engine at Coneygree Coalworks near Tipton, 1712.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Thomas Newcomen'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors

newcomen-engine-1712.detail: Pump rods hung in the mine shaft from that beam's far end. Steam from his boiler then re-entered, the rods' weight pulled its beam back, and so on, about twelve strokes each minute. Wasteful of coal, it suited collieries with fuel to spare, and hundreds were built across Britain and Europe before James Watt improved on it.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

longitude-act-1714.summary: In 1714 Britain offered £20,000 to anyone who could find longitude at sea, after four Royal Navy ships ran onto rocks off Scilly in 1707 and drowned nearly 2,000 men. Latitude could be read from the sun or stars, but longitude depended on dead reckoning, and on long voyages that guesswork killed; petitions from merchants and sailors pushed Parliament to act. The Longitude Act, given royal assent on 9 July 1714, offered £10,000 for any practical method accurate within one degree, £15,000 within 40 minutes of arc and £20,000 within half a degree. A Board of Longitude judged claims for 114 years; clockmaker John Harrison received more than any other claimant.

Mobbs, Paul; Unwin, Robert, 'The Longitude Act of 1714 and its Origins', Parliamentary History 35.2 (2016), pp. 152-170
sources.author: Mobbs, Paul; Unwin, Robert
sources.confirms: Abstract confirms the 1714 Act and its rewards.
sources.qualifies: Authors find the Act's origins multicausal; the 1707 Scilly wreck alone did not prompt it.

Harrison's marine timekeepers kept time accurately enough to compare local noon with home-port time, and his rewards included £10,000 in 1765; later acts rewarded lunar tables and Arctic exploration, and the scheme was wound up in 1828.

timoni-variolation-report-istanbul-1714.summary: Emanuel Timoni, a Chios-born physician trained at Padua and Oxford who practised in Istanbul, writes to John Woodward in December 1713 describing how for about forty years Greek and Circassian women there have engrafted smallpox: pus from a mild case is pricked into a child's arm with a needle, giving a light illness and lifelong protection. Philosophical Transactions prints his account in 1714. Giacomo Pylarini, Venetian consul at Smyrna, publishes a second report in 1715. Cotton Mather reads Timoni in Boston and backs inoculation there in 1721; Lady Mary Wortley Montagu has her son engrafted in Istanbul in 1718 and brings the practice to London. Folk inoculation was older still in Anatolia, the Caucasus and Africa, and in China by a different route.

west-africa-variolation-1716.summary: Communities across West and Central Africa, Ethiopia and southern Africa deliberately infected healthy people with matter from mild smallpox cases, scratching it into skin to produce a protective illness. Eugenia Herbert's 1975 survey found inoculation most established in Western and Central Sudan and Ethiopia, where it was often a specialist's trade. In Boston, Cotton Mather recorded in 1716 that his enslaved servant Onesimus, who had been inoculated in Africa, described this operation with an account confirmed by other Africans in the town. Mather's reading of Onesimus and of reports from Constantinople led to Boston's 1721 inoculation trial, which Zabdiel Boylston carried out.

sources.title: Herbert, Eugenia W., 'Smallpox Inoculation in Africa', Journal of African History 16 (1975)
sources.author: Herbert, Eugenia W.
sources.confirms: Earliest descriptions of African inoculation come from enslaved Africans in colonial America in the early and mid eighteenth century; practice most used in Western and Central Sudan, Ethiopia and Southern Africa

sources.author: Boylston, Arthur
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine

west-africa-variolation-1716.detail: Herbert argues that African practice arose independently of Asian and Ottoman inoculation and persisted into the twentieth century despite colonial bans. Boylston (a descendant) shows Mather identifying Onesimus as 'Guramantese' and dating his acquisition to 1706. Later Jennerian vaccination displaced variolation, but West African healers continued arm-to-arm practices. This date marks Mather's letter; African use predates it by an unknown span, so 1716 is approximate.

picture.credit: Zabdiel Boylston (1679–1766)

ottoman-tulip-era-1718.summary: From 1718 twelve years of peace opened the Ottoman court to Europe, with its first Ottoman-language press. Peace with Austria and Venice at Passarowitz on 21 July 1718 turned Sultan Ahmed III's court outward and homeward at once. His grand vizier and son-in-law, Nevşehirli Damat İbrahim Pasha, pushed trade and manufacturing, sponsored Istanbul's first Ottoman-language printing press in the 1720s, and sent Yirmisekiz Çelebi Mehmed to Paris in 1721; his descriptions of Versailles shaped Sadâbâd, a summer palace of canals and pavilions built at Kâğıthane in 1722 and 1723. Tulips, which the vizier loved, filled gardens, silks and paintings, giving later historians this period's name.

ottoman-tulip-era-1718.detail: Courtiers followed with their own pavilions. Fountains such as Ahmed III's of 1728 brought ornament and floral motifs that led into Ottoman Baroque. Resentment at courtly spending fed the Patrona Halil revolt of 28 September 1730, which deposed Ahmed and killed his vizier.

ottoman-variolation-montagu-1718.summary: In 1718 Mary Montagu had her son inoculated against smallpox in Turkey and took the idea home. Smallpox had killed her brother and scarred her own face in 1715. In Constantinople, where her husband was ambassador, she watched Ottoman women in March 1717 practise what she called engrafting: matter from a mild smallpox blister scratched into an arm or leg gave a mild case and lasting immunity. In March 1718 she had embassy surgeon Charles Maitland inoculate her young son, and she reached London that October determined to bring the method home. When an epidemic struck in April 1721 she had Maitland inoculate her daughter before witnesses, England's first such operation.

ottoman-variolation-montagu-1718.detail: Physicians resisted a folk treatment, but she won over Caroline, Princess of Wales. Seven condemned Newgate prisoners were inoculated in August 1721 and survived; Caroline's two daughters followed in 1722, and Montagu published a pseudonymous defence. Variolation could still kill or spread infection; Edward Jenner's cowpox vaccination later replaced it.

bubble-act-1720.summary: Passed on 11 June 1720, the Bubble Act (6 Geo. 1 c. 18) incorporated two marine insurers, Royal Exchange Assurance and London Assurance, and declared illegal and void any other business that raised money or sold shares like a chartered company without a royal charter or act of Parliament. Historians have read it as an attempt to stop speculation of the kind then inflating South Sea Company stock, or as Parliament guarding its own control over business. It made chartered status, and so parliamentary favour, Britain's gateway to large-scale ventures until its partial repeal in 1825.

sources.author: Harris, Ron
sources.confirms: Chapter summary: the Act is viewed as a watershed for joint-stock companies, from recognition 1689-1720 to mistrust after 1720.

bubble-act-1720.detail: Recent scholarship holds that its sponsors wanted to stop rival schemes competing with the South Sea Company for investors' money, since it passed before that bubble peaked. Enforcement was thin: one prosecution, in 1790, settled nothing of importance. Parliament extended it to its colonies in 1741.

mississippi-bubble-1720.summary: In 1720 John Law's Mississippi Company collapsed, and the French shunned banks for generations. Holders of state debt had swapped it for company shares, paid out in paper notes from Law's bank. Shares that stood at 500 livres in early 1719 reached 10,000. Selling turned paper into cash, France's money supply doubled and prices rose 23 per cent in January 1720 alone. By September shares were at 2,000 livres and by December at 1,000; Philippe d'Orléans dismissed Law before year's end, and he fled France.

Velde, Francois R., 'John Law's System', American Economic Review 97.2 (2007), pp. 276-279
sources.author: Velde, Francois R.
sources.confirms: Landing page bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Mississippi Bubble'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the event c. 1718-1720 and says the collapse occurred in 1720. It confirms that the scheme ended in financial disaster in 1720 as shares plummeted, but does not confirm that French people shunned banks for generations.

mississippi-bubble-1720.detail:
Law, Scottish gambler and financial theorist, had won the Regent's backing after Louis XIV's wars left France deep in debt. His Compagnie d'Occident, chartered in August 1717 with its Louisiana trade monopoly, bought France's East Indies and China companies in May 1719, then North African trade, royal mints and rights to collect direct and indirect taxes, financing each purchase with new shares underwritten by his Banque Générale. Shares traded in the open air on rue Quincampoix in Paris rose from par at 500 livres to 750 on 17 June 1719, 1,000 on 21 July, 2,000 one week later and 3,000 by 17 August.

By September 1721 shares were back at 500 livres. Company and bank went into receivership in April 1721 and emerged in March 1723 as a trading concern, with the French state paying 514 million livres to make it whole; it traded as French Indies Company until liquidation in 1770. Law ended his days gambling in Venice, where he is buried in San Moisè.

picture.alt: Crowds trading Mississippi Company shares in Rue Quincampoix, Paris, satirical print from Het Groote Tafereel der Dwaasheid, 1720.
picture.credit: Rijksmuseum, Public domain, via Rijksmuseum

south-sea-bubble-1720.summary: In 1720 South Sea shares rose eightfold and crashed; new companies were barred for a century. Because new stock was issued at face value, every rise in price left surplus shares to sell for profit, so directors talked up Pacific trade, lent buyers money against shares and handed stock to ministers. Shares went from £128 in January to almost £1,000 in early August, then fell back to about £100 by year's end, ruining thousands and dragging down banks that had lent on the stock.

sources.title: South Sea Company - Wikipedia
Temin, Peter; Voth, Hans-Joachim, 'Riding the South Sea Bubble', American Economic Review 94.5 (2004), pp. 1654-1668
sources.author: Temin, Peter; Voth, Hans-Joachim
sources.confirms: Abstract confirms the 1720 bubble and collapse using Hoare's Bank records.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'South Sea Bubble'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1720. Shares rose from 128½ in January to more than 1,000 in August, then collapsed. The page says shares were down to 124 by December, not about £100.

south-sea-bubble-1720.detail:
Robert Harley, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, created this company in 1711 so his government had a lender other than the Bank of England. Its monopoly on trade with Spanish South America meant in practice slave trading under Spain's asiento. One debt conversion in 1719 worked well enough that ministers sought something bigger; news of fortunes made in John Law's Paris added urgency. Annuitants were offered shares valued on an assumed 5 per cent return, and directors promised government £3 million in fees.

Selling began once August instalments fell due, and collapse coincided with Law's in France. By late September its price was £150. Parliament's inquiry of 1721 found fraud among directors and corruption in the Cabinet: Chancellor John Aislabie was imprisoned, both Craggs died in disgrace, and Stanhope and Sunderland were implicated. Robert Walpole, new First Lord of the Treasury, removed all 33 directors and stripped them of 82 per cent of their wealth on average, divided company stock between the Bank of England and the East India Company, and shielded King George. Its scandal prompted Cato's Letters.

picture.alt: Satirical allegory on collapse of South Sea Company shares, print made between 1722 and 1764.
picture.credit: Rijksmuseum, Public domain, via Rijksmuseum

yoshimune-lifts-book-ban-1720.summary: In 1720 Japan's shogun let Western books in again, and Japan learned European science in Dutch. From 1640 the Tokugawa government had forbidden most Western books, fearing Christianity, and from 1639 Dutch traders confined to Dejima island at Nagasaki were its only tolerated Europeans. In 1720 shōgun Tokugawa Yoshimune relaxed those rules. Japanese scholars began buying and translating Dutch scientific works and acquiring Western instruments, and Rangaku, Dutch learning, grew into a body of knowledge on medicine, astronomy and technology that kept Japan informed of European science until its ports opened in 1854.

sources.title: Rangaku - Wikipedia
Goodman, Grant Kohn, 'Tokugawa Yoshimune and Western learning', in Japan: The Dutch Experience (Athlone, 1986), pp. 49-65
sources.author: Goodman, Grant Kohn
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Tokugawa Yoshimune'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives no year or date for relaxing restrictions on Dutch books. It does not confirm that claim. It says Yoshimune’s inquiring spirit encouraged interest in Western science and that he imported a telescope from the Netherlands.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'rangaku'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives c. 1751-c. 1900 as the date range for Rangaku; it does not give a date for the 1720 event. It does not confirm Yoshimune’s 1720 relaxation of restrictions.

yoshimune-lifts-book-ban-1720.verification_note: Britannica confirms Yoshimune encouraged Western learning but gives no 1720 date for relaxing the book ban; Goodman's chapter is paywalled.
yoshimune-lifts-book-ban-1720.detail: Rangaku's first phase, from 1640 to 1720, was small and tightly controlled. It stayed confined to Nagasaki, where Dutch surgeons such as Caspar Schamberger treated officials and a modest trade in curiosities developed. After 1720 books on medical science were obtained, analysed and translated, setting off debates between followers of Chinese medicine and new Western anatomy. Telescopes, clocks, microscopes, maps and globes reached literate urban markets in Edo, Osaka and Kyoto, where some shops specialised in foreign goods. Its source credits this scientific base with helping explain Japan's rapid modernisation after American warships forced its ports open in 1854.

onesimus-variolation-boston-1721.summary: In 1721, when smallpox struck Boston, Mather urged inoculation and named Onesimus, an enslaved African, and African practice as his source; deaths among the inoculated fell sixfold. Inoculators took fluid from a pustule, cut skin and put in a drop. Most doctors, ministers and officials refused, but physician Zabdiel Boylston tried it, and of 280 people inoculated six died, against 844 of 5,889 who caught smallpox unprotected.

sources.title: Onesimus (Bostonian) - Wikipedia
Best, M.; Neuhauser, D.; Slavin, L., 'Cotton Mather, you dog, dam you!: smallpox inoculation, Boston, 1721', Quality and Safety in Health Care 13.1 (2004), pp. 82-83
sources.author: Best, M.; Neuhauser, D.; Slavin, L.
sources.venue: Quality and Safety in Health Care
sources.confirms: Full text: 1721 Boston inoculation campaign; bomb thrown at Mather 14 November 1721.

sources.title: Minardi, Margot, 'The Boston Inoculation Controversy of 1721-1722', William and Mary Quarterly 61.1 (2004), pp. 47-76
sources.author: Minardi, Margot
sources.confirms: OpenAlex abstract quotes Mather's account of Onesimus describing inoculation.

onesimus-variolation-boston-1721.detail:
Mather's congregation gave him Onesimus in December 1706; his birth name is unknown, and Mather described him as Guramantee. Kelly Wisecup notes he was probably inoculated before enslavement or during his Atlantic crossing, and that enslaved communities across the Americas kept up the practice. Mather listened in part because, as Margot Minardi writes, African inferiority had not yet been written onto bodies, and because he saw a cure as providential and as his route back to public influence.

Bostonians answered with fear: inoculating healthy people would spread disease, interfered with providence, and might be a plot by enslaved people to poison white citizens. Mather was publicly ridiculed for trusting an enslaved man's testimony. Boylston began with his six-year-old son and two enslaved people of his own; deaths in 1721 to 1722 ran about 2.2 per cent among those inoculated and 14.3 per cent among everyone else. Boylston's tomb wrongly names him first to bring inoculation to America. Onesimus later bought partial freedom.

fahrenheit-thermometer-1724.summary: In 1724 Fahrenheit published in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions a temperature scale that any thermometer could reproduce, with his method of making them and his fixed points: a mixture of ice, water and salt set 0 degrees, water with ice just forming 30, and body heat under the arm 90. His mercury-in-glass instruments, more accurate than spirit-filled ones, sold widely from Amsterdam, and their popularity carried his scale with them.

sources.title: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit
Fahrenheit, D. G., 'Experimenta circa gradum caloris liquorum nonnullorum ebullientium instituta', Philosophical Transactions 33 (1724), pp. 1-3
sources.author: Fahrenheit, Daniel Gabriel
sources.confirms: Fahrenheit's 1724 paper on boiling points measured with his thermometers.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1724 for developing the Fahrenheit temperature scale. It confirms the scale’s development in 1724, but does not confirm publication, reproducibility, or comparison of readings between observers.

fahrenheit-thermometer-1724.detail:
Born in Danzig to a Hanse merchant family and orphaned in 1701, Fahrenheit was apprenticed in Amsterdam and ran off to travel. In 1708 he met Ole Rømer in Copenhagen, who showed him his own scale and thermometer methods and told him demand for accurate instruments was high. He began mercury thermometers in 1713, settled in Amsterdam about 1717 to sell barometers and thermometers, and had standardised his manufacture by 1721. He visited England in 1724, was elected a Fellow on 5 May, and published five Latin papers that year.

His article was for two centuries the only description of his process. Ernst Cohen's 20th-century study of his letters to Herman Boerhaave cast doubt on it and showed his scale largely derived from Rømer's; W. E. Knowles Middleton attributes the confusion to an instrument maker hiding his methods. Water boiled about 180 degrees above freezing, and the scale was later redefined to make that interval exact, which is why body heat reads 98.6 today rather than his 96.

picture.alt: Dutch barometer and thermometer of about 1760, instruments of the kind Fahrenheit made in Amsterdam, decades after his 1724 scale.
picture.credit: Rijksmuseum, Public domain, via Rijksmuseum

gullivers-laputa-engine-1726.summary: In 1726 Swift's Gulliver's Travels mocked a professor whose engine wrote books by shuffling words at random. It is a frame twenty feet square covered in wooden blocks bearing every word of their language; pupils turn forty iron handles, scan jumbled lines for fragments of sense and dictate them to scribes. Anthony Bonner reads it as satire on Ramon Llull's Ars Magna, and Eric A. Weiss sees an early picture of machine-made text.

sources.title: The Engine - Wikipedia
Swift, Jonathan, Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World (London: Benj. Motte, 1726), Internet Archive
sources.author: Swift, Jonathan
sources.confirms: Catalogue of the 1726 Motte first edition containing the Laputa engine passage.

sources.title: Weiss, Eric A., 'Gulliver's Travels and the Engine', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 7.2 (1985), pp. 164-165
sources.author: Weiss, Eric A.
sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing
sources.confirms: Landing page bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Gullivers Travels'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates Gulliver’s Travels to October 28, 1726; it gives no separate date for the word-generating engine. The page does not confirm the record’s central claim.

gullivers-laputa-engine-1726.detail: In Swift's account every block is pasted with paper bearing all words in their moods, tenses and declensions, without order. At one sudden turn of its handles every word shifts; thirty-six pupils read lines softly and dictate to four scribes, and this is repeated three or four times. Its professor hoped, given public funds for five hundred such frames, to assemble all arts and sciences from broken sentences. Llull's medieval art had likewise combined terms mechanically to generate propositions, which is why Bonner takes Swift's passage as its parody.

muteferrika-press-1729.summary: In 1729 İbrahim Müteferrika printed the first book from a Muslim press in the Ottoman Empire, 250 years late. Printing with movable type had reached Istanbul through Jewish, Armenian and Greek presses, but no Muslim had run one; scribes and calligraphers defended manuscript culture. He then won Sultan Ahmed III's permission for non-religious books. His first, in 1729, was Vankulu Lügati, a two-volume Arabic-Turkish dictionary; by 1743 he had printed 17 works in 23 volumes.

sources.title: Ibrahim Muteferrika - Wikipedia
Sabev, Orlin, 'Selling the Books', in Waiting for Muteferrika: Glimpses of Ottoman Print Culture (De Gruyter / Academic Studies Press, 2018), ch. 4, pp. 147-201
sources.author: Sabev, Orlin
sources.confirms: Chapter: press output and sales 1729-1746, beginning with the Vankulu dictionary of 1729.
sources.qualifies: Sabev counts sixteen publications in the first period; the record says seventeen. Britannica dates the press's founding to 1727.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ibrahim Muteferrika'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1727 as the year İbrahim established a printing press; it does not give a date for the first book. It does not confirm that the first book was printed in 1729.

sources.title: Library of Congress Law Library blog, 'Ibrahim Muteferrika: First Muslim Printer of the Ottoman Empire' (2023)
sources.author: Library of Congress
sources.confirms: 1729. The page identifies Müteferrika as the Ottoman Empire’s first Muslim printer and says he printed his first work in 1729.

muteferrika-press-1729.detail: Born in Kolozsvár, now Cluj-Napoca, in 1674, Müteferrika took his surname from his post as müteferrika in Ahmed III's household during Ottoman Turkey's Tulip Era. He worked as diplomat, geographer and historian. His press used custom-made fonts, and its books, sometimes called Turkish incunabula, ran to between 500 and 1,000 copies each: dictionaries, histories, geographies with maps, and works by Kâtip Çelebi. Calestous Juma attributes printing's late arrival in Islamic lands to weight placed on oral transmission and on calligraphy's religious standing, with scribes resisting hardest. Religious texts stayed outside his licence.

picture.alt: Map of Japan printed in Kâtip Çelebi's Cihannüma by İbrahim Müteferrika's Istanbul press in 1732, three years after its first book.
picture.credit: İbrahim Müteferrika press, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

dojima-rice-futures-1730.summary: Osaka merchants had traded warehouse receipts for domain rice since 1697 at Dojima; in 1730 shogunate recognised this market and its book trading, in which contracts for standardised rice grades settled by cash difference at season's end without delivery. Ulrike Schaede's analysis finds clearing houses, margin requirements and daily price limits that match modern futures exchanges. Daimyo financed stipends by selling rice forward, brokers hedged, and price signals ran by flag relay to Kyoto and Edo. Dojima operated until 1939, and its candlestick price records inform charting methods still in use.

sources.title: Schaede, Ulrike, 'Forwards and futures in Tokugawa-period Japan: a new perspective on the Dojima rice market', Journal of Banking and Finance 13 (1989)
sources.author: Schaede, Ulrike
sources.confirms: Dojima book trading, clearing and 1730 recognition as a futures market

sources.title: Wakita, Shigeru, 'Efficiency of the Dojima rice futures market in Tokugawa-period Japan', Journal of Banking and Finance 25 (2001)
sources.author: Wakita, Shigeru
sources.confirms: Price efficiency tests on Dojima data
sources.qualifies: Differs from Schaede on degree of market efficiency

dojima-rice-futures-1730.verification_note: Schaede and Wakita differ on this market's efficiency, not on dates.
dojima-rice-futures-1730.detail: Schaede in 1989 and Shigeru Wakita in 2001 disagreed on how efficient Dojima prices were and how far book trading resembled modern derivatives. Both accept 1730 licensing and settlement by difference. Shogunate alternated between banning and tolerating speculation. Japanese economic histories date a formal futures market from that 1730 licensing.

picture.alt: Dojima rice market, Osaka, woodblock print from Naniwa hyakkei by Utagawa Kunikazu
picture.credit: Utagawa Kunikazu, Osaka Municipal Library digital archive

jantar-mantar-jaipur-1734.summary: Between 1724 and 1730 Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II of Jaipur built five masonry observatories in northern India, called Jantar Mantars (Barry Perlus, in Celestial Mirror, Yale, 2020); UNESCO dates Jaipur's site only to early 18th century, and its often quoted 1734 completion has no scholarly support. Jaipur's holds some twenty main fixed instruments. Its Vrihat Samrat Yantra, a sundial 88 feet high with gnomon angled 27 degrees to match Jaipur's latitude, casts a shadow moving about one millimetre per second and reads local time to about two seconds. Jai Singh's astronomers, at least 23 in 1735, worked there as Jaipur replaced Delhi as his main observatory and compiled Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, tables used in India for a century. UNESCO calls this site a meeting point of scientific cultures and inscribed it as World Heritage in 2010.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
Perlus, Barry, 'Jantar Mantar: Jai Singh's observatories', in Jai Singh's Astronomy / Yale volume (Yale, 2020), pp. 88-109
sources.author: Perlus, Barry
sources.confirms: Chapter abstract: Jai Singh II built his observatories between 1724 and 1730.
sources.qualifies: Perlus dates construction 1724-1730; the record gives 1734 for completion of the Jaipur site.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'The Jantar Mantar, Jaipur'
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: The page gives no specific year or date; it says the observatory was built in the early 18th century. It does not confirm the record’s central claim that it was completed in 1734.

jantar-mantar-jaipur-1734.verification_note: Perlus (Yale, 2020) dates Jai Singh's five observatories to 1724 to 1730, so about 1730 replaces an older 1734 date; UNESCO gives only early 18th century, and no source supports 1734.
jantar-mantar-jaipur-1734.detail: Its instruments follow Ptolemaic positional astronomy; Kapala Yantraprakara converts between two coordinate systems, and Yantra Raj, a 2.43-metre bronze astrolabe, was used once yearly for Hindu calendar reckoning. Damaged in Victorian times and restored, its instruments still work.

picture.alt: Brihat Samrat Yantra, giant stone sundial of Jai Singh II's Jantar Mantar observatory in Jaipur, built in the 1730s; photographed 2019.
picture.credit: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

norfolk-four-course-rotation-1730.summary: On light Norfolk soils, landlords and tenants settle into a four-year cycle of wheat, turnips, barley undersown with clover and ryegrass, then clover ley, removing fallow entirely. Turnips feed sheep and cattle through winter and their folding manures fields; clover fixes nitrogen for next year's wheat. Charles Townshend, second Viscount (1674 to 1738), retires from politics to Raynham in 1730 and promotes it so loudly he is remembered as Turnip Townshend, though rotation was established in Norfolk before 1700 and became common by 1800. Thomas Coke of Holkham (1754 to 1842) writes it into tenant leases and his sheep shearings carry it nationwide. Mark Overton dates England's surge in farm productivity to the century after 1750.

sources.title: Overton, M., Agricultural Revolution in England: The Transformation of the Agrarian Economy 1500-1850 (Cambridge University Press, 1996), ch. 3 'Agricultural output and productivity, 1500-1850', pp. 63-132
sources.author: Overton, Mark
sources.confirms: Standard survey of English farming 1500 to 1850 covering changes in rotation, output and productivity.
sources.qualifies: Argues the agricultural revolution took place in the century after 1750, later than Townshend's lifetime.

sources.title: Charles, D., Randall, J., Dove, R., Thompson, M. and Needham, T., 'Guest editorial: managing our soils: learning from the past to help feed a growing world population', Journal of Agricultural Science 161 (2023), 3-5
sources.author: Charles, David; Randall, John; Dove, Rosemary; Thompson, Mick; Needham, Teresa
sources.confirms: Names the Norfolk four-course rotation wheat, turnips, barley, clover, pioneered by Townshend (1674 to 1738) of Raynham and Coke (1754 to 1842) of Holkham, with clover fixing nitrogen and manure valued.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Norfolk four-course system'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Describes the sequence and states the rotation was established in Norfolk before the end of the 17th century and common by 1800.

sources.title: Eastern Daily Press, 'How modern Holkham farmers are reviving the principles of Coke of Norfolk'
sources.author: Eastern Daily Press
sources.confirms: Reports Holkham lease rules on rotation under Coke.

norfolk-four-course-rotation-1730.verification_note: Rotation has no invention date; it emerged in Norfolk over late 17th and 18th centuries. 1730 is Townshend's retirement to Raynham, used as anchor. Overton places that productivity surge after 1750.
norfolk-four-course-rotation-1730.detail: 1730 marks Townshend's retirement to farming rather than any invention; Dutch and Flemish farmers grew turnips and clover in rotation a century earlier. Gains came from keeping more livestock, so more manure and meat, and from cleaning weeds by hoeing turnips. Holkham leases set four, five and six course rotations by soil type; clover's nitrogen fixation and manure sustained soils.

picture.alt: Portrait of Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend, after Godfrey Kneller
picture.credit: After Godfrey Kneller, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

kay-flying-shuttle-1733.summary: In 1733 John Kay patented the flying shuttle, which let one weaver do the work of two; spinners could no longer keep up, and that imbalance spurred spinning jenny, water frame and mule. Weaving broad cloth had needed two people, standing at either side of their loom, passing weft thread back and forth by hand in its shuttle. Kay's shuttle ran on wheels along a board below the warp; tugging a cord jerked it from its box at either side across to its opposite, so a lone weaver worked wider cloth faster, one-handed.

sources.title: Flying shuttle - Wikipedia
Paulinyi, Akos, 'John Kay's Flying Shuttle: Some Considerations on His Technical Capacity and Economic Impact', Textile History 17.2 (1986), pp. 149-166
sources.author: Paulinyi, Akos
sources.confirms: OpenAlex bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'John Kay'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: May 26, 1733 (the patent date); the page also gives 1733 as the year. The page says Kay’s flying shuttle let one weaver weave fabrics of any width more quickly than two could before.

kay-flying-shuttle-1733.detail: Kay, from Bury in Lancashire, could not enforce his patent. He and his partners sued infringers repeatedly, but litigation costs outran any winnings, and makers of copied shuttles formed a Shuttle Club to fight his claims. By the 1750s his device was in use across English weaving districts; Kay was invited to France to demonstrate it, where guilds slowed its adoption, and Scottish weavers Joseph Alexander and James McKevin probably carried it to America in 1788. His son Robert Kay added a drop box, which let weavers switch among several shuttles carrying different colours.

picture.alt: Flying shuttles of the type John Kay patented in 1733, displayed at Bradford Industrial Museum; photographed 2009.
picture.credit: Linda Spashett, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vaucanson-digesting-duck-1764.summary: In 1739 Vaucanson's duck ate, drank and seemed to digest, that century's most famous automaton. He had drawn Paris crowds with his life-size Flute Player. He followed it with a gilded copper duck that quacked, drank, took grain from his hand, swallowed with a gulp and excreted what looked like digested food, claiming that a small chemical laboratory inside broke grain down. In 1844 magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin examined it and found two containers: one caught grain, another released green-dyed breadcrumb pellets loaded in advance. Voltaire still ranked it, with singer Le Maure, among France's glories.

sources.title: Digesting Duck
Jacques de Vaucanson
Pioneers' page: Jacques de Vaucanson
Jacques de Vaucanson: the father of simulation
Riskin, Jessica, 'The Defecating Duck, or, the Ambiguous Origins of Artificial Life', Critical Inquiry 29 (2003) 599-633
sources.author: Riskin, Jessica
sources.confirms: Vaucanson's duck, shown in Paris in the late 1730s, appeared to eat, digest and excrete, and became the emblem of early artificial life.
sources.qualifies: Riskin shows the digestion was simulated: the excrement was pre-loaded, not produced from the grain.

vaucanson-digesting-duck-1764.verification_note: Riskin (Critical Inquiry 2003) finds its digestion was a fraud, with pellets stored in a hidden compartment, and contemporary notices put its first showing in 1738 or early 1739, so a 1764 date does not fit.
vaucanson-digesting-duck-1764.detail: Contemporary notices place its first showing in 1738 or early 1739; one later account's 30 May 1764 unveiling date conflicts with Vaucanson's biography, which has him building his automata in 1738 and selling them in 1743. Vaucanson is credited with making the first flexible rubber tube while building his duck's intestines, and hoped some digesting machine could one day be made. Some of his automata passed to glovemaker Pierre Dumoulin, who toured them across Europe with great success; after his death in 1781 they were reported in Russia, rigged not to work. Vaucanson's duck is thought to have burned in 1879 in a private museum fire. Replicas by Frédéric Vidoni and David Secrett exist, and it appears in Hawthorne and Pynchon.

franklin-stove-1742.summary: In Philadelphia Benjamin Franklin designs a cast-iron, metal-lined fireplace with a hollow baffle and an inverted siphon flue that draws room air past hot iron and sends less heat up its chimney. He publishes it in 1744 as An Account of the New Invented Pennsylvanian Fire-Places, printed and sold by himself, and has his friend Robert Grace cast its plates. He declines a patent offered by Pennsylvania's governor, writing that as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours. Joyce Chaplin's 2024 William and Mary Quarterly article reads Franklin's stove as an early American experiment in material science. Cast-iron cooking stoves followed in the 1800s.

sources.author: Franklin, Benjamin
sources.venue: Evans Early American Imprints (University of Michigan)

sources.author: Chaplin, Joyce E.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of the stove's design and materials; bibliographic record with volume, issue and pages checked through Crossref, full text behind Project MUSE access block.

sources.title: The Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Inventions'
sources.author: The Franklin Institute
sources.confirms: Franklin stove dated 1742; metal-lined fireplace with hollow baffle and inverted siphon; never patented; quotation on enjoying the inventions of others.

sources.title: Library of Congress, 'Benjamin Franklin: In His Own Words. Scientist' (exhibition)
sources.author: Library of Congress
sources.confirms: Pamphlet of 1744 promoted a model manufactured by Robert Grace; much less wood needed.

franklin-stove-1742.verification_note: Franklin Institute dates this stove to 1742; a 1740 to 1741 design date comes from its account of his 1744 pamphlet, with Chaplin's article (pp. 219-254) cited as supporting literature.
franklin-stove-1742.detail: A Library of Congress exhibit shows Franklin's 1744 pamphlet and records that it promoted a model manufactured by Grace. The Franklin Institute gives 1742; Chaplin dates design to winter 1740 to 1741 and publication to 1744. Franklin claimed a room could be kept warm with a quarter of the wood and without an open hearth's draughts, claims Chaplin ties to a wider colonial anxiety about deforestation around Philadelphia, which she makes central to it.

picture.alt: Cast-iron Franklin stove, Metropolitan Museum of Art.
picture.credit: Unknown author, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

yalova-paper-mill-1744.summary: Having printed seventeen titles since 1729 on imported European paper, İbrahim Müteferrika persuades Mahmud I's government to found a paper mill at Yalakabad, modern Yalova, across the Sea of Marmara from Istanbul. Work begins in 1744 near streams at Elmalık; three master papermakers recruited from Poland build and run the mill and are paid to train Ottoman apprentices, and an order of April 1745 adds a second water wheel and supplies from state workshops. Müteferrika is appointed its director in 1745 and dies in January 1747. Paper watermarked from the mill appears in Ottoman manuscripts, but output was small, wages went unpaid and operations ceased after about a decade. Imports from Italy and France continued to supply Ottoman scribes and printers into the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Sabev, O., 'The Adoption of Printing in the Ottoman World', in The Müteferrika Press: Arabic Typography in an Ottoman Context (De Gruyter Brill, 2024)
sources.author: Sabev, Orlin
sources.confirms: In 1744 Müteferrika initiated a paper mill in Yalova, became its manager in 1745; initially run by three Polish masters; operated about a decade; he died late January 1747.

sources.title: Bayram, M., 'Water and Wire: A Survey of Watermarks Found in Manuscripts from the Ottoman Empire' (MRes thesis, University of Birmingham, 2020)
sources.author: Bayram, Merve
sources.confirms: Mill built 1744 to supply Müteferrika's press; Polish and Jewish papermakers paid to train Ottoman workers; workers often unpaid; mill failed to thrive.

yalova-paper-mill-1744.verification_note: Some museum accounts date the initiative to 1741 and operation to 1745-1760; Sabev gives 1744 for initiation and about ten years of operation.

picture.alt: Map from Kâtip Çelebi's Cihannüma as printed by İbrahim Müteferrika's Istanbul press, 1732
picture.credit: Kâtip Çelebi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

leyden-jar-1745.summary: In 1745 the Leyden jar stored electricity for the first time, so it could be carried and discharged at will. Before then electricity from friction machines leaked away as soon as it was made. Ewald Georg von Kleist, dean at Cammin cathedral, tried on 11 October 1745 to trap electrical fluid in a medicine bottle and found a shock far stronger than any machine gave. At Leiden, Pieter van Musschenbroek's acquaintance Andreas Cunaeus got the same result in 1745 to 1746 by holding a water-filled jar in his hand while charging it. Charge stored on glass's two faces could now be kept and released at will, the first capacitor.

sources.title: Leyden jar - Wikipedia
Pence, Charles H., 'Kleist, Musschenbroek and the Leyden jar', Isis 113.4 (2022), pp. 789-796
sources.author: Pence, Charles H.
sources.confirms: Abstract: von Kleist's jar October 1745; Musschenbroek's Leiden report January 1746.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Leyden jar'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives 1745 for Ewald Georg von Kleist’s independent discovery and 1746 for Pieter van Musschenbroek’s investigation.

leyden-jar-1745.detail:
A Leyden jar is a glass vessel with metal foil cemented inside and out and a terminal through its lid touching inner foil. Cunaeus, a lawyer, had ignored Dufay's rule that apparatus be insulated; his hand formed its outer conductor. Musschenbroek reported this to Réaumur in Paris on 20 January 1746, and Abbé Nollet, who sold Musschenbroek's instruments in France, read it to Paris's Academy in April, named it Leyden jar and marketed it to wealthy amateurs. That year he discharged one through 180 royal guardsmen before Louis XV, and later through a line of Carthusian monks.

Within months Winckler and Gralath were joining jars together. Between 1746 and 1748 Benjamin Franklin charged jars in series and built eleven lead-coated glass panes into what he called, in his 1749 letter, an electrical battery, first recorded use of that term. His dissectible jar showed charge sat on glass.

picture.alt: Plate of early experiments with Leyden jars from Abbé Nollet's Lettres sur l'électricité, Paris, 1753.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

la-mettrie-man-a-machine-1747.summary: In 1747 La Mettrie argued humans are machines, no soul needed: scandal then, AI's premise now. In L'homme machine, published in 1747, French physician Julien Offray de La Mettrie extended the machine to people and denied any soul distinct from matter. His evidence was medical: body and soul are one in sleep, both fail without food, and drugs alter mind as surely as flesh, so, he argued, each state of soul tracks a state of body. Karl Popper later noted that his doctrine outlived evolution and quantum theory, surviving as the thesis that man is a computer.

sources.title: Man a Machine
Vartanian, Aram, 'Introduction', in La Mettrie's L'Homme machine: A Study in the Origins of an Idea (Princeton, 1960), pp. 1-12
sources.author: Vartanian, Aram
sources.confirms: Text: L'Homme machine published at Leiden late in 1747 (title page 1748).

sources.author: La Mettrie, Julien Offray de

sources.author: Falvey, J. F.

sources.confirms: 1747. The page says L’Homme-machine developed La Mettrie’s materialistic and atheistic views, but does not explicitly confirm the record’s claims that humans are machines or that no soul exists distinct from matter.

la-mettrie-man-a-machine-1747.detail: La Mettrie wrote as a doctor observing how fever, diet and opium changed thought. He concluded that diverse states of soul correlate with those of body in every case, as he put it. Popper, discussing his claim, remarked that it was argued most forcefully in 1751, long before evolution was accepted, and that evolutionary theory sharpened it by blurring any line between living and dead matter. An English translation appeared in 1748 and a French-English edition in 1912.

lind-scurvy-trial-1747.summary: On 20 May 1747, in the Channel aboard HMS Salisbury, naval surgeon James Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy, lodged them together on one diet, and gave pairs of them one of six remedies: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, seawater, a spice paste, or two oranges and a lemon daily. Both on citrus were fit for duty within six days; the cider pair improved a little and eight others did not. Lind published his result in A Treatise of the Scurvy (Edinburgh, 1753) with a review of earlier writing on it. He did not grasp why citrus worked and recommended a boiled concentrate that destroyed most of its vitamin C. Britain's Admiralty issued lemon juice to its fleet only in 1795. It is cited as the first clinical comparison with concurrent controls.

encyclopedie-diderot-1751.summary: In 1751 Diderot and d'Alembert began the Encyclopédie, 28 volumes putting crafts beside philosophy. It gave crafts and trades as much detailed treatment as philosophy, with volumes of engravings showing workshops and tools. Church opponents attacked it as leading to irreligion; a royal edict suspended it in 1752, and Paris's Parlement had its privilege revoked in 1759 after volume seven. Work went on in secret, and its finished set ran to 28 volumes with about 71,818 articles.

sources.title: Encyclopédie
Diderot, Denis; d'Alembert, Jean le Rond (eds.), Encyclopedie, ou Dictionnaire raisonne (Paris, 1751-1772), ARTFL Encyclopedie Project, University of Chicago
sources.author: Diderot, Denis; d'Alembert, Jean le Rond
sources.confirms: Project page: 17 text volumes and 11 plate volumes published between 1751 and 1772; 74,000 articles.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Encyclopedie'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1751; the page says publication of the text began that year. Partly confirmed: it names Diderot and d’Alembert and says the first edition had 28 volumes of text and plates. It does not confirm the article count.

encyclopedie-diderot-1751.detail: Seventeen volumes of text appeared between 1751 and 1765 and eleven of plates by 1772, some 2,784 plates in all. Highly placed protectors, minister Malesherbes and Madame de Pompadour among them, let production continue after 1759 while officials looked away, judging their ban enough to satisfy churchmen. Title pages of volumes 8 to 17, released together in 1765, named Neuchâtel as place of publication, a principality safely outside France, though printing presumably continued in Paris. Officials seem to have required those last volumes to appear at once to limit publicity.

picture.credit: B. L. Prévost after C. N. Cochin, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

franklin-kite-lightning-rod-1752.summary: In 1752 Franklin drew electricity from a cloud with a kite, and buildings got lightning rods. Whether lightning was electricity had remained open; Jean-Antoine Nollet's speculations had made it Bordeaux's prize topic in 1749. Benjamin Franklin proposed drawing charge from clouds with a tall rod; lacking any spire high enough in Philadelphia, he used his kite instead in June 1752, with his son William's help. Loose fibres of its wet hemp string bristled as a storm cloud passed, he drew sparks from its key and charged a Leyden jar. Lightning, he concluded, was electrical, and rods could carry it harmlessly to earth.

sources.title: Kite experiment - Wikipedia
Franklin, Benjamin, 'A Letter of Benjamin Franklin, Esq; to Mr. Peter Collinson ... concerning an electrical kite', Philosophical Transactions 47 (1751-52), pp. 565-567
sources.author: Franklin, Benjamin
sources.confirms: Franklin's own kite letter printed by the Royal Society in 1752.

sources.title: Franklin Institute, 'Benjamin Franklin's Kite and Key Experiment'
sources.author: Franklin Institute
sources.confirms: June 1752; the page also dates Franklin’s account in the Pennsylvania Gazette to October 19, 1752. The page says the experiment demonstrated the connection between lightning and electricity.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'June 10 Benjamin Franklin Flies a Kite'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: June 10, 1752, according to tradition. The page describes Franklin’s kite experiment detecting electricity during a storm and capturing it in a special jar.

franklin-kite-lightning-rod-1752.detail:
His kite was never struck; one direct hit would probably have killed him. He held his apparatus by dry silk cord, which insulated him from its key, borrowed from Benjamin Loxley, and father and son sheltered in an open shed to keep silk dry. Franklin described his method in a letter printed in Pennsylvania Gazette on 19 October 1752 without saying he had done it himself; it was read to London's Royal Society on 21 December and printed in Philosophical Transactions. Joseph Priestley gave its fullest account in his 1767 History and Present State of Electricity, presumably from Franklin.

Thomas-François Dalibard had already carried out Franklin's rod experiment at Marly-la-Ville in May 1752. In August 1753 Georg Wilhelm Richmann was killed in Saint Petersburg attempting his own repeat, thought to be ball lightning's victim.

picture.alt: Benjamin Franklin seated beside his electrical bells with lightning striking outside, engraving after Mason Chamberlin's portrait of 1762.
picture.credit: After Mason Chamberlin, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

lisbon-earthquake-1755.summary: In 1755 an earthquake destroyed Lisbon; it was rebuilt on a grid with frames that flex. The churches had been full for All Saints' morning when the shaking began. Candles set fires that burned for days, and a tsunami swept its waterfront; much of Lisbon was destroyed. King Joseph I's minister, Marquis of Pombal, had corpses buried and survivors fed, then chose Manuel da Maia's plan to rebuild Baixa on wide gridded streets. Its new buildings carried an internal wooden lattice, their gaiola, that flexed in tremors, among Europe's earliest earthquake-resistant construction.

sources.title: Effect on society, economy...
Araujo, Ana Cristina, 'The Lisbon earthquake of 1755', Storicamente 17 (2021)
sources.author: Araujo, Ana Cristina
sources.confirms: Full text on the 1 November 1755 earthquake and Pombal's reconstruction with the gaiola frame.

sources.title: Lopes, Vieira, 'The 1755 Lisbon earthquake and management', Journal of Management History 20.3 (2014), pp. 278-291
sources.author: Journal of Management History author
sources.confirms: Abstract on the 1755 earthquake response.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Lisbon earthquake of 1755'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: November 1, 1755. The page does not confirm seismic-resistant rebuilding; it does not discuss Lisbon’s reconstruction.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Pombaline Lisbon (Tentative List)'
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: The page dates the earthquake to 1 November 1755. It says reconstruction began in 1756.

lisbon-earthquake-1755.detail:
Maia offered four options, from rebuilding as before to razing Baixa for his new plan; Pombal took the boldest. Prefabricated standard facades sped construction, and gaiola models were tested by having troops march around them to simulate shaking. Pombal also sent every parish questions: when shaking began and how long it lasted, whether buildings fell one way, how many died, whether the sea rose or fell first, how long fires burned. The priests' answers survive in Torre do Tombo archive, let modern scientists reconstruct events, and earn him recognition as seismology's forerunner.

Voltaire answered with his Poème sur le désastre de Lisbonne and with Candide's attack on this best of all possible worlds; Rousseau blamed dense city living for its toll.

picture.alt: Lisbon during its earthquake and fire of 1 November 1755, engraved print.
picture.credit: Rijksmuseum, Public domain, via Rijksmuseum

harrison-h4-chronometer-1759.summary: In 1759 Harrison's watch lost five seconds sailing to Jamaica, and sailors could fix longitude. A clock keeping home-port time gives longitude by comparison with local noon, which is why Parliament's 1714 Longitude Act had offered £20,000 for accuracy within half a degree. Harrison had built three large sea clocks before the watch. The Board of Longitude refused to accept one trial as proof and paid in instalments only after years of dispute.

sources.title: John Harrison
Betts, Jonathan, 'H4', in Time Restored: The Harrison Timekeepers and R. T. Gould (Oxford, 2006), pp. 81-103
sources.author: Betts, Jonathan
sources.confirms: Full text: 'H4 was completed in 1759'; two West Indies trials followed.
sources.qualifies: Jamaica trial sailed November 1761; Board paid the second half of the reward only in 1765 and 1773.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'John Harrison British horologist'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the Jamaica test to 1762, not 1759. It confirms that Harrison’s No. 4 marine chronometer was found to be in error by five seconds after a voyage to Jamaica, but does not say sailors could fix longitude.

sources.title: Royal Museums Greenwich, 'Harrison's clocks and the longitude problem'
sources.author: Royal Museums Greenwich
sources.confirms: The page gives no completion date for H4. It says Harrison commissioned a watch around 1751-52 and incorporated it into H4; William’s Jamaica trial was authorized in 1761.

harrison-h4-chronometer-1759.detail:
Harrison, Yorkshire-born carpenter turned clockmaker, had built H1 to H3 between 1730 and 1759 with frictionless grasshopper escapements and bimetallic temperature compensation. He then concluded that a watch beating rapidly would do better. H4 used diamond pallets and a remontoire to keep its drive even. His son William sailed with it in November 1761 and returned in March 1762 with the result. The Board of Longitude demanded another trial, to Barbados in 1764, then half its reward against surrender of all his timekeepers and construction of copies.

Larcum Kendall's copy, K1, sailed with James Cook on his second voyage and earned his praise; K2 went to Bligh on Bounty. George III tested Harrison's H5 himself in 1772, found it accurate to one third of one second per day, and urged him to petition Parliament, which granted £8,750 in 1773 when Harrison was 80. The full official prize was never awarded to anyone.

picture.alt: John Harrison's H4 marine timekeeper of 1759 on display at National Maritime Museum, Greenwich; photographed 2009.
picture.credit: Colonel Warden, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

bakewell-selective-breeding-dishley-1760.summary: Robert Bakewell (born 23 May 1725) takes full charge of his father's 440-acre farm at Dishley, Leicestershire, when his father dies in 1760, having managed it since about 1755. He separates rams from ewes and bulls from cows so every mating is chosen, inbreeds closely related animals to fix traits, culls failures and keeps records on each beast. From Midland longwools he builds New Leicester sheep, small-boned and barrel-shaped, fattening for the butcher after a second shearing at about 27 months against 39 for old Lincolns. He is the first to hire out rams and bulls on a large scale, which spreads his blood across England and lets him judge sires by their lambs; rams fetched 25 guineas by 1770 and hire income reached 3,000 pounds a year. The Dishley Society of 1783 polices the breed.

sources.author: Wykes, David L.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed reassessment of Bakewell's breeding methods, New Leicester maturity after the second shearing, ram letting and the Dishley Society.

sources.author: Humphreys, Jennett; Mingay, G. E.
sources.confirms: Gives birth 23 May 1725 at Dishley, 440-acre farm, management from about 1755 and full control after father's death in 1760, New Leicester traits, ram hire at 25 guineas by 1770 and 3,000 pounds a year.
sources.qualifies: Puts Bakewell's effective management from about 1755, before the 1760 inheritance used as anchor.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Robert Bakewell'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives 1760 inheritance, in-and-in breeding, ram letting and death on 1 October 1795.

bakewell-selective-breeding-dishley-1760.detail: His Leicestershire longhorn cattle and black cart horses had less lasting effect, but the method did: progeny testing, pedigree and breed societies all trace to Dishley. Border Leicester, Lincoln, Wensleydale and others descend from his stock, which also founded flocks in Australia and New Zealand. Critics then and since noted fatty mutton and reduced fertility from inbreeding. Bakewell died at Dishley on 1 October 1795.

picture.alt: Engraved portrait of Robert Bakewell of Dishley
picture.credit: F. Engleheart (engraver), published by Joseph Rogerson, 1849, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

industrial-revolution-era-1760.summary: From 1760 Britain made goods by machine in factories, not by hand, and output per person rose as never before. New iron and chemical processes, water power and then steam engines, machine tools and mechanised spinning, with textiles leading, multiplied output per worker. For the first time in history both population and average living standards began to rise together, though historians still argue over when ordinary wages improved.

sources.title: Industrial Revolution - Wikipedia
Allen, Robert C., 'Why the industrial revolution was British: commerce, induced invention, and the scientific revolution', Economic History Review 64.2 (2011), pp. 357-384
sources.author: Allen, Robert C.
sources.confirms: Abstract on Britain's wage and energy prices driving mechanisation in the 18th century; no 1760 start date.

sources.title: Allen, Robert C., The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (Cambridge, 2009)
sources.author: Allen, Robert C.
sources.confirms: Book page; no 1760 date.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Industrial Revolution'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page’s summary box date is 1733-1913. It also describes Britain’s economic development as 1760-1840 and the first Industrial Revolution as lasting from the mid-18th century to about 1830.

industrial-revolution-era-1760.detail: Why did Britain go first? Standard accounts list abundant cheap coal, farm productivity gains freeing labour, colonial markets and raw materials, stable politics and property rights, and banks to finance ventures. Economist Robert Lucas wrote that for once living standards of ordinary people underwent sustained growth, something earlier economists had thought impossible; others hold that improvement for most workers waited until Victorian decades. Steel, electricity and chemicals brought a Second Industrial Revolution from about 1870. Arnold Toynbee's lectures popularised the term after Louis-Auguste Blanqui's earlier use.

picture.alt: Coalbrookdale by Night, Philip James de Loutherbourg's 1801 painting of the Bedlam furnaces in the Shropshire ironworking valley.
picture.credit: Philip James de Loutherbourg, Science Museum, London, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

spinning-jenny-1764.summary: Around 1764 Hargreaves's jenny let one worker spin eight threads at once, the first machine of the cotton age. Kay's flying shuttle had left Lancashire weavers short of yarn. His left hand drew rovings out through a pair of clasped bars while his right turned a wheel that spun all eight. Yarn prices fell, Blackburn's spinners broke into his house and smashed his machines in 1768, and he fled to Nottingham, where he patented it in 1770.

sources.title: Spinning jenny
Allen, Robert C., 'The Industrial Revolution in Miniature: The Spinning Jenny in Britain, France, and India', Journal of Economic History 69.4 (2009), pp. 901-927
sources.author: Allen, Robert C.
sources.confirms: Abstract: Hargreaves's jenny of the 1760s paid in Britain's high-wage economy.

sources.title: Gragnolati, Ugo; Moschella, Daniele; Pugliese, Emanuele, 'The Spinning Jenny and the Industrial Revolution: A Reappraisal', Journal of Economic History 71.2 (2011), pp. 455-460
sources.author: Gragnolati, Ugo; Moschella, Daniele; Pugliese, Emanuele
sources.confirms: Abstract reappraises Allen's profitability argument.
sources.qualifies: Authors find the jenny would have been profitable in France too, against Allen's high-wage explanation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'spinning jenny'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page dates the invention to about 1764 and says Hargreaves patented the machine in 1770. It confirms that Hargreaves conceived the spinning jenny around 1764.

spinning-jenny-1764.detail:
Blackburn, with about 5,000 people, wove greys of linen warp and cotton weft that London finishers printed. Calico Act exemptions for fustians and 1736's Manchester Act permitting coloured cotton weft had shaped that trade. By 1750 carding and spinning earned nine shillings each of 36 paid for one 12-pound piece taking 14 days to weave. His jenny's coarse thread served as weft; its rovings still had to be carded and prepared by hand.

Hargreaves set up with Thomas James in Mill Street, Nottingham, making jennies in secret for one Mr Shipley. His patent (no. 962, 12 July 1770) collapsed when it emerged he had sold machines before filing; Lancashire manufacturers had offered £3,000. Stories of a daughter or wife named Jenny knocking over her wheel find no support in parish registers, and jenny probably abbreviates engine. Jennies grew to 120 spindles, stayed in use until about 1810 and gave way to Crompton's mule.

picture.alt: Spinning jenny of the type James Hargreaves built in 1764, engraving by Wilson Lowry, 1811.
picture.credit: Wilson Lowry, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

harunobu-nishiki-e-1765.summary: For New Year 1765, members of rival Edo poetry clubs commissioned private calendar prints (egoyomi) that hid long and short months in pictures. Their competition pushed block cutters and printers to use five, six or more colour blocks aligned by kento, small carved registration notches that hold each sheet in place, on thick hosho paper. Suzuki Harunobu designed many of these prints and, under patronage of hatamoto Okubo Kyosen, went on to publish commercial 'brocade pictures' that ended an era of two- and three-colour benizuri-e. Full-colour printing set conditions for Utamaro, Hokusai and Hiroshige and for print exports that reached European painters a century later.

sources.author: Bradel, Sabine S.
sources.confirms: Shift to nishiki-e late 1764 or early 1765; egoyomi exchanges; kento registration; Kyosen patronage

sources.author: Coaldrake, Kimi
sources.confirms: Harunobu's 1765 prints as technical innovation

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'nishiki-e'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Polychrome woodblock printing from 1765 associated with Harunobu

harunobu-nishiki-e-1765.detail: Sabine Bradel's 2025 open-access study in Asiatische Studien reassesses Harunobu's early career and dates shift to nishiki-e to late 1764 or early 1765, crediting kento with an increase in printable colours. Kento marks appear earlier, in 1740s, so 1765 marks adoption of full polychrome work rather than invention of registration.

picture.credit: Suzuki Harunobu, Cleveland Museum of Art

bengal-inoculation-holwell-1767.summary: In 1767 John Zephaniah Holwell, former East India Company surgeon, published an account of how itinerant Brahmin inoculators in Bengal protected children from smallpox. They dipped a needle in matter from a pustule, punctured skin on upper arm in a small circle, then prescribed a cold water regimen and diet for weeks. Earlier reports by Oliver Coult (1731) and a Dutch correspondent describe same practice. Practitioners moved village to village each spring, and mortality after inoculation was low. This Bengal method, with Ottoman and Chinese variolation, informed European practice before Jenner's cowpox vaccine of 1796.

sources.author: Arthur Boylston
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
sources.confirms: Bengal inoculation technique, Coult 1731 and Holwell accounts
sources.qualifies: rejects claims of ancient Indian origin; practice before about 1550 speculative

sources.author: J. Z. Holwell

bengal-inoculation-holwell-1767.detail: Boylston's review in Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine assesses India as a possible origin of inoculation and notes Coult's dating of Bengal practice to about 1580. He rejects claims of ancient Sanskrit descriptions of prophylactic inoculation as unsupported. Holwell's pamphlet is digitised by Wellcome Collection and Internet Archive.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0)

arkwright-water-frame-1769.summary: In 1769 Arkwright patented a water-driven spinning frame. He had used a model from 1765 based partly on a machine clockmaker John Kay had built for Thomas Highs. Rollers drew cotton out before spindles twisted it, and a water wheel drove 96 spindles at once, so its yarn was stronger and harder than any jenny's and could serve as warp. In 1771 he installed frames in his mill at Cromford on Derwent's bank, one of Britain's first buildings made to house machinery, where hours followed clocks and workers were employees rather than contractors.

Hills, Richard L., 'Sir Richard Arkwright and his patent granted in 1769', Notes and Records 24.2 (1970), pp. 254-260
sources.author: Hills, Richard L.
sources.venue: Notes and Records of the Royal Society
sources.confirms: Article dates the spinning-frame patent to 1769.

sources.author: Chapman, S. D.
sources.confirms: Abstract on factory forms before and at Arkwright.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'water frame'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1769. The page says R. Arkwright patented the water frame in 1769 and describes it as a water-powered spinning machine that produced cotton yarn suitable for warp.

arkwright-water-frame-1769.detail:
Arkwright's first mill, at Nottingham, ran on horse power; Cromford, begun in 1770 with partners, used river water. Combined with his carding machine it became the first factory running one continuous process from raw cotton to finished yarn, and Arkwright is credited with joining water power, machinery, continuous production and modern employment into one factory system. Until Samuel Crompton's mule of 1779 combined frame and jenny, his frame spun coarser counts.

Disclosing its design was punishable by death, yet Johann Gottfried Brügelmann obtained it and opened continental Europe's first spinning factory at Ratingen in 1783, also named Cromford, now a museum holding the world's only working water frame. Samuel Slater memorised its construction, evaded the 1774 ban on textile workers emigrating, left for New York in 1789 and with Moses Brown opened Slater Mill at Pawtucket in 1793.

picture.alt: Arkwright water frame made in 1775, held by Museum of Science and Industry, Manchester; photographed 2008.
picture.credit: Chris55, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

transit-of-venus-tahiti-1769.summary: Royal Society sent astronomer Charles Green with Lieutenant James Cook aboard Endeavour to observe Venus's transit across Sun on 3 June 1769 from Tahiti, part of a worldwide effort to measure solar system scale by parallax. At a fort on Matavai Bay's Point Venus, Green, Cook and Daniel Solander used Gregorian telescopes and a pendulum clock, with Tahitian hosts under chief Tutaha supplying food and labour. Their 1771 Philosophical Transactions report records contact timings that differed by tens of seconds owing to a dark 'drop' effect at Venus's limb. Combined with observations elsewhere, these timings helped produce solar distance estimates within a few percent of modern values. Cook's secret orders then sent Endeavour to search for a southern continent.

sources.title: Green, Charles; Cook, James, 'Observations made, by appointment of the Royal Society, at King George's Island in the South Sea', Philosophical Transactions 61 (1771)
sources.author: Green, Charles; Cook, James
sources.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society

transit-of-venus-tahiti-1769.detail: Orchiston's 2017 reassessment reviews Green's instruments, observing conditions and later use of data by Hornsby and Encke. Green died at sea in January 1771 before publishing his results. Point Venus also became a site of exchange and theft, with a quadrant stolen and recovered. Tupaia, a Ra'iatean navigator-priest, joined Endeavour from Tahiti afterwards, contributing geographic knowledge of Pacific islands recorded in his chart.

tupaia-chart-1769.summary: From 15 August 1769 Polynesian navigator Tupaia, sailing with James Cook, Banks and several officers, drew Cook a chart of 74 islands from memory. He devised a way to translate Polynesian wayfinding into compass logic: whichever island he placed at centre, his word avatea, noon sun, fixed its northern bearing. His chart shows linked voyaging routes from Rotuma and Tonga through Cook and Austral islands to Rapa Nui, and from Tahiti via Tuamotus and Marquesas to Hawai'i.

Eckstein, Lars; Schwarz, Anja, 'The Making of Tupaia's Map', Journal of Pacific History 54.1 (2019), pp. 1-95
sources.author: Eckstein, Lars; Schwarz, Anja
sources.confirms: Full text: the chart was made between August 1769 and February 1770 aboard Endeavour.

sources.title: British Library, Add MS 21593 C, chart of the Society Islands, July-August 1769 (catalogue entry)
sources.author: Banks, Joseph; Tupaia
sources.confirms: 1769; the date range is July-August 1769.

tupaia-chart-1769.detail:
Trained in Ra'iatea's schools of learning, Tupaia carried from his father and grandfather the bearings, sailing times and star paths to islands as far as Rotuma, Samoa and Tonga. Bora Bora warriors wounded him and drove him to Tahiti about 1763, where he became high priest and adviser to the Papara chief Amo and his wife Purea. Cook's Admiralty journal records that Tupaia said he or his ancestors had visited most islands on his chart, excepting Rotuma and Oahu.

Older research summarised by Joan Druett held that his own voyaging covered only 13 nearby islands; Lars Eckstein and Anja Schwarz read his chart as evidence of detailed knowledge across the Polynesian triangle, New Zealand probably excepted, and question whether Cook undervalued him. In New Zealand some Māori welcomed him as a tohunga, an expert, and gave him a dog-skin cloak. He died on 20 December 1770 of illness contracted at Batavia.

watt-separate-condenser-1769.summary: In 1769 Watt patented a steam engine that burned half the coal, cheap enough to run factories. Newcomen engines condensed steam inside their working cylinder, so every stroke chilled the metal and part of each new charge of steam was wasted reheating it. Repairing a model at Glasgow University in 1763, Watt saw that loss, and in 1765 conceived a chamber kept cold and under vacuum into which steam was drawn from a cylinder kept hot.

watt-separate-condenser-1769.detail:
Steam entered below the piston. At top of stroke an inlet valve closed and a passage to Watt's condenser opened, where water spray, about seven times the volume of condensed steam, absorbed its latent heat, and an air pump removed condensate and injected water. Atmospheric pressure then drove the piston down. John Roebuck took a two-thirds share, cleared Watt's debts and funded his prototype at Kinneil House, but Watt spent five years failing to find any cylinder bored true enough to seal without water above its piston.

When Roebuck's business failed, Matthew Boulton took his share in return for cancelling a £1,200 debt, moved Watt's Kinneil engine to his Soho works, and in 1775 had Parliament extend Watt's patent to 1800. John Wilkinson's boring machine of 1774, its cutting shaft supported at both ends, supplied cylinders accurate, Boulton wrote, to within one old shilling's thickness.

mechanical-turk-1770.summary: In 1770 Kempelen unveiled a chess automaton that beat challengers for decades. After watching François Pelletier's illusions at Schönbrunn in 1769, he had promised Empress Maria Theresa something better within a year. His Automaton Chess Player, finished in early 1770, showed a turbaned figure seated at its cabinet, whose doors opened to reveal clockwork. A chess master sat hidden inside: visible gears ran only one third of its depth, his sliding seat let him dodge each opened door, magnets under its thin board signalled every move, and levers worked the Turk's arm.

mechanical-turk-1770.detail: Each piece carried a small strong magnet, so corresponding magnets beneath the board swung as pieces moved and the hidden player could follow play on his own board by candlelight. Kempelen showed it reluctantly and dismantled it, but Joseph II had it rebuilt for a visit of Grand Duke Paul in 1781, and a European tour followed. After Kempelen's death in 1804 Johann Nepomuk Maelzel bought it, toured Europe and America, and employed masters including Johann Allgaier, Jacques Mouret and William Schlumberger. Napoleon is said to have played it in 1809. Edgar Allan Poe's 1836 essay argued a human must be inside. Fire destroyed it in Philadelphia in 1854, and Silas Mitchell then published how it had worked.

rongorongo-rapa-nui-1770.summary: Rongorongo consists of several hundred glyph types, including birds, humans and plants, carved in reverse boustrophedon lines on wooden tablets, staffs and a breastplate. Fewer than 30 inscribed objects survive, scattered in museums after missionaries noticed them in 1864; readers had died or been taken in Peruvian slave raids of 1862 to 1863. One tablet, Mamari, records a 30-night lunar calendar. A 2024 study radiocarbon dated wood of four tablets: three fell in nineteenth century, but one tablet's wood dates to about 1493 to 1509, which allows an independent script tradition predating European arrival in 1722. Steven Roger Fischer and others hold instead that Rapanui began writing after seeing Spanish documents signed in 1770.

rongorongo-rapa-nui-1770.detail: Fischer catalogued every surviving inscription in 1997 and argues for a procreation-chant structure in some texts, a reading many specialists dispute. Wood from a dated tree may have been carved much later, so 2024 dates bound only when timber grew. A 1770 anchor reflects a common argument that Spanish annexation ceremony, where chiefs 'signed' a document, provided a stimulus; older dates would push invention earlier. Script remains undeciphered.

cromford-mill-1771.summary: In 1771 Arkwright's Cromford mill ran day and night in two 12-hour shifts of 200 workers: the factory was born. Demand for spun cotton had outrun supply since 1733's flying shuttle, and jennies could not meet it. He chose Cromford because the Cromford Sough, draining Wirksworth's lead mines, and Bonsall Brook gave water all year to turn his frames; Jedediah Strutt, Samuel Need and John Smalley backed him. His mill was widely copied.

cromford-mill-1771.detail: Most employees were women and children, and its youngest was seven. Later Arkwright raised his minimum age to ten and gave children six hours of schooling a week so they could keep records their parents could not read. Because 200 workers exceeded what Cromford village could supply, he built housing nearby, among the first manufacturers to do so; Stuart Fisher calls it history's first factory housing development, with shops, pubs, chapels and a school. Its gate shut at exactly 6 am and 6 pm, and latecomers lost one day's pay and were fined another. Extended in 1785, Cromford Mill is now the centrepiece of Derwent Valley Mills, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

jaquet-droz-automata-1768.summary: By 1774 Pierre Jaquet-Droz and his workshop in La Chaux-de-Fonds had built three clockwork figures that write, draw and play music; a 2024 Delaware Press chapter dates their Writer to 1774 and Britannica captions it about 1772. Their musician presses keys of a custom organ; their draughtsman draws four pictures from cams encoding hand movements; their writer dips his quill and writes any text up to 40 letters, selected on a coding wheel, his eyes following each line. Because that wheel can be reset, this Writer counts among remote ancestors of programmable machines. Their firm's production ran from 1758 to 1811, spanning spectacle, luxury mechanisms and useful machines; Vaucanson's automata of 1738 had opened a Paris market for such devices.
