Their draughtsman shifts on his chair and blows dust off his pencil, drawing Louis XV, a royal couple thought to be Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, a dog captioned Mon toutou and Cupid in a butterfly-drawn chariot. Their writer, 70 cm tall, shakes his wrist after inking to avoid blots. These figures travelled and changed hands several times before Neuchâtel's History and Archaeology Society bought them in 1906 for 75,000 gold francs for its Musée d'Art et d'Histoire, where they still run.

kaitai-shinsho-1774.summary: In 1774 Japanese physicians published a Dutch anatomy book in translation, letting Western science in a century before Japan opened. Its plates matched what they saw, and they began translating next day. Only Maeno read any Dutch, and Japan then had no Dutch dictionaries, so they worked out meanings word by word, a process Sugita later compared to cryptanalysis. Kaitai Shinsho, four volumes of text and one of plates in classical Chinese, appeared from Suharaya Ichibee in 1774.

kaitai-shinsho-1774.detail: Their Dutch book was in turn translated from Johann Adam Kulmus's Tabulae Anatomicae, published in Gdańsk before 1722; they also consulted Bartholin, Blankaart, Veslingius and others. In 1773 they issued a five-page flyer, Kaitai Yakuzu, to test official reaction, and court physician Katsuragawa Hosan cleared their book with the shōgun's household. Odano Naotake, a samurai artist from Akita referred by Hiraga Gennai, redrew its plates in half a year. Maeno, aware of imperfections, kept his name off it. Afterwards Dutch comprehension advanced along with medicine; terms coined for this translation, among them shinkei for nerve, nankotsu for cartilage and dōmyaku for artery, remain in use.

cumming-s-trap-flush-toilet-1775.summary: Alexander Cumming, a Bond Street watchmaker, received British patent no. 1105 in 1775 for "a water-closet upon a new construction". Its soil pipe was bent into a recurved S twelve to eighteen inches below the bowl so a plug of water stayed in its bend and, in his words, "cut off all communication of smell from below", while a sliding valve emptied the bowl and refilled the trap with fresh water at each use. That water seal is still the principle in every toilet, sink and floor drain. Joseph Bramah's 1778 patent replaced Cumming's leaky slider with a hinged valve and sold in thousands. Thomas Twyford's one-piece ceramic washdown closet of 1883 and Thomas Crapper's siphon cistern patents made water closets cheap enough for ordinary houses.

hendesehane-naval-engineering-school-177.summary: After defeat by Russia in 1774, grand admiral Cezayirli Gazi Hasan Paşa backs a school of mathematics inside Istanbul's imperial shipyard. French archive records date its opening to 29 April 1775, in a disused galley shed at Tersane under French officer Baron de Tott's supervision, run by engineer Kermovan and an English convert known as Mustafa Ağa, with ten students, mostly serving captains. Lessons cover geometry, trigonometry, navigation and gunnery from translated French textbooks. Renamed Mühendishane-i Tersane-i Amire in 1781 and given a new building in 1784, it became Mühendishane-i Bahri-i Hümayun, the naval engineering school, and spawned a land engineering school at Hasköy in 1795 under Selim III's Nizam-ı Cedid. Istanbul Technical University traces its founding to this classroom. Older Ottoman accounts gave 1773, a date Kaçar and Beydilli have corrected.

hiraga-gennai-elekiter-1776.summary: In 1776 Hiraga Gennai rebuilt a broken Dutch static electricity generator in Japan and showed its sparks; he called it erekiteru, and IEEE recognises it as a milestone, Japan's first such device. In Edo he worked as pharmacologist, satirist, painter and inventor, producing his own thermometer and asbestos cloth. He exhibited his inventions in Edo and came to senior official Tanuma Okitsugu's notice.

hiraga-gennai-elekiter-1776.detail: Gennai was born Shiraishi Kunitomo about 1729. He prospected iron in Izu in 1761, helped Kawagoe Domain open an asbestos mine in 1766, improved charcoal furnaces and river boats, and wrote satires including Fūryū Shidōken den and Nenashigusa. His circle included physicians Sugita Genpaku and Nakagawa Jun'an, whose anatomy translation he helped by recommending its artist. In late 1779 he was arrested for killing two carpenters in a drunken rage and died of tetanus in prison on 24 January 1780; shogunate officials refused Sugita permission for a funeral, so he held a memorial without Gennai's body. His biography does not describe how his erekiteru worked.

watt-boulton-engines-1776-1776.summary: In 1776 Boulton and Watt's first engine began work at a colliery on half a Newcomen's coal. Parliament had extended Watt's patent to 1800 in 1775. A third engine ran at Stratford-le-Bow that summer, and their first sale went to the Carron Company's ironworks near Falkirk. These engines sold best where fuel cost most; Cornish mines ordered three in 1777.

watt-boulton-engines-1776-1776.detail: Wilkinson's boring machine made these engines possible: Boulton wrote in 1776 that its 50-inch cylinder at Tipton did not err by an old shilling's thickness. Boulton and Watt charged customers a share of coal saved against Newcomen engines. When a London brewer who used horses, not coal, wanted an engine, Watt needed another measure and defined horsepower; around 1784 he set charges at £5 per horsepower per year for his patent's life. Early Watt engines, like Newcomen's, still relied on atmospheric pressure to push their pistons; rotative motion, double action and parallel motion came in the 1780s.

wealth-of-nations-1776.summary: In 1776 Adam Smith argued that divided labour and free exchange rather than gold make a nation rich. Europe's trade then ran under mercantilist rules: colonial monopolies, tariffs, guild privileges and restrictions on labour, all meant to pile up national wealth. Division of labour, Smith added, is limited by market size, and self-interested exchange, guided as if by an invisible hand, served society.

sources.author: Smith, Adam
sources.confirms: Catalogue of the 1776 first edition, whose first chapter treats the division of labour.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'the Wealth of Nations'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors

wealth-of-nations-1776.detail: Smith's book drew on seventeen years of notes and took about ten years to write; it answered Colbert's mercantilism and the physiocrats alike. Its first edition sold out in six months, though David Hume told printer William Strahan it demanded too much thought to rival Gibbon's Decline and Fall. Five editions appeared in Smith's lifetime, in 1776, 1778, 1784, 1786 and 1789, and Edwin Cannan's team collated them in 1904. George Stigler called his extent-of-market theorem the core of a theory of firms and industry; Paul Samuelson found in Smith's use of supply and demand an anticipation of Walras's general equilibrium.

bengali-type-halhed-grammar-1778.summary: Nathaniel Brassey Halhed's A Grammar of the Bengal Language, printed at Hooghly in 1778, carried Bengali script in movable metal type for first time. Charles Wilkins, a Company writer, designed and cut punches, and Panchanan Karmakar, a blacksmith from Tribeni, cut and cast much of the fount and trained others. Bengali's conjunct consonants required hundreds of sorts. Karmakar later moved to Serampore mission press, where with his son-in-law Manohar he cut types for Bengali, Devanagari, Persian and other scripts used in dozens of languages. This fount started Bengali print culture, newspapers and textbooks that shaped nineteenth century Calcutta.

crompton-spinning-mule-1779.summary: In 1779 Crompton's mule spun yarn fine and strong enough for British cotton to rival India's. Hargreaves's jenny spun many threads but weak ones; Arkwright's frame drew roving through rollers for strong warp but needed water power. Between 1775 and 1779 Samuel Crompton of Bolton bred both together, hence mule. His machine held roving bobbins in a creel on its fixed frame and set spindles on a carriage that rolled out, drawing and twisting, then clamped and ran back to wind on. Rollers and carriage both evened thread, giving strong fine yarn for warp or weft. Crompton could not afford to patent it and sold his rights.

Catling, Harold, 'The Development of the Spinning Mule', Textile History 9.1 (1978), pp. 35-57
sources.author: Catling, Harold

crompton-spinning-mule-1779.detail: His first mule, built of wood with bands and pulleys, carried 48 spindles. It spun a pound of 60s count a day at 1,700 revolutions per minute on one sixteenth of a horsepower. He sold the rights to David Dale and went back to weaving; Dale patented and profited. Henry Stones of Horwich added toothed gearing and metal rollers, and once Arkwright's patents expired several makers developed it. Muslin supply rose, feeding Cartwright's power loom. The mule was the most common spinning machine from 1790 to about 1900; Richard Roberts's self-acting mule of 1825 made it automatic, carriages grew to 1,320 spindles and 150 feet, and Lancashire alone held 5 million mule spindles at peak.

iron-bridge-1779.summary: In 1779 cast iron's first bridge spanned the Severn at Coalbrookdale. Architect Thomas Farnolls Pritchard proposed one of cast iron to ironmaster John Wilkinson in 1773; Parliament authorised it in 1776, and Abraham Darby III cast and built it. Five sectional ribs spanning 100 feet 6 inches first crossed the Severn on 2 July 1779, raised from boats with a scaffold of derrick poles. Nearly 1,700 parts, 378 tons of iron, were joined with carpenters' dovetails and mortise-and-tenon joints, since no one had yet worked out ironwork joints.

iron-bridge-1779.detail: Pritchard, a designer of chimneypieces and funerary monuments, died in December 1777, a month after work began. Components were cast individually to fit one another rather than to standard sizes, with discrepancies of several centimetres between nominally identical pieces; the heaviest weighs over five tons. An iron bridge begun at Lyon in 1755 had been abandoned, and a 72-foot wrought-iron footbridge stood at Kirklees from 1769, so this was cast iron's first major bridge rather than its first idea. It opened to traffic on 1 January 1781; by the mid-1790s tolls paid shareholders 8 per cent a year, and Ironbridge town grew at its northern end. Closed to vehicles in 1934, it anchors Ironbridge Gorge World Heritage Site.

mysorean-rockets-1780.summary: In 1780 Mysore's army fired iron-cased rockets at the British, the first of their kind; Britain copied them. Rockets had been paper-cased in Europe and could not hold high pressure. Mysore's army under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan packed black powder into hammered soft-iron tubes about eight inches long and up to three inches across, strapped to four-foot bamboo shafts; iron chambers let a pound of powder carry almost 1,000 yards, with ranges up to two kilometres. Hyder Ali's rocket corps grew to about 1,200 men. At Pollilur in 1780 a stray rocket is thought to have detonated Colonel Baillie's ammunition and helped defeat East India Company forces.

mysorean-rockets-1780.detail: Tipu's manual Fathul Mujahidin, compiled by Mir Zain-ul-'Abidin Shushtari, assigned 200 rocket men to each cushoon, or brigade, of his 16 to 24. They were trained to set launch angles from cylinder diameter and distance to target, and wheeled launchers fired several at once. Some rockets carried pierced incendiary cylinders, others iron points or sword blades bound to the bamboo, which made them tumble unpredictably at the end of flight. They were used against the Company at Srirangapatam in 1792 and 1799. Rocket cases collected from Mysore went to the Royal Woolwich Arsenal, which began a rocket programme in 1801; William Congreve demonstrated his solid-fuel rockets in 1805 and published his Concise Account in 1807.

montgolfier-balloon-1783.summary: In 1783 the Montgolfiers' balloon carried people into the sky for the first time, and the age of flight began. Joseph and Étienne, paper makers from Annonay, believed smoke carried a buoyant gas, so they heated air under paper-lined cloth envelopes. After an unmanned flight at Annonay on 4 June 1783 and a sheep, duck and rooster lofted before Louis XVI at Versailles on 19 September, Étienne built with wallpaper maker Jean-Baptiste Réveillon a 1,700-cubic-metre balloon for people. He became history's first human to leave ground in one, in a tethered test in Réveillon's yard, most likely on 15 October 1783; Pilâtre de Rozier rose to 25 metres that same day.

sources.confirms: The page gives no date for a tethered ascent. It dates the first manned free flight to November 21, 1783. It does not confirm the record’s claim.

montgolfier-balloon-1783.verification_note: Annonay's flight of 4 June and a first manned free flight of 21 November 1783 are confirmed; no source records Etienne Montgolfier's tethered ascent.
montgolfier-balloon-1783.detail:
Joseph's first test was a wooden box 0.9 by 0.9 by 1.2 metres covered in taffeta, lifted by burning paper beneath it. Their Annonay balloon held nearly 790 cubic metres, weighed 225 kilograms and flew two kilometres in ten minutes. The animals survived their eight-minute, three-kilometre flight, so Louis XVI allowed human passengers. Réveillon's balloon stood about 23 metres tall and 15 across, painted deep blue with zodiac signs, fleurs-de-lis and suns bearing Louis XVI's face.

On 21 November 1783 Pilâtre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes made history's first free flight, from the Château de la Muette, about 900 metres above Paris for nine kilometres in 25 minutes, landing on the Butte-aux-Cailles. Ten days later Jacques Charles rose to about three kilometres in a hydrogen balloon of his own design.

mutis-botanical-expedition-1783.summary: In 1783 Charles III authorised a Royal Botanical Expedition in New Granada under Cádiz-born physician José Celestino Mutis, based first at Mariquita and from 1791 at Santafé de Bogotá. Over three decades a workshop of more than 40 painters, many trained locally in Quito and Bogotá, produced about 6,000 folio plates of Andean plants in tempera, using pigments made from local plants and minerals. Mutis studied cinchona species for quinine, built an astronomical observatory in Bogotá in 1803 and trained a generation including Francisco José de Caldas and Jorge Tadeo Lozano, several of whom led independence and were executed in 1816. Daniela Bleichmar reads the plates as an imperial visual inventory executed by American hands.

mutis-botanical-expedition-1783.detail: The plates, shipped to Madrid in 1816, remained unpublished until a joint Spanish-Colombian edition began in 1954. Mutis's correspondence with Linnaeus and his quina trade disputes with Sebastián López Ruiz are documented by Mauricio Nieto Olarte. Sebastián Molina-Betancur's 2023 book traces Mutis's teaching of Newtonian physics in Bogotá from 1762.

cartwright-power-loom-1785.summary: In 1785 Cartwright patented a power loom, and weaving, the last handcraft in cotton, moved into the factory. Spinning had been mechanised; weaving still depended on hand looms. Edmund Cartwright, a clergyman with no weaving background, patented his power loom in 1785, hand-operated and crude, but by 1787 he had versions driven by water and soon after coupled looms to steam, using levers to throw flying shuttles through their sheds. His machine did not pay, because looms had to stop while warp was dressed with size, yet over following decades others refined his ideas into reliable automatic looms.

cartwright-power-loom-1785.detail: Automatic looms had been proposed by M. de Gennes in Paris in 1684 and by Vaucanson in 1745, then forgotten. Grimshaw of Manchester licensed Cartwright's design and built a small steam-powered weaving factory in 1790, which burnt down. William Radcliffe improved the take-up in 1802; Thomas Johnson's dressing frame of 1803 solved warp sizing, and he ran 200 steam looms in Manchester by 1806; William Horrocks of Stockport hung the lathe from the frame in 1803; Richard Roberts's cast-iron loom came in 1822 and the Lancashire loom of Kenworthy and Bullough in 1841. Handloom weavers rioted in Lancashire in 1826. Cheaper cloth raised demand and exports and drew women and children into mills at low pay.

aboriginal-fire-management-observed-1788.summary: Aboriginal peoples across Australia have long lit small, cool fires in mosaics timed by season to clear undergrowth, flush game, encourage grass for kangaroos and protect camps and resource patches. Journals from 1788 at Sydney Cove, and later explorers, describe open, park-like woodland and constant smoke. Rhys Jones named this practice 'fire-stick farming' in 1969, and a 1998 review assessed its ecological evidence. A 2008 study combined Martu hunting observations in Western Desert with satellite imagery and showed that Aboriginal burning creates finer-grained vegetation mosaics than lightning regimes, raising small-game yields. Removal of such burning after colonisation changed fuel loads and fire behaviour in many regions.

aboriginal-fire-management-observed-1788.detail: Bill Gammage argued in 2011 from colonial paintings and diaries that burning shaped a continent-wide estate, a thesis praised and also criticised for overreach. Ecologists reply that regimes varied by region and that some open landscapes reflect climate and soil. Northern Australian savanna burning programmes now draw on Aboriginal practice to cut late-season wildfires and earn carbon credits. Fire management knowledge persisted through ranger groups and is being revived in southern states.

picture.credit: Joseph Lycett

lavoisier-elements-chemistry-1789.summary: In 1789 Lavoisier defined an element as what cannot be broken down and listed 33: modern chemistry began. Writing out fermentation as grape must = carbonic acid + alcohol, he gave chemistry its first equation and insisted on true balance between what enters a reaction and what leaves it, grounding conservation of mass.

lavoisier-elements-chemistry-1789.detail: Lavoisier showed that fermentation yields carbonic gas and spirit of wine. He preferred to call that spirit alcohol, after the Arabic, since cider and fermented sugar give it as well as wine, and called the reaction one of the most extraordinary in chemistry. His list ran from oxygen, azote and hydrogen through sulphur, phosphorus and charcoal to metals such as antimony, cobalt, platina and tungstein, and to earths including lime, magnesia and silex that later proved compounds. Robert Kerr's English translation, Elements of Chemistry in a New Systematic Order, appeared in Edinburgh in 1790 with 13 copperplates engraved by Madame Lavoisier. In France this principle is taught as Lavoisier's law: nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed.

nizam-i-cedid-1789.summary: From 1789 Selim III built an army drilled on European lines; the attempt cost him his throne. Defeats by Russia, sealed at Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 and again at Jassy in 1792, had convinced reformers that the Janissary-based army could no longer hold. Selim, sultan from 1789, headed them and convened a consultative assembly for tajdid, renewal. His new army was paid from a new treasury, Irad-i Cedid, fed by confiscated timar grants and new taxes on alcohol and wool. Contemporaries called only that army Nizam-i Cedid; its name later covered all Selim's reforms.

nizam-i-cedid-1789.detail: Ideas for military reform had occupied Ottoman statesmen for almost a century before Selim, and his biographers stress he was hardly their sole instigator. His predecessor Mustafa III had written in 1774 that his state had declined into meanness and vulgarity. Selim's new army demanded new taxation and uprooting of entrenched elites: absentee timar holders lost their licences, old taxes were redirected, and tariffs were reworked. Janissaries saw this threat to their privileges; in 1806's Edirne incident they joined local notables to lynch a judge announcing New Order deployments, then exploited resentment of Westernisation and higher taxes. Their coup deposed Selim in 1807, ending an era usually dated 1789 to 1807, though his army is judged an important step toward later reform.

sydney-smallpox-epidemic-1789.summary: In April 1789, fifteen months after First Fleet landed, colonists found Eora people dead and dying along Sydney Harbour shores with pustules of smallpox. Surgeon John White and Governor Arthur Phillip recorded bodies in coves and caves; one estimate held that half of Aboriginal people around Port Jackson died. Infection spread inland along trade and kin routes. Its origin is disputed: Noel Butlin weighed Makassan trepangers in north against First Fleet; Christopher Warren argues that variolous matter carried by fleet surgeons in bottles was deliberately or carelessly released; John Carmody contends that illness may have been chickenpox. Epidemic wrecked Eora society and cleared land British settlers then occupied.

sydney-smallpox-epidemic-1789.detail: Convicts and marines were largely immune from childhood exposure; one sailor, a Native American, died. Bennelong and Colebee survived, Colebee bearing scars. Warren compiled evidence that surgeon's variolation stock survived voyage in sealed bottles. Critics ask why no colonist reported release. Later epidemics in 1829 to 1831 and 1860s spread from northern contacts. No contemporary medical record distinguishes variola from varicella with certainty, which keeps debate alive.

merina-rice-dikes-1790.summary: In Madagascar's central highlands, Merina rulers mobilised corvée labour to dike Ikopa river, drain marshland and lay out bunded paddy fields fed by canals, converting swamp around Antananarivo into irrigated rice. Gerald Berg traces this hydraulic technology to roughly 1680 to 1750, and Gwyn Campbell shows rice surpluses after 1700 funding population growth and specialist artisans. Andrianampoinimerina, who united central Imerina from about 1795 and ruled to 1810, made control of water works and grain a basis of royal power, alongside arms imports and slave exports. Rice terraces and paddies still define highland landscapes.

merina-rice-dikes-1790.detail: Berg argued that irrigated rice let Merina kings command labour and build the monarchy, while Campbell's economic history sets the works within an island empire tied to Indian Ocean trade. Later king Radama I and his successors extended canals and dikes with forced labour, fanompoana. Dating relies on oral history collected in Callet's Tantara ny Andriana (1870s), so this year is approximate.

picture.credit: Cem Genco

us-patent-act-1790-1790.summary: In 1790 the United States passed its first patent law, giving inventors a limited monopoly in return for publishing how an invention works. Patentable subject matter was any useful art, manufacture, engine, machine or device, or any improvement not before known or used; successful applicants received sole right to make, use and sell their invention. A board of three cabinet officers judged each application and set its term, never beyond fourteen years. Fifty-seven patents issued before Congress replaced this statute in February 1793.

sources.author: Merges, Robert P.

us-patent-act-1790-1790.detail:
Thomas Jefferson, Henry Knox and Edmund Randolph, holding the State, War and Attorney General posts, formed that first Patent Board and granted patents judged sufficiently useful and important. Fees totalled about four to five dollars: fifty cents to file plus ten cents per hundred words of specification, two dollars for producing the patent, one dollar for affixing the Great Seal and twenty cents for endorsement. Applicants supplied a written specification, with drawing and model where possible, detailed enough for someone skilled in the art to use the invention.

Samuel Hopkins received the first patent on July 31, 1790, for making pot and pearl ashes; potash went into glass, soap, cloth dyeing, saltpetre and gunpowder. This Hopkins came from a town north of Baltimore, not Pittsford, Vermont, as often supposed. Three patents issued in 1790, thirty-three in 1791, eleven in 1792 and ten in 1793. Board meetings were irregular and each application needed careful inspection, so review advanced slowly; Congress dropped examination in its Patent Act of 1793. Records of these patents burned in 1836.

leblanc-process-1791.summary: In 1791 Nicolas Leblanc patented a way to make soda ash from salt; glass and soap could be made in bulk, and the chemical industry began. It answered a prize of 2,400 livres offered in 1783 by Louis XVI and France's Academy of Sciences, because alkali was vital to glass, textile, soap and paper makers and western Europe had imported it since deforestation made wood-ash potash uneconomical. His first plant, built that year for the Duke at Saint-Denis, began producing 320 tons of soda yearly; France's Revolution denied him his prize money.

leblanc-process-1791.detail:
Salt was first treated with sulfuric acid to give sodium sulfate, called salt cake, plus hydrogen chloride, a reaction Carl Wilhelm Scheele had discovered in 1772. Leblanc's contribution was its second step: salt cake mixed with crushed limestone was heated with coal, whose carbon reduced sulfate to sulfide, which then reacted with limestone to yield sodium carbonate and calcium sulfide, together called black ash. Water leached out soda ash, in a step termed lixiviation.

French revolutionaries seized his plant with Louis Philippe's estate in 1794 and publicized his trade secrets. Napoleon returned it in 1801, but Leblanc lacked funds to repair it against rival soda works and killed himself in 1806. French producers made 10,000 to 15,000 tons yearly by the early 19th century; Britain practised his process most widely, from a Losh family works at Walker on Tyneside in 1816. Britain's Alkali Act later forced conversion of waste calcium sulfide to carbonate, and Solvay's process gradually made Leblanc's obsolete.

buttonwood-agreement-1792.summary: On 17 May 1792 twenty-four New York stockbrokers and merchants signed a pact to deal only with each other, cutting out auctioneers, and to charge no less than one quarter percent commission. Legend places its signing under a buttonwood tree outside 68 Wall Street near Tontine Coffee House, and today's New York Stock Exchange counts it as founding. Peter Eisenstadt (Prospects, 1994) showed this account is largely legendary: it distorts what happened at that meeting, and claims that Buttonwood established any exchange are without foundation. Library of Congress's research guide likewise calls signing under a tree myth. Brokers had met two months earlier at Corre's Hotel to bring order to their trade, worked from offices and coffee houses, and from 1793 did business inside Tontine Coffee House at Wall and Water streets.

buttonwood-agreement-1792.detail: New York Stock Exchange archives hold its original, and a plaque on Wall Street Hotel's side, at Wall and Pearl streets, marks its site. Eisenstadt traces how Buttonwood legend endured for more than a century.

chappe-semaphore-1792.summary: In 1792 Chappe demonstrated his optical telegraph to legislators; by 1794 his towers sent a message 230 kilometres from Lille to Paris in under an hour. Relay towers stood within sight of each other, each carrying pivoted arms whose positions spelled symbols that operators read through telescopes and repeated onward. Revolutionary France, at war on several fronts, appointed Claude Chappe Ingénieur-Télégraphiste in summer 1792; its Convention funded the Paris-Lille line in 1793, and it opened in July 1794. Its first telegram, on 15 August 1794, reported France's capture of Condé-sur-l'Escaut from Austrian forces; eventually 556 stations covered 4,800 kilometres, in use until the 1850s.

chappe-semaphore-1792.verification_note: Field dates French optical telegraphy from 1793; France's Convention funded a Paris-Lille line in 1793, it opened in July 1794 and its first telegram reached Paris on 15 August 1794, while 1792 saw only a demonstration to legislators.
chappe-semaphore-1792.detail:
Work began in mid-1790, when his brothers and he sought some way for central government to receive intelligence and send orders in the shortest possible time. Claude considered sound, smoke and even electricity, dropped for want of insulation that could withstand available electrostatic sources. Their first public demonstration, on 2 March 1791 between Brûlon and Parcé, 16 kilometres apart, used modified pendulum clocks with ten-numeral dials, synchronised and read against black and white panels through telescopes, with numbers looked up in a codebook; Chappe later saw that synchronising signals alone could carry messages. Twice Paris mobs destroyed his apparatus at Place de l'Étoile, suspecting royalist signalling; his brother Ignace's election to the Legislative Assembly helped their cause.

A message's first symbol passed through 15 stations to Lille in nine minutes, and a complete 36-symbol message took about 32 minutes depending on weather. A 50-station line to Strasbourg, 488 kilometres, followed in 1798. Half a century later electrical telegraphs, cheaper, swifter and more private, replaced semaphore lines, which could not cross wide water without an island relay.

murdoch-gas-lighting-1792.summary: In 1792 William Murdoch lit his house with gas made from coal; within 15 years gas lamps lit London's streets. Murdoch, Boulton and Watt's senior engine erector at Redruth, was trying to replace light from oil and tallow. Accounts from 1794 describe his small retort of heated coals with a three or four foot iron tube, through which gas passed to an old gun barrel and was lit. His Redruth house became the first home lit by gas; in 1805 he fully lit Philips and Lee's cotton mill in Manchester, the first factory so illuminated, whose 50 gas lights soon grew to 904.

murdoch-gas-lighting-1792.verification_note: Accounts agree Murdoch began experimenting with coal gas in 1792 at Redruth, lit part of Soho Foundry in 1798 and Philips and Lee's mill in 1805; his first public demonstration is dated 1802.
murdoch-gas-lighting-1792.detail:
Dates are uncertain: most sources place his first practical demonstration between 1792 and 1794, and about a decade earlier Jean-Pierre Minckelers had used gas lighting on a practical scale. Murdoch spent following years testing the quantity and quality of gases from different substances and ways to transport, store, purify and burn them; William Fairbairn recalled him filling a bladder at a gasworks and walking home by its flame, discharged through an old tobacco pipe stem.

Back in Birmingham from 1798 he lit part of Soho Foundry's main building, probably not permanently, and in 1802 illuminated its exterior to celebrate peace at Amiens. The Manchester mill took four years from proposal, as he made large-scale lighting practicable and cost effective. His 1808 paper to the Royal Society, Account of the Application of Gas from Coal to Economical Purposes, earned its Rumford Gold Medal. Boulton and Watt dominated factory lighting by 1809 but left streets and homes to rivals such as his former assistant Samuel Clegg and Frederick Albert Winsor.

macartney-embassy-1793.summary: In 1793 the Qianlong emperor rejected Britain's request for open trade. Envoy Macartney sought new ports for British trade, a permanent embassy in Beijing, a small coastal island for British use and looser restrictions on merchants at Guangzhou (Canton); Britain, paying silver for tea, brought clocks, telescopes and weapons to display its ingenuity. He met Qianlong at Chengde on 14 September 1793, kneeling once rather than performing a full kowtow. Qianlong refused all of these requests, writing to George III that his empire lacked no product and needed no outside manufactures.

sources.author: Hevia, James L.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'George Macartney Earl Macartney'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The page gives no specific year for the rejection. It says Macartney was sent to China after becoming a viscount in 1792; a caption depicts the embassy in 1793.

macartney-embassy-1793.detail:
Macartney and Henry Dundas had anticipated dispute over court ritual. Dundas instructed him to accept ceremonies that did not compromise his sovereign's honour, and Macartney offered to kneel on one knee as before his own king; Qianlong's edict of 8 September allowed one prostration instead of nine. In an imperial yellow tent before several thousand attendees, Macartney knelt once, exchanged gifts and presented George III's letter. Qianlong's reply called Europeans barbarians and ordered the king to tremblingly obey and show no negligence, treating him as a subject, which angered king and public in England; critics there said the embassy had acknowledged its own country's inferiority, and caricatures showed Macartney debasing himself.

Historians long read this failure as China's refusal to modernise. Fuller archives published in the 1990s challenged that reading: Qing officials appear as competent political operators who placated British power in India with unspecified promises to avoid conflict and loss of trade, and failure owed less to kowtow refusal than to incompatible world views. Courtiers noted flexible steel swords and six brass cannon among gifts, but a model steam engine stayed unpacked and went to Dinwiddie for India. The East India Company was then beginning to grow opium in India for sale in China against its silver deficit.

cotton-gin-1793.summary: On 14 March 1794 Eli Whitney received United States patent for a cotton gin that pulled fibre through wire teeth on a revolving cylinder and narrow slots in iron breastwork too small for seeds, while brushes swept lint from those teeth. Britannica dates his invention to 1793, when he built it in Georgia and applied for patent that October; Angela Lakwete (Inventing the Cotton Gin, Johns Hopkins, 2005) dates it to 1794 and shows that gins existed for centuries before him: an Asian hand-cranked roller gin reached America in the seventeenth century, and enslaved Africans built foot-powered models, but rollers could not clean short-staple upland cotton. Southern mechanics soon turned his design into saw gins. Cleaning fifty pounds of lint daily where hand work managed one, it made cotton hugely profitable, fixed southern states on cotton and institutionalised slavery (Britannica).

cotton-gin-1793.detail: Picking became its bottleneck, and planters bought more enslaved people to expand production: enslaved people in America rose from around 700,000 in 1790 to about 3.2 million in 1850, and cotton output from 750,000 bales in 1830 to 2.85 million in 1850. Whitney's patent was not validated until 1807; Hodgen Holmes, Robert Watkins, William Longstreet and John Murray held improvement patents by 1796, and years of suits against planters copying his design left him little profit. P. J. Federico (Technology and Culture, 1960) reconstructed patent papers lost when Whitney's records burned in 1795 and America's Patent Office in 1836.

hwaseong-fortress-geojunggi-1794.summary: From 1794 Korea built Hwaseong Fortress with pulley cranes designed by Jeong Yak-yong, cutting the labour of lifting stone. It housed and honoured remains of King Jeongjo's father Crown Prince Sado and apparently prepared a move of his capital away from court factionalism. Architect Jeong Yak-yong, later a leader of Silhak (practical learning), combined Korean and Chinese fortress designs with contemporary science: brick as building material and efficient pulleys and cranes. Its 5.74-kilometre wall, enclosing town, palace and defences together, took 700,000 person-hours, and workers were paid rather than conscripted.

hwaseong-fortress-geojunggi-1794.detail:
Earlier Korean practice built a simple town wall plus a separate mountain refuge for wartime. Hwaseong, answering collapse of Korea's front line in the Imjin War, united wall, defensive fortress and town centre, with four main gates serving as town gates, secret gates for sorties, and two sluicegates over the Suwoncheon stream. Its wall stands 4 to 6 metres high and originally enclosed 1.3 square kilometres, built higher on flat ground than on its two hills.

Construction cost Korea's treasury 870,000 nyang and 1,500 sacks of rice in wages, where earlier government works had relied on corvée labour, another mark of Silhak influence. Jeongjo moved people to Suwon at state expense with ten years' tax exemption. Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, published in ten volumes in 1801 shortly after his death, documented plans, tools and supervisors, and guided reconstruction from 1970 after severe Korean War damage; UNESCO listed fortress and palace in 1997.

appert-canning-1795.summary: From 1795 Nicolas Appert kept food edible for months by sealing it in jars and boiling them, the start of canning. He packed food into glass jars, sealed them with cork and sealing wax and immersed them in boiling water, succeeding with soups, vegetables, fruit, juices, dairy products, jellies, jams and syrups. Bacteriology did not yet exist, so Appert never understood why heat worked, yet his method was simple enough to spread widely. In 1804 his House of Appert at Massy, near Paris, became the world's first food bottling factory.

appert-canning-1795.detail:
Appert had been arrested in April 1794 during the Terror and escaped execution. His early containers were champagne bottles, imperfectly sealed with cheese and mineral lime, before thick, large-mouthed glass bottles took produce ranging from beef, fowl, eggs and milk to prepared dishes; homemakers probably already used similar techniques, but Appert was first to work at industrial scale, and in later years he switched to an autoclave. Exhibiting bottled fruit and vegetables in 1806 won him no reward.

In 1810 the Interior Ministry's Bureau of Arts and Manufactures paid him 12,000 francs ex gratia on condition he publish; L'Art de conserver les substances animales et végétales appeared that year in 6,000 copies, the first book on modern food preservation. The same year Peter Durand in Britain patented preserving in tin cans, and in 1812 Bryan Donkin and John Hall bought both patents and began producing preserves. Prussian and Austrian forces later destroyed his Massy factory, and he never prospered despite the grant.

condorcet-progress-1795.summary: In 1795 Condorcet, in hiding from the Terror, argued that knowledge would keep growing and human life keep improving without limit. France's Convention had voted his arrest in 1793 for criticising its proposed constitution, and he sheltered in Madame Vernet's Paris house. Caught at Clamart, he was found dead in his cell at Bourg-la-Reine two days later. His widow Sophie de Grouchy published his Sketch in 1795. It narrates civilisation as progress in science, ties that progress to human rights and justice, and foresees rational society shaped entirely by scientific knowledge.

condorcet-progress-1795.detail:
Condorcet had championed free markets, public education, constitutional government, equal rights for women and people of all races, and welfare. Elected as Paris deputy to France's Legislative Assembly in 1791, he became its secretary and belonged to no faction. His earlier mathematics of voting produced his jury theorem, that any group whose members are each more likely right than wrong grows more reliable as it grows, and Condorcet's paradox, that majority preferences among three or more options can cycle.

His death remains unexplained: most accepted is poison supplied by his friend Pierre Jean George Cabanis, though some historians suspect murder. Thomas Malthus wrote An Essay on the Principle of Population in 1798 partly against Condorcet's views on perfectibility of society.

metric-system-1795.summary: In 1795 France defined the metre and the gram by law, decimal units meant for all people and all time; most of the world now uses them. Its metre was one ten-millionth of Earth's distance from North Pole to Equator through Paris; its gramme was pure water filling a cube one hundredth of a metre on each side at melting-ice temperature. Delambre and Méchain were still surveying between Dunkirk and Barcelona, so a provisional metre of 443.44 lignes served meanwhile. Platinum prototypes made in June 1799 entered France's National Archives, and in December 1799 this system became by law France's sole system of weights and measures from 1801.

metric-system-1795.detail:
Earlier proposals, after Huygens's pendulum clock of 1656, had tried pendulum length as natural standard, but gravity varies by place and calibrated clocks differed. Revolutionary France's panel chose Earth's dimensions instead, using Picard's 1670 survey and Cassini's of 1718, and assigned working groups to measure latitude difference and triangulate between Dunkirk and Barcelona, measure baselines, verify seconds-pendulum length at 45 degrees, weigh distilled water in vacuum, and publish conversion tables. Because one gramme was too small for practical use, its thousandfold, named kilogramme, became base unit of mass, alone among SI base units in carrying a prefix. Greek prefixes marked multiples, myria, kilo, hecto and deka, and Latin ones fractions, deci, centi and milli.

Paris's mètre des archives measured 443.296 lignes and its kilogramme des archives 18,827.15 grains of livre poids de marc; both platinum copies served as standards for about 90 years. People kept using old measures. Napoleon's mesures usuelles of 1812 restored customary names as round metric multiples; in 1837 France's new Assembly reimposed its laws of 1795 and 1799, effective 1840. The Treaty of the Metre in 1875 produced international metre and kilogram artefacts and created CGPM, which launched SI in 1960.

picture.alt: Woodcut Usage des Nouvelles Mesures, Paris, 1800, teaching the metric units introduced by the law of 1795.
picture.credit: L. F. Labrousse, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

wootz-steel-1795.summary: In 1795 Pearson analysed wootz, the Indian steel of Damascus blades, and steel chemistry began. Wootz had been made in southern India since the mid-first millennium BC, its banded pattern formed by sheets of microscopic carbides. Traded westward as cakes of steely iron, it became associated with Damascus steel. Smiths heated black magnetite ore with carbon from bamboo and leaves of plants such as avārai in sealed clay crucibles inside charcoal furnaces until slag was gone. High-carbon alloys were little known in Europe, and in 1795 Pearson made the first chemical examination of wootz, publishing in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.

wootz-steel-1795.detail:
Production centres included Golconda in Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. Excavations at Kodumanal near Karur, capital of the Cheras, revealed furnaces and crucibles on a trade route to the west coast through the Palakkad Pass. An alternative route smelted wrought iron first, then heated and hammered out slag. Its name traces to ukku in Kannada and Telugu and urukku in Malayalam.

Samples sent by Helenus Scott reached Sir Joseph Banks, Royal Society president, in 1790 and went to several experts. Research into wootz fed English, French and Russian metallurgy: Faraday measured 0.01 to 0.07 percent aluminium and with Stodart supposed it essential, which T. H. Henry later traced to slag; Royal School of Mines analyses in the 19th century recorded 1.34 percent combined carbon; and Pavel Anosov in Russia reproduced wootz with nearly all its properties by four documented methods. Indian rajas' jewelled daggers at London's Great Exhibition of 1851 and its 1862 successor were prized above all for their steel.

jenner-vaccination-1796.summary: In 1796 Jenner showed that mild cowpox protects against smallpox, killer of one in ten: the first vaccine. He scraped pus from cowpox blisters on milkmaid Sarah Nelmes, infected by a cow named Blossom, and inoculated it through two small cuts in James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son. Phipps had fever and some unease, nothing more. On 1 July Jenner gave him variolous material, routine variolation, and no disease followed; later challenges also failed to infect him.

jenner-vaccination-1796.detail:
Smallpox mortality reached 20 percent in towns and cities, where infection spread more easily. Variolation, deliberate infection with smallpox matter, was then routine protection, and Jenner himself had undergone it as a boy with lifelong effect on his health. Others preceded him: John Fewster realised by 1768 that prior cowpox gave immunity, and at least five investigators in England and Germany between 1770 and 1791, among them Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty in 1774, tested cowpox on humans. Phipps was case 17 in Jenner's first paper, which the Royal Society did not publish; after revisions he published 23 cases, including his 11-month-old son Robert, in his 1798 Inquiry into the Variolae vaccinae known as the Cow Pox, naming cowpox variolae vaccinae, pustules of the cow. Some conclusions were right, some wrong.

Medical opinion deliberated at length before accepting vaccination. Parliament granted him £10,000 in 1802 and £20,000 five years later after the Royal College of Physicians confirmed its efficacy; Spain's Balmis Expedition of 1803 to 1806 carried vaccine to the Americas, the Philippines, Macao and China; Britain banned variolation and offered free vaccination in 1840; and in 1980 the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated, with vaccination an essential component.

lithography-1796.summary: In 1796 Alois Senefelder invented lithography, printing from a flat stone with grease and water. He drew his image in grease, oil or wax on smooth limestone and treated it with gum arabic and weak acid, which made bare stone attract water; dampened and rolled with oily ink, the stone took ink only on the drawing, which then transferred to paper. Early use was mostly musical scores and maps, and flat plates allowed longer, more detailed print runs than intaglio or letterpress.

lithography-1796.detail:
Lithography takes its name from Greek lithos, stone, and graphō, to write. Nitric acid in the gum solution forms a hydrophilic calcium nitrate layer on unprotected stone, while durability of the drawing depends on the lipid content of its medium. Technical problems slowed adoption; Specimens of Polyautography in 1803 gathered experimental works by British artists including Benjamin West and Henry Fuseli, in the 1820s Delacroix and Géricault took it up, and Goya produced his last prints in Bordeaux.

Godefroy Engelmann's chromolithography of 1837 used a separate stone for each colour, every pass needing careful register, and suited flat colour areas of period posters. Lithography largely replaced engraving for English commercial maps after about 1852, having printed British army maps during the Peninsular War. Offset lithography, which transfers ink through a rubber cylinder, keeps paper dry and runs at high speed; since the 1960s most books and magazines, especially colour-illustrated ones, have been printed this way.

macarthur-merino-wool-1797.summary: In 1797 ships Reliance and Supply brought a few Spanish merino sheep from Cape Colony to Sydney, bought by Henry Waterhouse and William Kent. John and Elizabeth Macarthur, Samuel Marsden and others crossed these with Bengal and Cape fat-tailed sheep and selected for fine fleece. Macarthur shipped wool samples to London in 1807 and secured land grants at Camden; by 1820s New South Wales exported more than 100,000 kilograms of wool yearly, and by 1850 Australian wool dominated British imports. Garran and White's 1985 study shows this was a collective effort of many breeders, with Elizabeth Macarthur managing flocks during John's long absences, rather than one man's foresight.

macarthur-merino-wool-1797.verification_note: Date of merino arrival is secure; credit is disputed, with Garran and White rejecting Macarthur-as-founder narrative repeated in Nature (1934) and popular histories.
macarthur-merino-wool-1797.detail: A 1934 Nature note repeated Macarthur's claim as founder of Australian wool industry. Garran and White, using flock records and letters, argue that Macarthur promoted his own legend, that Marsden and Waterhouse were equally early, and that pastoral expansion onto Aboriginal lands after 1820 mattered more than any single flock. Wool suited a colony far from markets: high value, non-perishable and easily shipped. Pastoral frontier drove dispossession and frontier violence across southeastern Australia.
